Against Newton, who had declared the production of colourless images by the combination of two or more refracting media impossible, Euler appealed to the human eye, which possesses such an achromatic combination; and the achromatic lenses were in fact then invented.

(1) Eth. IV. Preface p. 201.

(2) See "Ueber Spinoza's Grundgedanken und dessen Erfolg" in the author's historische Beiträge zur Philosophie. vol. 2. Vermischte Abhandlungen. 1855. p. 35 ff. p. 53 ff.

Is it then possible to set the end aside if one [p. 44] transforms it, as Spinoza does, into a mirror-image of desire? Representing, on this opinion, proceeds from the necessity of the efficient cause. Through representing there arises a desire, an impulse, and the desire clothes itself in the semblance of the end. If we go into this more closely, the end lies in the background of the impulse. The impulse is, as it were, the longing of the unfulfilled end. The desire for nourishment rests on the destination for nourishment and on a whole structure of concepts of end realised in the organism. The impulse of the eye towards light, the desire of the soul for knowledge, designates the indwelling end. Hence such an explanation does not suffice. Spinoza dissolves the end into an insubstantial echo of the efficient cause only because it threatens to break through necessity.

(1) Cf. Spinoza's correspondence with Oldenburg Epist. 3 ff.

(2) Euler in the Denkschriften der preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. 1747.

It is, finally, vain to argue against the end from the concept of God, as Spinoza does. If God posits the ends and himself sets the goal, he is in this neither dependent on something external, as on a fate, nor does he lack anything, since he has everything from himself.

The ill-treatment of the end, the noblest of all concepts of nature, avenges itself in Spinoza in its consequences. The rigid representation of whole and part, not the more spiritual one of life and members, runs through his thoughts. For him all error, all evil, arises in that we think and act in so far as we are determined only as parts. Multiplicity, which springs up with the parts, is for him therefore the mother of evil, and everything strives back into the *one* substance, whereas conversely, where the good is placed in the end, the good exists only through multiplicity. The ethical, which consists in free devotion to the higher end, must in Spinoza be transformed into the deed of the efficient cause, whereby everything maintains its essence and seeks what is useful to it. The [p. 45] sharpness of evil is blunted, in that it is placed only in negation, which coincides with the essence of the determinate and individual. The right of each thing is equated with its power. According to nature each thing has as much right as it has power to be and to be active.¹ And this too is consistent. For power is nothing but the efficient causes, in so far as they are compressed into one point and tensed within themselves. Only with the recognition of the divine end does the grounding of right raise itself above the flat and barren representation of physical power. When, finally, Spinoza sketches the natural history of the passive states of the soul from the fundamental thought that the mind strives to maintain itself in its being and is conscious of this striving: here too the physical cause alone is supposed to work towards the equilibrium of self-preservation. And yet here, in the whole that is to preserve itself, as in the essence of the whole generally, the end comes plainly to light. The end underlies the affect.

(1) Eth. VI. 24. p. 219. ed. Paul.

The annihilation of the end, the sole dominion of the efficient cause, is accordingly the most significant characteristic of the Spinozist system, and could far rather be called its atheism than the dreaded proposition that God is the immanent cause of things. The intellectual love of God, which, following from necessary and eternal knowledge, is the pious enthusiasm of this view of the world, has a finer name than content. Certainly at the right moments our knowledge so exults that the love of God is the consummation of its joy. But where does it do so? Only there, we think, where in the small as in the great the harmony is revealed to the mind which is the beautiful appearance of ends full of thought. Spinoza does not know this, and without [p. 46] it the delight of knowledge is only joy in one's own power or cunning, which knows how to become master, at least in spirit, of the stern force of the efficient cause. There remains only the cold recognition of a necessity without life and love.

(1) Tract. polit. c. 2. p. 307. ed. Paul.

(2) In the third book of the Ethics.

Spinoza's harsh severities are an indirect proof of the significance of the end in our view of the world.

5. Since we accordingly recognise the fact of the end and its determinations, we turn to its derivation.

Kant, who in his *Kritik der Urtheilskraft* investigated the nature of the end more deeply, must be heard first on this question.

Kant begins with the distinction of the determining and the reflecting power of judgment.¹ Whereas the determining power of judgment subsumes the particular under a given universal, the reflecting power seeks the universal for a given particular; whereas the former proceeds like the judge to whom the law is prescribed, the latter, like the legislator, draws up the rule from the cases.

Since the reflecting power of judgment is to ascend from the particular to the universal, it needs a principle which it cannot draw from experience, precisely because this principle has to ground the unity of all empirical principles and the possibility of their systematic subordination. It takes it from its own understanding and considers the empirical laws according to such a unity, as if an understanding likewise, though not ours, had given them for the benefit of our faculties of knowledge, in order to make possible a system of experience according to particular laws of nature. Thus there results the end, through which nature is so represented [p. 47] as if an understanding contained the ground of the unity of its manifoldness. For the end is the concept of an object in so far as the concept at the same time carries within itself the ground of the actuality of the object. The end is therefore only borrowed from us, nothing but an analogy, nothing but a guiding thread for extending natural science according to a new principle. As we cannot at all see a priori the possibility of such a causality of nature according to ends, so we cannot properly observe the ends in nature as intentional either. Accordingly the purposiveness of nature will be only a subjective principle of reason, in that it works regulatively for the human power of judgment, but does not constitutively determine anything about the nature of objects.² As in the practical sphere the point of view of a maxim gives direction and consistency to the motley play of human actions, without a law of the matter itself needing thereby to have been attained: so the concept of end, through which sensible phenomena receive a spiritual order, is such a maxim for the reflecting power of judgment, as it were a human attempt to become master, in its own way, of the infinitely manifold things. 2

(1) Cf. Kritik der Urtheilskraft. Introduction p. XXIII. ff., 1st ed. 1790, cf. p. 329. Kant's Werke in Rosenkranz's edition IV. p. 17 ff., cf. p. 287.

Thus Kant regards this whole principle. What he gives with one hand in the investigation of the far-reaching end, he takes from us with the other, in that he lets the end appear only like a gleam of light which we ourselves cast upon things, without its being the stimulating, enlivening light through which things come to be and grow.

Kant cannot do otherwise. The closed consistency of his whole view demands it so. Were the end something in things, were the understanding accordingly the architect of the [p. 48] world: then with the end known the thing in itself would be known, and this so carefully veiled image of the gods would be unveiled. If Kant makes space and time into forms of human intuition, the categories into root concepts of the human understanding, the unity of things asserted in judgment into a consequence of the unity of human self-consciousness, the idea of the unconditioned into a mere spur and goad of human knowing, so that it chases after a phantom that recedes ever further into the distance: then Kant must in a similar way degrade the concept of purposiveness into a human maxim. So the knowing human being wanders about, cut off on all sides from things, yet in lawful accord with himself. But is it then to be enough if a clock merely keeps regular time with itself, regardless of whether it goes by the sun, the great clock of the world?

(1) Cf. Kr. d. U. p. 291. p. 332. Kant's Werke IV. p. 259. p. 289.

(2) Kr. d. U. p. 335 ff. Kant's Werke IV. p. 291 ff.

We therefore examine the grounds and the inner coherence of the view.

Just as, according to Kant, space and time are supposedly unable to be empirical because they condition the possibility of thinking particular spaces and times, and hence condition the whole of experience: so the principle of purposiveness is supposed to be transcendental and not to stem from experience, because it is destined "to ground the unity of all empirical principles under likewise empirical but higher principles, and thus the possibility of their systematic subordination to one another." These proofs run parallel; and hence the same leap is to be recognised here that was pointed out above in the view of space and time. If space and time are subjective forms, or if the representation of space and time is generated by our own act [p. 49] in order to apprehend the objects of experience: it by no means follows from this that space and time have nothing to do with things. Rather the fundamental forms will overlap in such a way that the representation of them is produced by the mind just as they themselves are produced by things. The subjective and the objective express only relations, and therefore the realm of all possibility cannot be so split that what is subjective is not objective, and what is objective is not subjective. We find the same mistake again in the view of the end. Granted that this principle grounds experience and therefore, born in advance from the mind, does not first come into us from experience: this does not prove that the end has no actuality in nature. Its subjective origin testifies not at all against its objective significance.

(1) Kr. d. U. Introd. p. XXV. Kant's Werke IV. p. 18.

(2) Above vol. I. p. 164.

But that things of nature, Kant continues, ¹ serve one another as means to ends, and that their very possibility is sufficiently intelligible only through this kind of causality—for such an assumption we have no ground whatever in the universal idea of nature as the sum total of the objects of the senses, and with this mode of explanation we lose ourselves in the transcendent. Certainly, if Kant strictly restricts nature to the "sum total of the objects of the senses" and thereby tears it away from thought: then the efficacy of the end cannot be seen from such a concept, delimited in advance; but neither can it be refuted from it, since the presupposition is only arbitrarily formed. What is supposed to lie of the transcendent in such a mode of explaining nature thus only soars beyond the narrow bounds within which nature, as though it were nothing but the flat fact of the senses, has been unlawfully enclosed.

(1) Kr. d. U. p. 263. Kant's Werke IV. p. 239.

(2) Kr. d. U. p. 351. Kant's Werke IV. p. 303.

[p. 50] What worth, then, would such a merely regulating, but nothing establishing, concept of the end have? The point of view of the end would have solely the function of bringing order into the confused mass of inflowing representations, a clever order, bound as strictly in unity as a feudal constitution; but it is only our order, not the order of the world, it is only the makeshift of our understanding, not the law of things. We connect representations according to the rule of the end without seeing that the things, whose deputies the representations are, grip one another in the same connection. In this merely subjective significance the thought of the rule falls away from itself. If a rule, as e.g. in geometrical constructions, in arithmetical calculations, in grammatical relations, is destined to form a thing according to it (a figure, a number, a sentence): then the rule plainly touches the origin, and thus the innermost nature, of the thing. What guided the understanding in the universal rule presents itself in the thing as a determinate and individual phenomenon. The end that is "regulative, though not constitutive" falls short of this simple efficacy of a rule. But there are rules, one may say, which, like rules of gender, bring together according to mere appearance even what by the origin of the thing would scarcely belong together, merely in order to come to the aid of memory with a short formula for extensive particulars. Is the rule of the end to mean no more than this? Does one wish to degrade it so low, merely in order to withdraw it from things? And even if one were to bring oneself to that, that external rule of appearance would still stand at a higher level, because it does not let itself be deprived of saying something about things. If the end is to form only a rule in knowing, without at the same time being the rule of the thing: then instead of a necessary concatenation of things it yields only a contingent connection made by the mind.

[p. 51] What does it actually mean, then, when Kant asserts that the concept of combinations and forms of nature according to ends is at least *one* principle more for bringing its phenomena under rules where the laws of causality according to its mere mechanism do not suffice? What worth has it when "entirely new prospects" are promised us from it? This one principle more, these new prospects, are truly a wealth of a peculiar kind. Otherwise a principle is supposed to simplify knowledge; in this case it brings only complication, in that it attempts an interpretation of phenomena which directly contradicts the acknowledged principle of the efficient cause. It brings discord instead of unity. And if the contradiction is not meant so seriously, because the principle is after all only a subjective connection: then the whole principle is not much better than that of an alphabetical arrangement or of some other synoptic sequence. It is then only the principle of a registry, so that the mind may find its way about in the voluminous files of the world. The human mind, which directs itself by this rule of the end given in advance, becomes virtually an index of things according to a scheme sketched in advance. It is then no principle of fathoming, which is nonetheless what the cause of the end gives itself out to be, but only a principle of convenient survey.

In declaring the end a regulative but not constitutive concept, Kant places it beside the idea of the unconditioned, which according to his doctrine works in the same way.² Has the a priori rule, which modestly renounces the law of the thing, the same sense in both cases? If within the efficient cause the idea of the unconditioned spurs the mind not to rest in the limited and individual, but to advance from the part it has grasped to the conditions: [p. 52] then this motion remains within the same circle of the view. The idea declared regulative works in fact only subjectively, in that it nowhere grants rest to the sluggish understanding and enlivens the activity of investigation. But with the regulative concept of the end it is otherwise. This does not drive onward along the path already taken of the explanation attempted from the nearest efficient cause, but suddenly turns the whole consideration around and compels the understanding, which wants to comprehend things from things, to fall out of its role, as it were. This transformation has a right to be called a rule only if it leads into the truth. But if the end is nothing in things, then it projects things askew into our mind; and the end is not an enlivening rule of inquiry but a falsifying distortion of the view. Hence Kant errs when he writes: "if only we abide by this presupposition as a merely regulative principle, even error cannot harm us." The assumption that the end is regulative but not constitutive is in contradiction with itself, since it can only be an actual rule if at the same time it posits the truth of its mode of consideration.

(1) Kr. d. U. p. 265. Kant's Werke IV. p. 240.

(2) Kr. d. r. V. p. 536 ff. Kant's Werke II. p. 400 ff. Kr. d. r. V. p. 715. Kant's Werke II. p. 532 ff.

How, further, does the end, declared to be a subjective mode of connection, stand in relation to the other subjective elements of the Kantian philosophy? If the end were a necessary form of our knowledge in the sense in which space and time are the form of intuition and synthetic unity the form of judgment: then the end, like these, would have to appear everywhere and without exception as the necessary stamp of grounding. Without choice the end would always be there wherever we seek the cause of phenomena, as space is always there where we intuit outwardly, and time where we observe inwardly, and unity where we connect two concepts in judgment. Just as, according to Kant, [p. 53] all these forms prove their subjective and a priori nature by the fact that we cannot unchain ourselves from them in our mental activities: so the end too would have to carry this thoroughgoing necessity within itself. In vain do we look about for such a mark. The end is rather first called to aid where the explanation by the efficient cause breaks off. When the object itself compels the inquiring understanding to give up the path it has taken, then the possibility of the end offers itself, as a supplement, so to speak. Where, therefore, the subjective rule of the end is to be applied is decided by the essence of the thing, and the rule therefore cannot close itself off within the narrow circle of a merely subjective mode of consideration, and determines itself from the object. Thus Kant's view leads beyond itself.

(2) Cf. Herbart's Einleitung §. 132. p. 243 f. (according to the 3rd ed.).

It happens to Kant once more within the same domain that the concepts spill over the carefully staked-out boundaries. So it happens in the investigation of the beautiful. Since the beautiful arouses satisfaction through the concord of the faculties of knowledge, since it awakens a harmonious play of the powers of representation, since it brings, e.g., the directions of imagination into accord among themselves or formative intuition into accord with the understanding: it is supposed, according to Kant, to carry within itself the form of purposiveness without the representation of an end. In so far as the cognitive powers are harmoniously moved, the object is there, as it were, for them and falls under the form of purposiveness; but the end, which as concept is the producing ground of the object, is nonetheless lacking. Beauty is not the cause of the possibility of the thing.

Here too Kant labours in vain to separate the concepts by strict boundary lines of the faculties. The concepts do not lie spatially beside one another, but work into [p. 54] one another. When Kant distinguishes free beauty, in which the imagination plays, as it were, with itself, e.g. the splendour of colour in the blossom, from beauty bound by the concept, in which the imagination enters into agreement with the understanding: then in the latter the teleological power of judgment intervenes determiningly in the aesthetic. Beauty of this kind is, as it were, the concept appearing; and in the concept a mode of appearance lies preformed and intimated for the designing imagination. The beauty of the male body, e.g., is measured against the concept of male strength and dignity, against the idea of man, as it were. Formal purposiveness, as according to Kant it comes forward in the concept of the beautiful, tacitly takes its determining ground from real purposiveness.

(1) Cf. Kr. d. U. p. 352. Kant's Werke IV. p. 303 f.

Thus the end cannot be restricted to a merely subjective and regulative form of judging, and everything depends on the concept being the indwelling, shaping soul of things, and the soul, as Plato puts it, being earlier than the body.

The deed corresponds to our representation. We act upon things according to the purposiveness we have apprehended, and things answer in accordance with this action. We thus apply constitutively the concept of end, which was supposed to be only regulative (e.g. in healing, in the training of the body, in education), and the nature of things suffers, demands and confirms this procedure.

In this way we are compelled to relinquish the Kantian view of the end.

6. In Hegel's derivation of the end the following moments come into consideration.

The concept has developed itself into the syllogism. The syllogism is mediation. Through its motion this mediation is sublated. Nothing is now in and for itself, each thing only by means of another. The individual is a universal, and indeed because it has particularity in it at the same time; the [p. 55] universal is truly universal only through its realisation in the individual, and particularity is the unity of both. The result is therefore an immediacy that has issued from the sublation of mediation. As the moments interpenetrate, being issues forth as a thing that is in and for itself, that is sufficient to itself: objectivity.¹

Objectivity is at first only immediate, as every concept must first free itself from immediacy. The moments still subsist in independent indifference as objects outside one another. Their unity is still only an external one. So it is in the sphere of mechanism.

The objects appear in this external pressure and impact as non-independent, but within a greater independence; for objectivity as a whole relates itself negatively to itself and thereby generates the relation of non-independence in the individual objects. Hence arises the concept of centrality, in which the object itself is related to what is external.²

The non-independence of the object reveals itself in the striving towards the centre. Since this striving is a striving towards the determinately opposed object, the centre itself thereby falls apart, and its negative unity passes over into objectified opposition. Centrality is therefore the relation of these objectivities, negative and tensed against one another. Thus chemism results, in that the object is posited in its existence as differentiated against its other.³

In chemism there is an inner totality of both determinatenesses, and there therefore appears the impulse to sublate the opposed [p. 56] one-sided subsistence of the object and to make itself into the real whole in existence. From the difference of the opposites there arises a neutral product, and the neutral is again kindled into differentiation.

(1) Logik III. p. 169 ff.

(2) Cf. Encyklopaedie §. 195 ff.

(3) Logik III. p. 200. 209 ff.

These processes are external, and they appear as independent of one another. As they pass over into products, their finitude shows itself, just as, conversely, the process exhibits the presupposed immediacy of the differentiated objects as a null one. Thus the externality and immediacy in which the concept of the object was sunk are negated. Through this negation it becomes free and is posited for itself over against that externality and immediacy. This objective free concept is the end.¹

The end is now in itself directed towards the determinateness of externality, and its simple unity is the unity that repels itself from itself and preserves itself therein, a cause which is cause of itself, or whose effect is immediately the cause.² By making itself into the other of its subjectivity and so objectifying itself, it sublates the difference of the subjective and the objective and closes together only with itself.

But the end is at first only finite and external, because the content of the end is called forth by the given object and the material for its realisation must be sought in the world as it is found. The end is thereby as contingent as the object is a particular one.

The execution is assured in the means, which is subject to the concept. For the concept is this immediate power, because it is self-identical negativity, in which the [p. 57] being of the object is determined throughout only as an ideal one.¹ For since the concept is the truth of substance, and substance repels itself from itself and remains with itself in the things that thereby arise: this power of substance is also the power of the concept, and therefore for the end, the concept that has become free, the means are present without qualification.

(1) Logik III. p. 217 ff.

(2) Cf. Kant's determinations and above vol. II. p. 21 ff.

Thus the objective is made conformable to the end as the free concept. But as soon as the end is attained, the one-sidedness of the finite shows itself. Nothing has been brought about but a form posited externally on the material. The attained end is therefore only an object which is in turn means or material for other ends, and so on to infinity. What was just now end is now again means; and these concepts relieve one another. The end is thus the same as what the means is; and the concept of the end as such has not yet attained any true objectivity. This progress to infinity, this relativity of the executed end, this emerging identity of end and means points to a new stage—the idea; it is the absolute unity of the concept and of objectivity, reason, which is the eternal intuiting of itself in the other, the concept which in its objectivity has carried itself out, the object which is inner purposiveness, essential subjectivity.

At these stages objectivity ascends from the pressure and impact of mechanism to the full victory of the end that pervades the world.

For the assessment of this course we single out the following points. What matters here is the rigour of the derivation and not the semblance of the result.

That transition from the disjunctive syllogism into [p. 58] objectivity, from the syllogism unfolded through all its moments into the essence that is self-sufficient through reciprocal development, may be left to rest on itself, although on closer consideration it would show itself to be untenable; for nothing in it drives outward, as objectivity demands. But we need a conceded presupposition, so that we are not compelled to unravel the threads of the fabric ever further backwards.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 207-209.

(2) Cf. Encyklopaedie §. 158.

Chemism is derived from the centrality of mechanism. The objects are determined against one another, and as the centre falls apart, they relate themselves to one another in reciprocal excitation. Can such a transition from the solar system, in which centrality reaches its apex, into the combinations of acids and bases, from astronomy into chemistry, be so much as divined anywhere in nature? The dialectic attempts its connections on its own account and therefore does not reach the course of coming-to-be. The thing does not come to be in this way; but perhaps the thought of the thing does, which logic undertakes to present in its eternity. That may be, although it is not to be seen why the development of the thing and the development of the thought should here fall apart in such a manner that the connection is nowhere to be seen. Mechanism and chemism have at least this in common, that in both the efficient cause reveals itself. Combination and separation occur upon external excitation. The substances seize one another and let one another go, seek one another and flee one another. The forces of things play with one another. Or are we to take it thus, that the substances, determined for one another, together realise their concept, and to see a proof of this in the definite numbers of the proportions of combination? This difference of conception is easily illustrated by a single example. We take the example from Goethe's *Wahlverwandtschaften*. If one puts a piece of lime into dilute sulphuric acid, the acid seizes the lime [p. 59] and appears with it as gypsum. The proportion of combination is definite. 100 parts of sulphuric acid combine with 71 parts of lime to form gypsum. In this process, it seems, exciting forces are active, properties of the substances which meet one another and bring about compositions or separations. Then the concept nowhere appears here as though it hovered freely above the process, as though it went before it determining it. It is the process of the efficient cause, and the concept only follows it and is only drawn out of it. Such is the view if one lets the experience of chemism have its way by itself. Conversely, one would present it thus. Lime and sulphuric acid are each one-sided by themselves; they are meant to combine into gypsum as into a higher formation. The proportion of combination vouches that the concept, measuring both substances against each other, preceded the process. Then the governing end shows itself already in chemism. Gypsum is to come to be; lime and sulphuric acid are determined for this; the separate parts (lime and sulphuric acid) are to be comprehended from the thought of the whole (the gypsum). Were one to take chemism thus, it would already be teleological, and the end would then have to spring forth in the transition from mechanism to chemism. Since this does not happen, it cannot be Hegel's view; nor is it otherwise the view of science.

From what moments, then, does the efficient cause of chemism give birth to the end? The stage of chemism negates itself in that the processes pass over into products and the products into processes, and this alternation runs on into infinity. Through this negation the concept sunk in the object becomes free for itself. But of what kind is the negation? The chemical factors (to take it more generally and not to stop at the substances of the properly chemical sphere) do indeed show their lack of independence in being thrown into a necessary process. This lack of independence is [p. 60] however only a lack of power, only a dependence on another efficient cause. It is therefore a negation within this domain; the one force is limited and conditioned by the other. If we cancel this negation, the thought of the end by no means appears thereby. Since the negation of the chemical process takes place by physical means, we remain only within the efficient cause. Chemism is blind, like mechanism. How does the foreseeing end come out of it? How does the external play of combinations turn over into thought? It is nowhere shown how the concept sunk in the object is driven forth out of it, and indeed in such a way that it now is for itself and before the object, and determines its future. This reversal of the relation is nowhere grounded here, and yet the end is determined as the cause whose effect is cause! Perhaps what is missed here is placed in the infinite progress of chemism. To be sure it runs on; to be sure one can interpret it as itself, without a hold, seeking a hold. But what hold? Nowhere in it is the end, this transformation of the scene, nowhere in it is the thought that is free for itself so much as intimated. What is specific to the end has here no premises.

Something essential is further added in the progression. From chemism, which is indeed taken in the wider sense altogether, the dialectic does not proceed immediately to the organism, as nature, say, translates the chemical processes in the lungs and in the stomach into organic ones. The intermediate link for the dialectic is teleology, the external end, which realises itself in an external material found already at hand. The life of nature has the end more inwardly within itself. The external end appears only in the free choice of man, and as it were only as the freest blossom that the inwardly purposive, organic life is able to bear. According to the course of development which we observe, [p. 61] this external end, often a contingency of thought, is later than the internal one, in which freedom and necessity go together. Let us grasp the difficulty as it really is, without volatilising it into generality. How in all the world is the external, that is, the human end to form itself out of the negation of chemism? What a chasm lies between!

And now the means of the external end. Whence is the power put into its hand, if now the subjective concept, drawn out of the object, having become free for itself, stands over against the object? "The concept is this immediate power, because it is the negativity identical with itself, in which the being of the object is determined throughout only as an ideal one." The concept has inherited the power of substance; since the objects are selfless over against substance and substance governs in them, the being of the object vanishes before the concept without resistance. Hence the end triumphs over things, so that they become its means. This seems consistent. But one thing has been overlooked, and indeed the most important. That concept which in this sense is called the negativity identical with itself, like substance itself, is the infinite concept. Against this, according to the course of the system, the being of the object can offer no resistance of any kind. But the end that is being spoken of is finite and external; and precisely in this limitation it must have forfeited that power. Hence the manner in which the possibility of realisation is ascribed to the finite end is only a semblance.

Can the derivation then perhaps demonstrate how the infinite end (the idea) could realise itself? This development would have greater significance than that one; and though the right thing would not then have been accomplished in the right place, what is most essential would have been given in advance. To test this hope we must go back to the source of the plenitude of power which the concept has received. Everything [p. 62] depends on how the concept has become the truth of substance.

We consider this point in its naked simplicity.¹ Substance is not active against something, but only against itself as a simple element without resistance. In repelling itself into the accidents, it is causal. The substances arising thereby react against the first substance and act and react among themselves. In this reciprocal action the one is what the other is, cause and effect; they are identical. This pure alternation with itself is necessity unveiled. As substance runs its course through causality and reciprocal action, it becomes evident that independence is the infinite negative relation to itself, so that what is as independent and actual is only as the identity of substance. Through this reciprocal motion, which remains with itself, the truth of necessity is freedom and the truth of substance is the concept. In that substance remains with itself in the accidents, it is not blind but is the concept.

Substance passes over into substances and therefore finds itself again in them. In reciprocal action the one and the other are cause, the one and the other effect. The one is what the other is. Substance therefore remains identical with itself. This remaining-with-itself is the concept.

This derivation is merely formal; the content is set entirely aside. What the substances are, what the reciprocal actions produce, has no influence. This is the consolation of substance, that what comes out has again the form of substance and is just as much effect as cause; the one is what the other is. This formal, wholly external equalisation of reflection is the guarantee that substance [p. 63] remains with itself; and from this stem freedom and the concept. But if the substances rebelled, if reciprocal action broke out into a war, that relation of like form, that grounding of identity with itself, would always be the same. Substance could even then still be content with itself; for even then substances would still arise in causality; even then, in action and counteraction, the one would be what the other is; both passive and active. But what a thin concept of being-with-itself, what a powerless freedom, what a contentless concept!

(1) Logik II. p. 221. cf. Encyklopaedie §. 150 ff.

(2) Cf. above vol. I. p. 62ff.

From this formal identity and from no other are freedom and the concept derived; for the sake of this identity the concept, like substance, is "the negativity identical with itself." The premises give nothing further. But from such a formal identity no power stems. In it the concept has, as it were, only the role of looking on, as substance, in the production of causality and in the action and reaction of reciprocal action, finds identical relations (forms of existence) again. Yet in the end there is need of the concept that predetermines and governs the content of existence. In that identity which has been demonstrated, the concept is neither conscious nor certain of the thing.

Thus the concept as this "immediate power," against which the being of the object has no power, dissolves away when one leads the concept back to where it came from in the system.

The treatment of the end has received a far-dazzling logical semblance from the fact that the end is traced back to the determinations of the syllogism. Subjectivity concludes itself together with objectivity in the terminus medius of the means. This side will be discussed further below in the doctrine of the syllogism.

[p. 64] Finally, the manner in which the finite end raises itself to the infinite end of the idea still demands a particular consideration. The end attained becomes means to another. The concepts of end and means become identical; the one is what the other is; and in this identity they exchange with one another into infinity. Hence the truth of the finite end is the idea, the absolute unity of the subjective and the objective. Two moments are active here: first that identity, in that the end attained offers itself as the material of another, so that the difference of end and means vanishes; for what was just now end now becomes means; then the course into infinity. That identity is no real one, only a logical one of reflection, not a pregnant one, as for example a seed, but a dull and flat one, like an external comparison. It says nothing at all; for in one relation something is end, in another means. End and means can become really identical only in the absolute whole. This concept is neither produced nor conditioned by that one. The progress into infinity, too, means little. For nowhere is there a direct compulsion to bend this advancing series of ends round into a circle, which is what would first matter. The alleged identity of end and means drives toward this just as little as the identity of the something and the other in their mutual relation drives from the so-called bad infinity to the positive infinity that returns into itself.¹

Thus Hegel's derivation is at no point sufficient to develop the inner possibility of the concept of end and to ground the necessity of its dominion.

7. For those who declare the end to be merely subjective, a mere category of human thinking, there is, in face of the evident facts of the organic and the ethical, which compel us to comprehend them under the [p. 65] end, only *one* way out. They must show that what appears to us as purposive stems in itself from the blindly efficient cause.

(1) Cf. above, the dialectical method, vol. I. p. 57 ff.

The oldest attempt has been preserved for us by Aristotle¹ in some hints taken from Empedocles. If we bring it from its fragmentary presentation into a whole, it appears, with some inserted thoughts which we do not strictly pass off as Empedoclean, roughly as follows.

In the strife of love and hate, of the combining and separating forces, elements and shapes meet. If they come together in such a way that, combined, they cannot maintain themselves, the formations perish in the moment in which they arose, as when, for example, a piece of a bull collided with a human face. But the elements and shapes which, meeting one another, so agree and so fit together that they can maintain themselves, remain; they have indeed come to be without an end, but once they have come to be they hold their ground, and in self-preservation they exhibit end and purposive activity. Because we men, we may add by way of supplement, know only of such formations as can maintain themselves—for the ill-fitting ones, which perished in arising, we do not know at all—we regard harmonious activity according to an internal end. The atomists, who explained the living and the lifeless from the shape, position and order of the atoms, must have proceeded similarly with the blind motion that brings the atoms together.

What Aristotle objects against this view, in emphasising that the phenomena of nature are constant and always occur, but that the coincidence of chance can yield nothing lasting, does not suffice, because [p. 66] the constant is provided for by the fact that only such formations remain as can maintain themselves, while all others have perished and do perish. To be sure, it will become harder and harder to attain the lasting through chance if that capacity for self-preservation, invented by chance, must extend so far as to explain the preservation of the kind as well, and thus, for example, propagation. Yet whoever once does not shrink from assuming that thousands upon thousands of formations perish before *one* remains (experience nowhere finds their remains and traces) has, in the hypothesis, gained the abiding and the lasting.

(1) Phys. II. 4. p. 196a 20. II. 8. p. 198 b 29.

Where chance, incalculable in the individual case, plays into causality, the human understanding calculates in general, as in dice or in card games, the probability that this or that combination will occur, and even expresses it in numerical ratios. With the growing number of elements which can unite, and unite each time in a different order, with the greater and yet bound composition that must be attained, with the more precise result that is in question, the probability of turning the end of nature into a play of nature sinks in a scarcely measurable, scarcely expressible ratio. Even the ancients, who did not know the rapidly and mightily rising ratios of the calculus of permutations and combinations, indicate what is right in a happy image. It is not probable, they say, that letters of all kinds thrown together and poured out, mingling as chance would have it, should compose a poem, so that in this way sense would come from the senseless. Perhaps it is still more difficult to assume that from the blind coincidence of chemical and [p. 67] physical elements and forces any organ of the body, for example the bright, sharp, comprehensive eye, or even the concordant sum of the organs, the body as a whole, could spring, than that from letters blown together a book in which one might read thoughts should arise, as if by a chance that cancelled itself and turned into its very opposite. This path of haphazard gives us no hope of insight into how the seeing could arise from the blind, the precision of the organic, the persistence of what agrees, the satisfaction of life, and even self-conscious thought from the motley, confused jumble. The infinitely growing improbability is equivalent to impossibility.

(1) Hoc qui existimat fieri potuisse (that from the chance collision of atoms an ordered world should come to be), non intelligo, cur non idem putet, si innumerabiles unius et viginti formae litterarum vel aureae vel qualeslibet aliquo coniiciantur, posse ex his in terram excussis annales Ennii, ut deinceps legi possint, effici. Cicero de natura Deorum II. 37.

8. Against this tendency, which explains the end from chance, Aristotle already, especially in the second book of the Physics, attempted to demonstrate the end as an original principle. He does not, indeed, succeed in everything he undertakes to prove. But just as he profoundly recognises the end in the facts of organic nature and clearly turns it outward, for example in the treatise on the parts of animals, so he has also successfully employed his acumen for the metaphysical grounding. He does not succeed, after the definition of chance which he aptly gives,¹ in demonstrating the end really as what is prior and presupposed by chance. For in his consideration the possibility remains open, which he does not investigate, that the concept of end, prior to chance, which we measure by the end, is prior only in us and dwells only in the judgment of man at all. What is lacking in him is the investigation whether the [p. 68] end holds universally or how restrictedly it holds, and yet this investigation was necessary, since he acknowledges the efficient cause and, in the mathematical in particular, lets it act alone. His consideration of the end in nature after the analogy of art remains in the first instance an analogy. But it has a deeper point of support. Human art evidently works for ends, but its ends are not self-devised; it only continues the ends in nature, in that it strives to supplement and complete what remained defective. This inference back from the ends of art to the ends of nature has an illuminating clarity. But concerning the origin of the end, whether it is to be comprehended in the Empedoclean manner from chance or in the Aristotelian from understanding, he determines nothing. In this respect it is important to supplement this consideration by the preceding one.

(1) Phys. II. 5. 6. p 196b 10 ff.

(2) Phys. II. 6. end p. 198 a 5.

9. In grounding the concept of end we distinguish the logical and the metaphysical side of the task. It is incumbent on us first to investigate how we know. If in doing so we must reach over into the nature of being in so far as the question is how thinking and being are mediated and how being in its actual nature is appropriated by thinking, then in the certainty that the end is there already lies a metaphysical knowledge, which would complete itself if it could be shown how the end comes to be in being.

We continue first with the former.

The position of motion and that of the end are essentially different. Motion, the original act of mind, was in general intelligible by itself; the end is not. It presupposes something to which it relates; at the least the shaping motion, as in mathematical problems, or the material world, which it animates with mind. Just as [p. 69] the end in its execution is surrendered to external being, so it already arises in relation to that being and is therefore to be comprehended only in the midst of experience. In treating of the end, therefore, we have leapt over the whole physical world, which we receive as something given by virtue of the original motion, and we require these empirical elements as a condition.

(1) Phys. II. 8. middle p. 199 a 15, cf. polit. VII. 17. p. 1337 a 1.

If we set thinking and being over against each other, then, presupposing the possibility of mediation, there results a twofold relation of cause. Either being acts on thinking, the thing on the concept, or thinking acts on being, the concept on the thing.

We deliberately keep in view only the reciprocal relation of cause from thinking to being. Since we have shown a living intermediate link in motion, we are thereby entitled to speak of such an overreaching activity at all.

The causality which keeps itself merely within the one or the other circle, in being or in thinking, we designate as the efficient cause. In thinking too? It may seem strange to extend the efficient cause to this domain of freedom. And yet it must be done, provided that the added condition is taken strictly. Where thought copies external things, it has received an excitation from the opposite circle and appropriated what is foreign. In such a case the physical nature of thinking cooperates, but already it no longer acts within itself and oversteps its sphere. But when thinking at first follows the projecting motion, or demands an accompanying image for the concept, or, as in the so-called association of ideas, determines the course of representations according to the sequence of time or the point of view of similarity, or, in the play of wit, lets the free reciprocal excitation of representations have its way, representations which there repel or attract one another as in chemical elective affinity: then we have [p. 70] before us, as it were, the physiological nature of thinking, and we may here, although in a higher domain, speak of the efficient cause just as we determine, in the very midst of the service of the end, the efficient cause of the organs, for example the function of individual parts of the eye. We presuppose the efficient cause in this whole extent and ask further about the twofold relation designated above.

If being acts on thinking, the fact on the process of understanding, there results in this relation the ground of knowing (causa cognoscendi). If thinking acts on being, the concept intervenes in the process of becoming, there results, on the contrary, the end (causa finalis).

In the first case the effect of the real process becomes the cause of the logical one. For what is the later in being, thought produces the earlier; and it is at least the intention to undo the process of being in thinking and then to let the fact come to be once more, mentally, out of the producing ground. For example, the beautifully curved, mighty line and the wonderful play of colours of the suddenly rising rainbow strike the astonished mind. This appearance becomes an impulse to reflection. In the fact the understanding wishes to read the producing ground and then to project the appearance from the ground.

In the second case the activity of the logical process becomes the cause of the real one. Thinking, already filled with the appearances, posits an effect and asks, so far as it has insight into the real process, how this is to be attained. The effect is what is willed, and for the sake of this effect the cause from which it proceeds is willed. This cause is only the secondary, but what is necessary through the end. Evidently two things work together here. First, what is has been transformed into thought, and thereby the [p. 71] cause and effect of the real process have been known. Then, out of this thought and this knowledge, a power over the effect is acquired. Only in that a real organ which it governs is subject to thinking itself is thinking able, therefore, to intervene determiningly. For example, a tangent is to be drawn to a curve, say the circle. This problem contains the end and in it the end-point, the goal to be attained by a real activity. In so far as thinking possesses insight into geometrical formation and commands an organ that produces the figures, it can project and carry out the process that produces the tangent.

In the first case the copying motion excited from without, in the second the prefiguring motion, is the active intermediate link. There the representation of the antecedent arises from the reality of the consequent, here from the representation of the consequent the reality of the antecedent and thereby likewise that of the consequent. There thought goes backward, here it reaches forward. There the ground of knowing (causa cognoscendi), here the knowledge of the ground is the living impulse.

The possibility of this twofold reciprocal action between thinking and being lies always in the mediating motion. Hence it also happens that the efficient cause is intuited under the direction whence, the end under the direction whither (whereto).

Just as we know external motion only through the mind's own motion, so we know the external end which nature has realised only because the mind itself projects ends and can therefore copy ends.

When the end is worked out in the process that realises it and brought to knowledge as a free power, there shows itself in this the profundity of investigation, the transfiguration of the blind course of the cause. When the end [p. 72] is set as a problem by the mind and this problem is happily solved, there shows itself in this the genius of invention. But the former stage is possible only through the latter.

Thus the end intervenes in the sciences as a second a priori. Problems of mathematics, problems of mechanics and technology are free products of the mind hastening ahead of what is given. This a priori direction enters into the very midst of the empirical sciences. We may designate it only relatively as an a priori; for the elements with which the end operates are given to it; but out of them it creatively produces something new. Even in pure mathematics, where content and form are a priori, the end of the problem will presuppose elements as given, and it receives them no differently than when it otherwise receives them from experience.

Because the mind in this way projects and carries out ends, it is able, going backwards, to understand those that have been projected and carried out. Let us now ask what compels it to leave the track of the efficient cause, which nevertheless offered itself to it as the first in the producing motion, and what vouches to it that the form of the end belongs not merely to its manner of consideration but to the thing itself.

The question is similar to that at the beginning, when motion was posited as what is common to thinking and being; but it is more difficult. There everything pressed toward the assumption of motion, unless we wished, within us and outside us, to fall into the opposite, rest and death. Here it is not made so easy for us. The knowledge of the efficient cause is under way; it might even seem that we are being led into the arms of a dualism if we open a second path in the end.

The necessity of giving up the efficient cause in its blind sole dominion, or rather of subordinating it to a higher ground, lies, however, in the impotence of the efficient cause itself. Where it suffices, we need no other [p. 73] ground; and without its help the end is a phantom. But if, in face of phenomena such as those of organic life, explanation by the efficient cause founders, the mind must try another path. To be sure, at this standpoint the possibility still remains open that the efficient cause, more deeply investigated, may dissolve the view of the end into a semblance. Such an attempt must be expected. Until then, however, the incapacity of the efficient cause is the indirect proof of the necessity of the end. Light cannot be comprehended from darkness, and therefore we posit it as an activity of its own.

But light reveals itself, and that is its proper proof. So too the end. When the continuity which is the essence of the efficient cause breaks off in time and space, when what has been interrupted restores itself to unity only in a higher thought, then this whole found again is the proper guarantee. Efficient activities that run apart, manifold directions that divide even to the point of opposition, now appear in surprising connection. They form a whole, just as they are determined by the whole. The thought of the whole is before the parts, the thought of the effect before the cause; this complete reciprocity between whole and parts has in itself a self-proclaiming clarity as soon as it is illuminated by the kindred mind.

To every end there belongs a realising process, which consists in the concatenation of efficient causes. Now if there were a derivation from the efficient cause which ended with a formation of the end, for example man, this could be either the realisation of the willed end or else the development of a blind force, and the inference back would be doubtful. But such a situation will not easily occur. In order to solve the simplest geometrical problem, for example to draw a circle through three points which [p. 74] do not lie in a straight line, we make several different starts. We draw straight lines from one point to the other as future chords, we erect perpendiculars from their midpoints, we take the radius from the point of intersection to one of the given points, and with it we describe the circle sought. On the side of the efficient cause there is here discontinuity; no continuation in the same direction of force; we start and break off and do so again. But the starts from different points are preformed in the end, the pervading thought of unity, and in this preforming thought a continuum is restored. In the steady development of the organic we do not see these breaks, which we perceive externally where we ourselves carry out the end; but we notice, in the differentiation through the germ, in the shaping and arrangement of the cells, in the different formation of the different members, the different directions laid down in advance.

The end, indeed, as the invisible thought, cannot be observed like the external appearance; but it is nevertheless present in what can be observed, as the soul of the appearance. Itself a thought, it is accessible only to thought. But has it on that account less actuality? No grounding stands better. Within the efficient cause, too, the producing ground in its simplicity mostly lies beyond the motley, confused appearance, for example the generating cause of the wonderful world of colours beyond the rays that touch the eye. Just as in all such cases theory must try itself against the appearance until it covers it, just as it must agree with itself and enter again as a member into the concordant unity of the rest of knowledge, so the end has to fulfil the same conditions of a hypothesis. In this way it confirms itself in itself and in the system.

[p. 75] No strict criteria can be given, like an external measuring-rod. Since the end presupposes given elements and comes to execution only by means of the physical cause, it must, in order to be known, sustain a struggle with this cause. The broken thread of the efficient cause, the bold leap of the appearances, drives us at first to seek again the lost unity through the thought of the end; but the question arises ever anew: is the thread of physical activity really broken, or is the supposed leap of the appearances perhaps only a quicker step? The discontinuum is perhaps, more deeply investigated, a continuum, and the apparent continuum, on sharper consideration, divides into the members of the end. Because the sudden leap of the appearances urges us to leave the quiet course of the efficient cause, it happens that precisely chance, as in divination, counts as a sign of the end. In the old belief Iris, appearing as at a magic stroke, becomes the messenger of the gods, thus the bearer and herald of the end, until astonished wonder dissolves and freer consideration conjectures in her the mirror-image of the sun.

We must not fail to recognise the share of motion in the thought of the end. If motion was the original activity of mind, it will be taken up into the intuition of the end.

In the many-shaped, intertwined forms of motion we intuit efficient causes.¹ Where they subordinate themselves to the end, many are active together. The manifold play of combination which must be tried in order to find the significance of the individual causes for the end becomes possible only through freely projecting motion. The end thereby clothes itself in a peculiar intuition. The various forces working for *one* end (the [p. 76] efficient causes) must incline together toward *one* point and point toward it in their direction. This point, in many cases only ideal, but intimated and necessarily posited by the course and order of the forces, designates for intuition the unity of the ends in the fullness of the serving forces. This convergence of directions accompanies the end in such a way that where it cannot be demonstrated in the appearance, the end too is not to be recognised. The divergence of directions, which, followed out absolutely, leads to complete dissolution, scatters the forces which the end has to gather, and is in the appearances the sign that they withdraw from the dominion of a higher unity.

(1) Cf. above vol. I. p. 340 ff.

If in this way the intuition of motion, in determining itself more precisely, takes the end up into itself, then the categories projected from motion will also appropriate the end and thereby pass over into denser shapes of the concept. We shall therefore attempt later to present how these categories develop through the end.

10. Were the consideration of ends to complete itself, one thing more would have to be added from the metaphysical side.

We have attempted to show that the end is actual in nature and becomes knowable, or, what after the preceding considerations is the same, a thought at the ground of things, which directs and guides the forces.

At the beginning of our investigations it could not be asked how motion comes to be in being; for that already required motion. With the end, which presupposes efficient causes as its means, it is otherwise, and the question how the end comes to be in being at all has its right. For this, so far, only the ideal premises have been known, above all that anticipation of the whole before the parts, of the effect before the cause, possible only through thought, and that consistency in the demand for means, possible only through thought. But knowledge of the real [p. 77] side has lagged behind. Nowhere in nature do we observe the point at which thought takes hold of and seizes force and leads it toward its ends, and speculation is nowhere able to show it. The consideration that seeks the internal end grounds the ideal in the real; but it still lacks knowledge of how the ideal comes into the real, enters into the real. Just as the ancients represented Helios standing boldly on his chariot, guiding the horses of the sun with his hand, but gave the hand no reins, the instruments of human tractive force, so the thought of the end governs the efficient forces with invisible reins. The human thought of the end disposes of the executing hand, and the hand initiates that real process which corresponds to the consistent projection of the means. For the process in nature the correspondence breaks off at this place, and it is chiefly into this gap in knowledge that the doubt throws itself which regards the end with disbelief. It is not impossible that our knowledge may one day be completed. For now let it suffice to know what we know and what we do not know.

We remarked at the beginning that all knowledge rests on a community of thinking and being, and in agreement with this we have found in the end that our thought, which projects ends, understands the ends realised in being. Here too we must not leave a doubt unmentioned.

"A concept at the ground of things," it is asked, "similar to ours?" Our concept, it is asserted, is only a certain "motion or affection of the pulpy mass in the skull," our concept is mediated through and through, and this is supposed to become equal to the original divine one?

We disregard the crude conception which calls the mysterious, probably most profound organ a pulpy mass because it is still not understood, and puts thought in the shade because thought dwells in it. It is to be [p. 78] wondered at how the original motion, which no adherent of blindly efficient causes denies, becomes so free and conscious in the human mind that with it the mind copies and appropriates external motion and creates geometry; and yet it happens. The agreement is likewise to be wondered at when the composite organisation helps the simple principle at the ground of things to be known and human thought to reach the thought in being; and yet it happens. In art, in experiment, in practice this agreement confirms itself, in that things answer harmoniously to the deed which accords with the end that has been grasped. We wonder at this agreement, which is the highest achievement of the internal end, but after our investigations we cannot doubt it.

11. A further remark offers itself here, which is perhaps not unimportant for psychological development. It has already been pointed out in passing¹ that the organs of motion act in the most intimate agreement with sight. When the eye strives into the distance, that is an ideal motion, while the bending and stretching of the joints, walking and grasping, actually traverse space and can therefore be designated a real motion. Sight directs the organs of motion, and these carry out the direction. The ideal motion here reaches over the real, the directing over the producing and advancing. The one motion is taken up into the other, and here, as it were externally, in the schema of motion, the dominion of the end over the efficient cause presents itself. This intuition runs like a guiding image through the whole domain of the end and is still recognisable even in the most spiritual heightening of intention.

(1) Cf. vol. II. p. 7.

[p. 79] The following detailed note is intended to enter into a theory of the present day, which seeks to remove the end from the consideration of nature, so far as it concerns the validity of this concept. For since in the foregoing the end has not been constructed in some a priori way, but sought out in the actual and its knowability then demonstrated, the investigation must ask whether this basis in organic life has in fact been withdrawn from it.

Note. 1. The theory of the end presented here may well be called, as has been done, the anthropomorphic one; for it can make the end, which runs through nature as a fact, comprehensible only in the way in which man exercises it, through thought and will at the ground of things. No other way of comprehending it has yet been found.

The inference that something is true because it is anthropomorphic opens the door to every deception, every semblance; it is the fallacy of the thoughtless crowd and of our impetuous affects. The inference, on the other hand, that something is untrue because it is anthropomorphic bars all access to knowledge; for foreign things disclose themselves to thinking only in the activities which we consciously exercise and which at the same time, even if blindly, underlie things; it matters only that they prove themselves as such. In this way mathematics, springing from the constructive motion of our mind, thus subjectively (anthropomorphically), penetrated into material things and their forces; and in the same way the end, a fundamental concept of human reason, becomes comprehensible in things. If the former is not doubted in its results, it gives the latter, for its part, a share in its certainty.

The more recent natural sciences in particular make war on the anthropomorphic end.

2. Since Darwin wrote his book on the origin of species by means of natural selection, or the preservation of favoured races in the struggle for life (1859), since this book of luminous empirical research drove on to its metaphysical consequences in Germany, the victory of efficient causes has been celebrated and the concept of end removed from the world or left to human poetic invention.

This means more than when Spinoza declared the concept of end to be a human invention and yet afterwards took it up again as an auxiliary concept. It means more because, instead of the abstract generality which Spinoza pronounced, today the full and entire labour of the natural sciences, labour in the almost [p. 80] immeasurable domain of the concrete, has been summoned to make the proposition true.

It is a new piece of German philosophy of nature, and indeed distinguished from the former one in that it does not construct from generalities, but demonstrates the ground plan in the given material and keeps itself open to every correction by what is given. Such earnest work on the genesis of organic life, on the family tree of beings, will be mistaken in its intention only by one who does not know the need of research for unity and development. It is the business of the natural scientists to exercise criticism in particulars and to test the hypothesis of the principle. In investigations which turn on the value of the concept of end, it cannot be avoided to examine the new view with regard to this fundamental concept. It is incumbent on them to guard a concept which, if mistaken in nature, would also be mistaken in the ethical. It is a fact in the history of philosophy, attested by Socrates and Plato and Aristotle, that with the concept of the end in nature the inner vocation of man was more deeply known, and the concepts of the organic and the ethical mutually deepened and illuminated one another. In what follows we leave the hypothesis standing as such and ask only how the concept of end stands in relation to it.

3. We must first recall the main features of the theory.

Deeply grasped analogies have not seldom guided inventive science, and a thoroughly carried-out twofold analogy forms the essence of Darwin's doctrine. The one is the analogy of the origin of varieties for the origin of species in the vegetable and animal kingdoms, the analogy of artificial selection for the breeding of new varieties for the assumption of a natural breeding through selection for the production of new species. The other is the analogy of competition in the market of life, which awakens and heightens forces, or of the wars for power in history, for the animals struggling with one another for the necessities of life, which in this struggle test their forces, increase them and acquire new ones.

The gardener who aims at a particular colour of blossom in a species of flower selects the seeds of those individual plants which tend toward this colour, for example, among the white-blossoming ones, those that are turning reddish. He sows the seed of these plants in isolation and proceeds with the seed of these plants again according to the same point of view of selection. The selection of seeds from plants blossoming redder and redder leads, through repetition, to the goal. A variety with red blossoms arises. Pigeon breeding, whose practice goes back to ancient Egypt, [p. 81] has, in the long time of its existence, through artificial selection in pairing following an intention, produced varieties which differ so essentially in their habits, performances, their ornament, in the transformation of their structure and even in their anatomical characteristics, that they could pass for different species; and yet it is shown that they all descend from a single wild parent species, the blue rock pigeon. The races of dogs are another example. Sheep breeding and horse breeding succeed in a similar way in attaining and fixing particular properties through selection in breeding. Suitable conditions of life, which are supplied to plants or animals through cultivation, for example to plants a soil mixed with the right substances, to animals better nourishment, assist breeding. In these examples, which extend as far as the human hand tends plants and animals, it is shown what continued artificial breeding is able to accomplish through inheritance in producing varieties which can grow so in their differences that they come to equal species.

The question now is how a similar process could form itself in nature. In place of the plan of men another impulse enters, the struggle for life, the struggle for the necessary conditions of existence, which creatures wage among themselves. Plants contend with one another for the space of soil which they need for their roots, for sunlight and moisture, without which they do not thrive. Animals contend with their enemies, who seek them as food, with beasts of prey and with parasites; they contend with their own kind living in the same place for the means of life; they contend against hostile influences of every sort. The stronger or craftier conquer; the others succumb, are displaced and themselves perish. Germs of life produced a thousandfold, blossoms, seeds, eggs, the young of animals, animals as prey for food, perish, and the life laid down miscarries in this war of all against all before even *one* of these germs of life, favoured by circumstances in the struggle for existence, attains full development. In this struggle for life the victorious beings develop their forces in the direction that is useful to them; they cultivate their strength and pass it on with habit to their descendants. We take up an example which is offered to us. Where plants struggle with lack of water, those individuals which have hairy leaves have an advantage; for they are able to draw moisture from the air to themselves. As the plants with barer leaves perish, the hairy ones pass on their property and increase it in a natural drive. As the hairiness increases and [p. 82] therefore draws the sap to itself and takes it away from other parts, the plant is transformed in other respects too. Reciprocal action with the whole environment, in this struggle for life, stamps shapes and forms upon creatures. It stimulates the forces, in that it combats or favours them, and through inheritance, through the series of generations in which the differences grow, it gradually forms constant species.

In this process two things work together: adaptation and inheritance.

Adaptation to the conditions of life, which every organism practises, the self-activity with which it wins from the external what it needs for its existence, entails alterations of its shape, of the structure of its organs, which become permanent through inheritance. Thus, for example, a gilled salamander from Mexico, which lives and reproduces in water with its water-breathing organs, was observed in the Paris Jardin des Plantes. A number of the animals crept out of the water onto land; they lost their gills and were now transformed into a gill-less salamander form that breathes through lungs. Conversely, parasites, originally independent organisms, feeding on foreign force upon the ground of foreign life, lose the organs they no longer use. Through this adaptation to the condition of life creatures become more manifold and perfect and heighten themselves in their formation. Even composite organs of the utmost perfection, such as the eyes, have on this view developed in the struggle for life, through adaptation to the elements, from the first eye-spots of the lowest beings. The psychical is connected with this. Through taming, which compelled animals to adapt to the house, domestic animals such as the dog have been weaned of wildness. The division of labour, which shows itself in the self-preservation of the individual where the organs develop out of the general life for particular functions, for example those of the senses, throws itself outward in animals when, as with the bees, the ants, the swimming colonies of hydromedusae, animal states form, in which the individuals unite for the struggle for existence and build and form themselves differently according to the determination of their functions.

Natural selection works through adaptation and heredity; it works through the strength and excellence of the being toward a higher strength and excellence of the same.

More recent geology intervenes in this explanation of the species forming themselves in the struggle for existence. In investigating the earth's crust, it acquaints us with an unmeasured past in the formation of the ground on which the world of the organic [p. 83] is built up, as, for example, in the basin of New Orleans a series of buried cypress forests has been found one above another as lignite beds, separated by intermediate layers, and in individual forests of these strata tree trunks with five thousand annual rings. In the main geological periods, which some would reckon by millions of millennia, the successive generations, which continued themselves even through the divisions of the periods, had sufficient time, in the struggle for life, to lay down and carry out the division of labour, and to add up from generation to generation the differences they had acquired and to fix them through habituation and inheritance. Nature has time to accomplish its breeding through selection, which needs favourable chance. On this view each formation designates not a new and complete act of creation, but only a scene, for the most part torn out quite at random, from a slowly proceeding drama; for the intermediate forms which could represent the continuum have perished in the same struggle for existence, and we know only what was able to preserve itself.

The comparative history of development of living beings in the embryonic states serves to confirm descent. For the egg of the higher animal, at first not different from the egg of the lower, passes from stage to stage through the forms which are proper to the embryo in the series of preceding creatures, as, for example, the embryo of a tortoise in the sixth week is compared with the embryo of a chicken on the eighth day after conception. It is assumed that the development of species and genera, which required many millennia, is compressed into short periods in the development of the embryo, for example of man.

This theory led its originator to a few first created species, which, developing, underlie the world of life in its innumerable forms.

The drive toward unity led further in Germany. The mechanical origin of all creatures from matter, which is eternal, is supposed to be the necessary consequence, and *one* spontaneous generation by physical or chemical means the necessary presupposition. No end intervenes in the whole process of origination. Everything is the work of efficient causes. The family tree of the creature, which branches out, leads from the monera, the lowest microscopic beings, solely through development in the struggle for existence up to the mammals, and from the lowest mammals through the apes to man in *one* uninterrupted line. This natural system represents the descent that actually took place, not [p. 84] merely a kinship in concept but a kinship in flesh and blood. Nature had time, but it is itself only *one*, the nature of the causes efficient in matter. Every other view of it is dualistic; the end, a transcendental formation, founds this discord. The monism of matter is victor and a new epoch of mankind begins.¹

With this claim the theory works among us today.

4. The hypothesis, seeking in the bent of its essence the logical unity in infinite manifoldness, and indeed along the most proper and most significant path, the path of genesis, already fulfils the vocation of a hypothesis in that it furnishes the guiding thought for observations and inquiries and comparisons, and is thereby scientifically fruitful, even apart from the success of its metaphysical consequences.

It is no doubt aware where its gaps and its questions still lie. If we are not mistaken, some have already been noticed by the natural sciences.

All life is supposed to stem from physical and chemical conditions; this presupposes the possibility of a spontaneous generation, an origination of the first organic thing out of the inorganic. Such a thing belongs only to the belief of natural science in its beginnings, when it as yet knew no rigour of knowledge through experiments and abstractions, through reliably exclusive trials.
