The hypothesis must consistently presuppose a primordial generation, a spontaneous generation, a generation without parents, which is what the expressions generatio aequivoca, generation from the heterogeneous, designate. But as yet no example has been demonstrated; chemistry, which does indeed produce some organic products, has as yet let no organism come into being; up to now this has been denied to it. The lowest, first living beings, the monera or protists, are there, but their origin from the forces of matter has not been demonstrated.

The hypothesis must lead to the conclusion that related kinds are capable of producing hybrids and that the hybrids as such are fertile. Just as the individuals of the varieties, which are the basis of the analogy, mate fruitfully with one another, so too the individuals of the species would have to do so. Only thereby would the intermediate forms and transitions be explained, or only thereby would the production of new properties be made possible. Up to now the trials have not had success to the extent that the hypothesis leads one to presuppose. The old theory has [p. 85] in the capacity for reproduction a testimony to the constancy of species.

(1) Ernst Haeckel natürliche Schöpfungsgeschichte. Berl. 1868. p. 15 ff. p. 19. p. 306. p. 487.

(2) Cf. J. B. Meyer der Darwinismus. Two articles in the preussisch. Jahrbücher 1866.

The hypothesis requires new hypotheses in many respects in order to carry through the unity and the continuously progressing descent. Experience lacks the intermediate forms that must be presupposed for the theory, as, for example, the intermediate forms between the apes now living and the human beings descended from them and arisen in the struggle for existence. One may assume that they have perished and that perhaps their fossil remains will one day be found, perhaps brought to light from the bottom of the sea. Up to now experience does not keep pace with the theory, and there are gaps enough.

Thus up to now the theory lacks the necessary proofs and evidence precisely at the real nodal points of development.

5. It is a question for natural science whether, the remaining premises being presupposed as true, the principle of adaptation in the struggle for life and the favouring of contingent circumstances suffice to explain the immeasurable manifoldness of species in their form and articulation; for the powers to which, for example, the animal must adapt itself are relatively uniform: the atmospheric air, water, the products of the soil, light and warmth. How are the circumstances to be thought that drew forth this property and no other? and how did they vary in such manifoldness as to drive forth such manifold formations? It is not enough to operate with the universal of adaptation alone; it will be necessary to demonstrate it in the particular and under the particular circumstances; only then will one be able to judge whether it is in fact possible that, for example, the genesis of the compound and yet precise eye becomes comprehensible from the instinct of adaptation and from heredity. This will have to hold still more for the organ of the brain, still unriddled today, the bearer of consciousness and of the higher functions.

6. For the construction of the natural system the fact of heredity suffices in the first instance; but it remains a question for natural science whether inheritance, which is indeed a fact renewing itself everywhere, really becomes intelligible from matter, which is, after all, said to be the same. Is it enough, in order to comprehend inheritance from matter, that we see reproduction take place in the lower animals through division of the same matter? The division of the same matter into other individuals does not explain the propagation of the form that governs the matter and prepares and adapts to itself the future conditions of life.

Even if the human egg, like every mammalian egg and [p. 86] every animal egg, is in the first instance a simple cell; if this cell divides into two halves, these divide again and, growing, bring forth by continued division a heap of cells out of which the germ or embryo is formed; if then, out of the simple germinal form, the differences of the organs emerge through a series of developments, and these differences correspond in the order of development to the systematic articulation of the classes; and if in man only towards the end of germinal life, and only shortly before birth, those differences become recognisable which distinguish the mature human germ from the mature germ of the most nearly related tailless ape: then the theory sees in this developmental history of the human individual a brief, compressed repetition of the developmental history of the blood-related vertebrate stock. This may well be too much. Were there in this process a real repetition, and not merely a passage through the external forms, one would have to expect that, for example, the seven-month human child, if it were born and cared for, would become an ape and not a human being. The external shape cannot do it if the essence driving within is a different one. Hence this principle of knowledge drawn from the developmental history of the egg, this dazzling piece of evidence for the hypothesis, requires some restriction in the strength of the proof.

7. It is possible that research in natural science will fill up, in these directions, the gaps that still exist. But we must further follow the consideration of principle which compelled us to enter into this new design of German philosophy of nature.

In the first place, matter, and indeed matter alone, is presupposed. If matter is the principle (matter in the first instance in general, a universale taken wholesale, which requires closer determination), then it is consistent to hold the principle, as necessary energy, to be eternal. But if matter is the principle of plurality, then over against it a principle of unity is just as necessary, and it is therefore just as consistent to declare the principle of unity to be just as eternal; and if we ask more closely what this principle of unity is, and we find that it is concept or idea or end, then it is just as necessary to posit this ideal element as the eternal. The question of the relation of the two to each other would then first yield the right view of the principle; for they are not at variance, but plurality is subordinated to unity.

Such universal inferences, however, natural science gladly leaves to the inferring metaphysics. The theory leaves the question of the eternal, in which the span of time vanishes, [p. 87] undecided, and begins with a determinate point in time, with the cooling body of the earth, back to which it infers, and over against it with the light and warmth of the sun.

8. The theory begins with what it infers backwards from established facts. But it does not show how out of the inorganic an organism, out of the non-sentient a sentient self, comes to be. The struggle for life always presupposes a unity for which the whole exerts itself. We do not yet ascribe sensation to the plant, but the plant that wrestles for existence works for itself as a whole. Where the root of a tree strives into the depths, but on rocky ground covered with a thin layer of earth cannot go deep and perpendicular, it adapts itself to the given conditions and goes horizontally in the soil all the further and the more branched. The tree thereby preserves itself. Where the animal fights for existence, it has the centre of a whole in the feeling of life, in pleasure and pain, which are for it the immediate indications of a furtherance or an impairment of its existence. From this centre the striving proceeds; in it the lowest animal possesses a self. How out of carbon and oxygen and nitrogen, which do not live and do not feel, there comes to be in combination something living, like the plant, or something sentient, like the animal, or something conscious and self-conscious, like man: this neither the old atomists, such as Lucretius, nor the materialists of the last century, such as La Mettrie, nor the German continuers of Darwin, equipped with more means of explanation, have shown up to now even by approximate surmise. So long as this chasm between the non-sentient and the sentient exists, the ideal, whose kernel is the inner end, has its station in this gap. And should an experiment ever succeed that showed the transition, then at this point the end would grow forth, the end which would have been matter and would from then on become the regulator of the world. But we are not yet so far.

The struggle for life is a struggle for ends, for without such no self can be thought. The self exercises its defensive activity according to the measure of its ends, the ends without which its life would not subsist, and it draws to itself the materials and the conditions of its life according to the same measure, felt by it. The animal enjoys its essence in the functions of the ends that underlie its existence. In the strivings of the animal which spring from affects, such as fear or anger, or take place for the sake of affects, such as the satisfaction of pleasure, the inner ends of its own essence make themselves known.

9. The struggle for life, which calls forth new forms of [p. 88] activity and new organs and fixes them through inheritance, is in this direction called adaptation. The struggle for existence produces, for example, in animals the teeth or the lungs or the gills which the being needs, and teaches in instinct the cunning by which it conquers, in that it accommodates itself to the conditions of life and wins furtherance from them out of their own nature.

The concept of adaptation leads to the end; there lies in it only another name for the formative end. Through adaptation the theory gains a means which tacitly presupposes the concept of end. A tool, such as the drill, is adapted in its construction to the human hand, a lens to the structure of the eye. The hand is to guide the tool and heighten its capacity in it; the eye is to see a sharper or larger image. The end lies open to view in this adaptation. If adaptation in plants and animals makes itself known in the interaction with the climate, with the surrounding nature, as when a gilled newt, transferred from the water to the land, transforms itself into a being breathing with lungs, or when the wading birds, such as storks, cranes, snipes, have long legs and long bills in keeping with the ground on which they seek their food: then adaptation behaves no differently therein. Ends are plainly there. But since adaptation gives the species the constant property only through long inheritance, since adaptation goes on in unmeasured time, in which the small modification gradually adds up to a large one, adaptation, where it positively creates real tools and invents means, has merely broken up the execution of the *one* end running throughout into the smallest steps. If it could ever be demonstrated that through adaptation and inheritance in the struggle for life the artful, intelligent eye of man had been formed out of the light-spot of the lowest animals, then the *one* end would have worked through aeons and reached its goal little by little in the smallest beginnings and stages. Adaptation, in the interaction of the individual with the conditions of life of its surroundings, has the self-activity and the habituation of the living being as *one* of its factors, and the being exercises these according to the ends that condition its life. Adaptation is no knocking into shape from outside. The Greeks called the beautiful, measured against the necessity of self-preservation, the superfluous, and designated the beautiful by the superfluous (περισσόν). If one applies the truth of this expression to the human eye or the human ear, and if one thinks, in the one case, of the rods and cones of the retina, which according to the physiological interpretation serve for the harmony of colours, and, in the other, of the Corti corpuscles, which act for the striking of the [p. 89] nerves tuned to a tone; if then feelings of harmony are conditioned by both, feelings which seem to be there only for their own sake: then we find it hard to accept that these profound dispositions have worked themselves out merely through the struggle for life favoured by circumstances. In any case it will have to be shown what trait in the struggle for life, what disharmony in the conflict of the being with its conditions, gave existence to these pieces of evidence of ideal harmony, to the beautiful, which belongs to perfection and not to the necessity of existence.

10. The struggle for life, which through exercise of force, through adaptation to the real conditions, through division of labour in unmeasured time, gradually leads to greater perfection and wins thousandfold life from every corner of the world, presupposes a germ that should preserve itself and defend itself and multiply itself. In this germ, then, the future world of life, the life of the aeons on the earth, is enclosed, just as in the acorn the thousand-year oak that developed out of it lay enfolded. The theory posits such beings, the monera, the protists. It is all one whether the seed of the annual plant proves its force and develops its essence for *one* year, the acorn for a thousand years, or the generative germ of all life, the moneron, through periods of time that may count by millions of years; time does not alter the concept, any more than space alters the concept of the ellipse, whether it be described by a planet or, according to the same law, by a pencil. Every moneron or every protist is pregnant with the possibility of a world of life, on condition that it is compelled by its material surroundings into the struggle for existence. Out of the acorn, in interaction with light and air and moisture of the soil, comes this oak and no other being; and out of the moneron, in a similar, only manifoldly modified interaction, comes this infinitely branched world of life which descends from it. The point of the beginning is only pushed back. Leibniz, who did not yet lead man back through the race of apes to the moneron, who stopped at the first-created man as the eternal germ of the human race, once made a remark to the effect that God, in Adam, thought and willed the history of the world. According to Leibniz's thought, the plan of providence lies in the first man. Leibniz, for whom the concept of end and power in the series of efficient causes were harmoniously attuned, would today, if he held the [p. 90] concatenation that has been discovered to be correct, have extended the thought he conceived of Adam, and, stretching the history of men into the history of the living in all the forms of its multiform existence, would have stopped before the moneron and read and admired in it a greater plan. A chance, a favouring by chance, he would not concede, not even chance in the restricted sense in which there is no chance within the necessity of efficient causes, but only chance as the unforeseen, measured against some arbitrary end.

(1) Cf. Briefwechsel mit Arnauld. Ed. by Grotefend 1846. Letter 10 p. 40.

11. Since cells have been found to be the first formations of life, the question has been raised whether the cell, as first unity, already falls under the concept of the individual. One has, however, returned to the old measure of the end. The individual has accordingly been defined as a unitary community in which all the parts work together towards a homogeneous end or are active according to a determinate plan. The subordination of the parts to the unity of the whole is determined by this concept, and the more manifoldly this articulation serves the whole, the unitary community, the more perfect the individual appears.¹

Is the inner end, by which the individual is here measured, to be only a principle of knowledge for man? only a mark by which we recognise the individual? as we recognise, for example, the right angle by an arc of 90º, the quadrant of the circle, while the circle has nothing to do with the concept of the right angle as one of two equal adjacent angles. This is not the meaning.

12. The concept of end goes deeper. Even if we were to leave it undecided for a few moments that it is the generating principle, the principle that conditions the plan, it is nevertheless indisputably the preserving, healing, perfecting principle. If, for example, we use an organ in accordance with its end and the end of its parts, and maintain and protect the unity and interaction of the parts, we preserve the organ. The physician grasps the inner end of the parts in relation to the whole when he seeks successfully to remove an obstruction or to initiate a new formation. The disease of the organism fights against the hostile influences in the sense of preservation, and the vis medicatrix naturae works in the sense of the whole, hence of the concept of end. Where the physician prevents, he averts the disturbance of an end; where, in the course of the disease, he assists the furthering forces, he does [p. 91] so according to the measure of the end; where, finally, he has the task of replacing a deficient force or a missing limb, he does so in the sense of the end that has suffered impairment, as, for example, in the sense of the end that refraction has in the eye, when he corrects the range of vision with a lens. Thus the end works in healing. When the teacher of gymnastics strengthens the motions of the body and trains them to manifoldness and beauty, or when the educator leads the pupil towards his inner destination and harmoniously stimulates the faculties of his mind, then the end works perfectingly.

(1) Virchow über Atome und Individuen.

Were the end ever driven out of the generation of the living and replaced, as in Empedocles, by a concurrence of chance, it would still remain causal in preservation and perfection.

But it is more correct to conclude that preservation and generation, which go together, also have the same ground in their origin.

13. When, having arrived from the moneron at man, we look back and survey the course which the struggle for life took in unmeasured time, it is the course from being to better being (ab esse ad melius esse); and the struggle for life, the arouser of force for the end of the self, is the means to the strengthening and elevation of the self, and, thought universally, the means of development towards better being. Consistently, one will continue this intuition into human life. One will ascribe the arousal of the inventive force, as is done (cf. above II. p. 11 f.), to the need of man, born defenceless, in the struggle for food, in the struggle with nature. One will, with Hobbes, place the war of all against all at the beginning of things, in order thereby to bring men to feel the necessity that many subordinate themselves to the unconditional power of *one*; one will perhaps, with Spinoza, take self-preservation as the basis of ethics too, and, so that a strengthened power of the community may be possible, demand justice as a means of concord; one will let the needs of man refine themselves, and thereby perfect themselves, in the competition of egoistic forces, the morality of a one-sided political economy.

But one will not prevent thinking man, as soon as he gains room, from thinking himself, from grasping in the ends of his essence a value above all values, from conceiving the concept of the person, and from seeking the spiritual conditions of the world-order in which he may find himself and, in the struggle of his affects and representations, preserve and hold himself.

If, now, one sees the theory which explains the creation of life [p. 92] through adaptation and inheritance in the struggle for life dissolve, through adaptation, into ends, into nothing but small steps of ends, all of which, however, were governed through the aeons by *one* end running throughout, the end of self-preservation, which in the eternal wrestling and straining of beings divides itself as the unity into many ends, pervading the tools; and if thinking man now grasps this great unity, from the moneron up to himself, as a world-order, all the more as an order since it goes from being to better being: then he will ask himself whether this development, governing billions of years, merely appears in his head, the head of erring man, as the grandest mirror-image there is, while in itself it is a product deaf and blind, like carbon and oxygen and nitrogen or the law of gravity or of the refraction of light, or whether, on the contrary, a plan of eternal origin makes itself known here. The word "plan" we take from the natural scientists, and we consistently extend it from the natural-historical developmental history of man or of an animal or of a plant to the developmental history and the genealogical tree of life in general.

If development in the struggle for existence keeps to *one* direction, and thus strives towards *one* goal, this consistency, which runs through unmeasured times, vouches for the reality of the driving end. The spectacle of development, which a thought underlies, has become greater, but the thought rules in the end as before.

Natural science is unhindered in its intuition in going its great and successful way out of its own need; whoever wished to hinder it would not merely toil in vain, but would also lack trust in the reason in the world-order which science explores. What it yields can stand in contradiction with this only temporarily or only apparently.

Thus, for example, one seeks to prove from the squandering of the germs of life in nature that no inner end governs the formation of life, but that only the favour of chance makes it possible. On a blossoming tree many blossoms blow away, and before *one* sets and becomes fruit and bears seed, many perish. From numerous eggs animals of the species could arise, but many are destroyed or consumed, only a few are fertile, and still fewer individuals preserve themselves for development in accordance with nature. By the standard of human understanding, which does nothing uselessly, husbands its means, and seeks to create much with little, but not little with much, there appears here the opposite of a purposive formation. Hence only the efficient cause, and chance in the struggle of efficient causes for existence, is supposed to be what ultimately determines; a fool, it is thought, is he who, in the face of this simple [p. 93] consideration of the germs of life lavishly scattered and carelessly destroyed, believes in an inner end in the process of life. However, the consideration is only a consideration from the standpoint of the part and not of the whole. For in the whole, the perishing of germs of life too will have its significance. If the sure plan demanded this path and no other, if only on it was development towards the higher possible, then one would be demanding the impossible in wanting it otherwise; it is the only purposive path if it yields the best that was possible. The necessary is then the good.

The struggle for existence has often before been noticed as the stern background of life. Heraclitus called war the father of all things, and Jacob Böhme spoke of the grim quality of God over against gentle love. But this did not prevent them from recognising therein the sway of a divine power. The same Heraclitus who declared war the father of all things declared the invisible harmony mightier than the visible, and Jacob Böhme proclaimed in the necessary disunion the dawn in its rising.

Struggle is the arouser of force, the impulse to invention; but what gives shape in adaptation, what invents and tests, is neither co-posited in the struggle nor to be found in matter as such, for it cannot be thought without end and means.

The question of the inner end in nature is no idle question. Where it finds an answer that becomes knowledge, it becomes causal in art, in ethics, in religion.

That the search for a plan does not make knowledge divided against itself, and that the question of the end produces no dualism, is evident from the unity for which the end strives. Knowledge of it curtails no knowledge of forces, but grounds in them an intuition of higher unity. Thus the monism of matter, the sole dominion of efficient forces, which seeks to build itself up on the overthrow of the ideal, is a premature song of victory.

From the considerations here attempted it may emerge that German Darwinism, which wants to let the end perish in the efficient cause, does not do away with it, but itself presupposes it. What it demonstrates of the struggle for existence as the arouser of forces fits itself, as means, into the end.

12. The two directions of comprehending knowing have now been pursued, one of which is turned towards the efficient cause, the other towards the end. In both a wonder shows itself at first glance. For in the [p. 94] fathoming of the efficient cause, thought goes backwards, out of the present into the vanished past, out of the surface of existence into the depths of becoming; and in the projection of the end, by means of that first process, out of the present into the future, which as yet is not. Thus thought, in its vigorous act, triumphs over the power of time. How this can happen, however, has been discussed above.

[p. 95]

## X. DER ZWECK UND DER WILLE. — X. END AND WILL.

1. The last investigations turned on the objective end, and indeed on the inner end, i.e. one which so orders the parts and forces of an organism into agreement that it constitutes its essence and preserves it and the genus.

In the impulses which experience offered to set the end above the efficient cause (the causa finalis above the causa efficiens) as the proper principle, there lay still more; there lay in them a concept which comes about only on the foundation of the end.

For it might be thought that the end, imprinted on the world and carried out through the world, made it into one great machine, in which, much as in a planetarium turned by the hand of the astronomer, all motions ran their course according to the alien thought, as if at the finger of God. But in those considerations of organic nature life confronted us, and the concept of the ensouled goes hand in hand with the concept of the living.

The inner end is the properly individuating principle of the world. From the standpoint of the efficient cause we measure substance as peculiar according to the law of formation [p. 96] that underlies it, as, e.g., the individual crystal according to the geometrical laws of chemism that give shape in space. But when formation takes place through the end, out of the whole, and when the realisation and preservation of the whole has become the task set by the unity thought beforehand, then the individuating principle, i.e. the principle that strives toward a relative whole, presents itself in this more sharply.

Every end is directed to individual activities in space and time; it wills what is individual. Though itself a thought, it does not remain in a universal that hovers there like something merely possible. If space and time alone are taken as the individuating principle, then its essence is found only in this, that a separated multiplicity is produced for our consideration, and no concern is taken whether and through what the separated gathers itself together as a whole. From the inner end there follows separateness in space and time, but from separateness there does not yet follow a true individual. Already in the machine the end sets off the whole cleanly and roundly; yet the moving force, or the will that directs it, remains external to it; and to that extent one will still call it selfless and not an individual in the same sense as the product of nature, which is a natural end.

Only with the concept of the end in the living does the proper sense of a self come forth. We merely lend a self to the lifeless from ourselves. When, for example, we say that the water cuts its way for itself, this is indeed meant to express that the force which hollows out the deepening of the way belongs to the same water that flows in the deepened bed. But that it is the same water which cuts the way and uses the way is only an appearance, since we take the water flowing through as a whole; strictly speaking, it is some waves that cut the way and others that afterwards flow through it; the first wave that forces its way through makes the way for others that follow; for it, it is not yet a way. Only in the living, [p. 97] where moving force and inner end coincide, where what the active being does turns to its benefit or to its harm, does the self come fully into its right, as, e.g., when we say that the tree itself puts forth its blossoms. In the concept of the self lie one's own acquisition and possession, or one's own loss. The coincidence of force and end in the same subject conditions the concept of the self, and only with the self is the individual present in the higher sense.

In plants the end appears as individuating by making itself known in assimilation, in the transformation of inorganic matter into organic, in the plan of the type, in the propagation of the genus. In the animal it shows itself by producing more and more centralised formation, and its significance rises inwardly in sensation, in desire, outwardly in the many-membered instruments, until in the thinking and willing human being it itself presents an ethical destination.

In this whole sphere of life we have the general phenomenon that motions are directed toward a goal and that what directs dwells in what is directed and moves along with it. In the machine what moves and directs remains outside. Now what, regarded from the side of the thing, is the end, forming, building, steering, that is in the individual (subjectively) the soul, realising the end, sensing, desiring, thinking. To that extent the soul can be defined as a thought of an end realising itself. In the machine such a thought is realised; in the living it realises itself.

We may compare the definition of the soul in Aristotle, who calls the soul the entelechy of the body,¹ i.e. the realisation, according to the inner end, of what is laid down in the body, or more exactly, the first entelechy of the body, whereby it is indicated that the soul is the realising [p. 98] force which contains the capacity for activity and first brings forth the realisation as act. This definition does indeed attach to the body, in which the ends appear, and the body is that from which the view starts; but this is not meant to take the body as the first and the soul as its accident; rather, just as in general the energy (the actus) is what determines, and not the capacity as such (the potency), which is rather determined according to the energy, so in this intuition the soul is the prius, and in it lie the ends for which the body is the instrument. Thus Aristotle says in a comparison,¹ which at the same time contains a partial representation dependent on the soul: "If the eye were by itself a living being, seeing would be its soul. For this activity is its essence according to the concept, and the outer eye is the body of seeing; and when seeing leaves the eye, it is no longer an eye, but an eye only in name, like the painted eye or the eye of stone." The essence according to the concept clearly expresses the determining end as what is original.

(1) Ueber die Seele II. 1 ff.

(1) Ueber die Seele II. 1. §. 9. p. 412 b 18.

If we now call the soul a thought of an end realising itself, the expression is at first only formal. The content of the end, e.g. assimilation, sensation, thinking, is not thereby stated, and we take it from what is given. But the form nevertheless carries something essential in itself. From this determination there flows, e.g., the fundamental drive of all life, self-preservation; and when the determination opens up what lies bound within it, there still springs in man, out of its unity, will and knowledge: will, inasmuch as the end contains an ought, and knowledge, inasmuch as the end, itself a thought, drives to thinking; and will and knowledge demand each other into unity out of the same fundamental determination. The form further contains a subordination, and hence the possibility of a [p. 99] system of ends, such as comes forth in the higher life of the soul. By presupposing the thought that something higher is to come about than the means itself, it purifies the conception of the merely empirical fact and gives it a higher direction. Every determination of value for the individual depends on the legitimate end.

In systems in which the end does not occur at all, or, as in Herbart, only incidentally, one must, to be sure, determine the concept of the soul otherwise, if one admits it at all. One then mostly starts from the unity of self-consciousness, thus already from the highest stage of the life of the soul; and by inferring backwards one determines the soul as a simple being, not merely without parts but also without any multiplicity in its quality, which, though it is not anywhere and not at any time, nevertheless has spatial and temporal relations, corresponding to its inner state in the being-together of beings. In the connection of this doctrine 1 it is not explained how the soul, e.g. the human soul, as something simple in being-together with others, in reaction against other things that are, can have so many-sided, internally diverse, infinitely manifold a counter-action; and something spaceless and timeless that has spatial and temporal relations is still less clear, still less free from contradiction, than the concepts of experience, which are supposed to suffer from contradictions. The objective semblance, the assumption of which has been refuted above, does not suffice here.

If the soul is a thought of an end realising itself, [p. 100] then unity, and to that extent simplicity, is thereby the first; but relations to space and time are at the same time demanded by the realisation.

(1) Cf. e.g. Herbart Lehrbuch zur Psychologie. 3rd ed. 1850. §. 150ff. Wilh. Fridolin Volkmann Grundriss der Psychologie vom Standpunkte des philosophischen Realismus und nach genetischer Methode. 1856. §. 5 ff.

(2) See above I. p. 205ff. The discerning reader will easily see what repercussion the above critique of Herbart's synechology (I. p. 173ff.) has on his rational psychology (loc. cit.). If the former is correct, the latter is incorrect. Cf. the author's "Historische Beiträge zur Philosophie" vol. 3. p. 97 ff. "über die metaphysischen Hauptpunkte in Herbarts Psychologie."

Only with the concept of the end is there formed the possibility of self-preservations, which Herbart applies to everything that is; for before it there is no self in the proper sense, but only the reaction of a law of formation. Only with the concept of the end is there the possible opposition of inner and outer, which in Herbart already appears in matter; before it, the inner, even if hidden from us and withdrawn, is still an outer, because spatial. To that extent even Herbart's view carries within it an analogue of the determination by ends, but admittedly without intention and without warrant.

2. The end, the centre of the activities, is accordingly not alien in living beings, as it is in the machine; it becomes their own; in the various gradations of beings it is desired, sensed, thought, willed; and when we say: the soul desires, senses, or at a higher stage the soul (the mind) thinks, wills, then the soul is therein the thought of an end realising itself.

We call these activities reflexive activities, since they proceed from the living being and take place for the living being, and posit the end of the efficient cause in the being itself. In them the being is an end to itself. The desiring animal desires for itself and wills to still its need; the sentient being, which becomes aware of increased existence in pleasure and of diminished existence in displeasure, therein senses itself; the thinking human being thinks himself, and without thinking himself, without his self-consciousness, he thinks nothing else either; the willing human being wills what he wills as his deed. That the end, which in the machine too is the ultimate unity, becomes in the living the centre which in its realisation affirms itself, senses itself, thinks itself: this is the higher and the new [p. 101] that makes itself known here and that we understand in other beings only from ourselves.

The end itself, which is here presupposed as the general foundation, already raises this phenomenon above the possibility of its being explained from blind forces. What is peculiar to reflexive activity, in which at once something other appears to the being and the being appears to itself, points no less beyond efficient causes.

The external motions of matter, the so-called organic stimuli, which come from outside, are incommensurable with the peculiar nature of the activities of the soul (sensation, desire, thinking).

The sensation of pleasure and displeasure is a familiar phenomenon to us; at every moment we are caught up in it, and yet, so long as we understand only forces of motion, it is incomprehensible to us. Every physical activity takes place spatially, acting out of itself upon another through change of place. But the feeling of pleasure is a reaction of force upon itself, and not, say, in such a way that force as such heightens itself therein and becomes more intensive in opposition to the extensive. The swiftest motion we can think is in and for itself still dull and blunt. The sensation of pleasure indicates in the individual life an end furthered for it by force, and yet it is no mere sign, but something of its own in itself. When we speak of a reaction of force upon itself or upon the active being, of reflexive activity, the expression is spatial, but we understand it only if we substitute something non-spatial. In pleasure or displeasure the being is no longer a stranger to its doing.

The sensation of pleasure takes place in the perception, e.g., of something external, and on closer consideration the incommensurability of the inner process with the outer becomes clear here too. The tense string, when struck, sounds; here the tension of the string is external, the excursions of the string are [p. 102] external; the sound waves propagate themselves externally. When they penetrate into the ear, the animal hears. But neither in the chemical composition of the nerve nor in the tension and position and mobility of its parts can the ground be found why a sound wave in the nerve could produce anything other than a vibration similar to itself; one does not see how through the nerve it could transform itself into a conscious sensation, how it could cease spatially as motion and rise again as sensation, as sensation of something external and as sensation of the life moved thereby in pleasure or displeasure. The leap from the last state of the material element to the first dawning of sensation is a leap across the greatest chasm.¹ No adherent of material efficient causes has explained it.

With the feeling of pleasure, expansion is the mimetic, physiognomic effect; with displeasure and grief, contraction. Poetic minds such as Campanella regarded expansion as pleasure and constriction as displeasure in general, and in the lifeless too. But the accompanying phenomenon does not express the essence of sensation. The heated iron bar expands and the cooling one contracts. But no one suspects pleasure or displeasure in it.

It remains for psychological investigations to show how, in human development, self-consciousness attaches itself to self-feeling in pleasure and displeasure. If some of our representations are marked with pleasure or displeasure, while others, and by far the majority, float along free and more indifferent to our self-feeling, then we stand over against these as more foreign and count the former within the circle of our ego, especially insofar as we were causal in them. They form the empirical material of our empirical ego.

In self-consciousness we appear to ourselves, and this [p. 103] appearing to oneself, which begins with self-feeling, is comparable with nothing in the material; higher than self-feeling, self-consciousness is still further removed from the material. Already as a reflexive activity it remains unexplained. It has been proposed to assume that the motion communicated to the nerve in sensation makes a circuit in the brain, and that this return of consciousness to itself can thereby be comprehended. But the circuit, even if it could be demonstrated, explains nothing. The point moving in a circle does not become anything other by describing this motion and no other; it remains as external as it was. Its path returns into itself; but it does not thereby come to itself, so as to know itself. In this explanation the metaphor of language, which speaks of self-consciousness as a motion returning into itself, has been made into what is proper and original; and such an explanation detaches itself, along with the image, which is only a sign, from the essence, and melts away.

(1) H. Lotze medicinische Psychologie oder Physiologie der Seele. 1852. p. 180 f. Mikrokosmus 1856. I. p. 160 f.

In self-consciousness unity is the first, much as in the end, in which unity produces multiplicity. In the midst of the manifold of our activities and states we feel ourselves as one, equal to ourselves. In the infinite representations which the open senses unlock for us at every moment, self-consciousness does not lose itself; rather, certain of itself, it hovers freely and purely above them. This unity, equal to itself, which makes itself known to us at every moment, continues through time and in the changing relations to space, and extends itself into that abiding identity with itself which, proper to self-consciousness, stems from no external experience.¹

This nature of the self-conscious mind, superior to matter, also makes itself known in the logical fact that [p. 104] there are, as our investigations have shown and will show further, concepts a priori which cannot be explained sensualistically from experience.

(1) Cf. above Part I. Section VII. p. 286 ff.

So far as knowledge of matter reaches at present, it does not reach to self-feeling and self-consciousness, which are phenomena without their like. Were one, on the analogy of the advancing electrical physiology of the nerves, to make our sensing and thinking into electric sparks, or, as Alexander von Humboldt once put it with telling irony, into an electric thunderstorm discharging itself in the brain: still the electric sparks know nothing of themselves. The lightning shines for us, but not for itself.

If the end forms the foundation of these phenomena, if the soul is a thought of an end realising itself in individual existence, then the soul is not result but principle. Its appearance, conditioned by the body, is result, but its essence is principle, in a way similar to that in which the thought of a geometrical problem does indeed appear in the system of lines which realises it, yet is the principle of that very appearance. Were it only result, then it would have to be explained how the unity of life, sharp and precise in the manifoldness of forces, how self-consciousness, ruling in calm freedom over the agitated impressions, could arise out of a multiplicity coming together by chance. That this is not thinkable has been shown earlier. The system of lines in a geometrical problem, simple compared with the intricate and yet harmoniously unified phenomena of the life of the soul, never stems from multiplicity. The shipwrecked man who on the lonely shore perceived geometrical figures in the sand recognised in them the nearness of the human mind, in which the unity of thought is what determines. How could we read anything else out of the revelations of the soul?

If our investigations have not erred, then the soul is [p. 105] not, as in Kant, veiled from itself by merely subjective forms, by space and time and the categories, so that, always only appearing to itself, it would remain constantly hidden from itself in its essence. The inference back from appearance to essence has its place here too; and the identity which belongs to no thing and only to self-consciousness has, in the connection of the results so far, a deeper significance. If in the rational psychology against which Kant took the field there was squeezed out of it what does not lie in it, then this basis was misused and the bow was drawn for a goal further than it can carry. But we must nevertheless regard the identity of self-consciousness as something real, and indeed as something in which an ideal announces itself, inexplicable from our knowledge of the material.

Thus the appearance of the soul is result, but its essence is principle.

3. We must leave it to psychology to pursue this general concept within the range of its wide extension, in the ascending series of the living kinds, and to carry it through into the essence of man. It is to be admired in what abundance of forms such a thought of an end realising itself appears ever otherwise, ever new, and in the animal kingdom is directed toward winning from all elements and all situations of the external conditions the self-enjoyment of existence. The inexhaustible theme of the manifold feeling of pleasure varies itself in ever new ways as the task of a thought of an end realising itself, and nature becomes alive in order to rejoice in existence in countless forms. Sensation, fused with desire, becomes ever richer and more significant in the ascending kinds of animals. Let the above exposition borrowed from Cuvier¹ serve here as an example, the exposition of the strivings and sensations in herbivorous and carnivorous animals, distinguished according to [p. 106] two opposite sides and manifold in themselves. The fundamental desire in the self-preservation of life clearly expresses the inner end which reveals itself in the structure of these animals and asserts itself in all their activities.

(1) See above II. p. 8 ff.

But in animals the driving thought is still hidden from itself. The underlying end is blindly desired and, as it is attained or missed, blindly sensed in pleasure or displeasure. Further than this they do not come, since, working and fighting for self-preservation or playing with the abundantly offered conditions of life, they pass their existence blindly.

Otherwise with man, whose essence it is that he think, and that thinking pervade desire and sensation and draw them up to itself. Through thinking he is capable of the universal, and this conscious universal raises man above the animal, by entering determiningly into the blind stirrings of the life of the self and, conversely, taking up what is one's own into itself.

In opposition to the blindly organic in nature, we designate what flows from this peculiarly human source as ethical.

The question is how far the principle for the ethical lies in what has preceded, or how far the organic is the same and how far not.

4. The inner end becomes easily recognisable in the ethical.

The ethical rises out of the organic as a higher stage. Just as without the thought at the ground of things, e.g. in the life of an animal kind or in the function of a member, e.g. the eye, the hand, there is nothing organic and no organ, so without a directing end, without an inner destination, without a thought for the sake of which life is there, there is no ethics. Without it ethics would lack its peculiar essence. [p. 107] It would become a mechanics of human forces meeting one another, a physics of the self-preservation of the one colliding with the self-preservation of the other. Without the inner end branching out, the idea of action would be lacking.

If we recognised it as a character of the organic that the whole is before the parts and that the whole determines the parts, then the same character appears in the ethical, whether we consider the individual human being in agreement with himself or the community, e.g. of the state, of which the individual becomes a member.

In this connection one sees how important it is that already in nature the thought that subordinates the forces to itself be recognised and acknowledged. Physics and ethics will breathe their spirit each into the other. A shallower or deeper physics will make ethics shallower or deeper, and the reverse also shows itself, although physics, which in the system is the necessary presupposition of ethics, will determine ethics more powerfully than ethics in turn determines physics.

In the history of philosophy the systems of mechanical (atomistic) physics (Epicurus, the système de la nature) show an affinity with hedonism or the morality of well-understood egoistic interest. In more recent times Herbart, without drawing in the inner end, founded practical philosophy on five ideas, which express what is concordant among the elements necessary to action and are supposed to have their evidence in the aesthetic approval they arouse. It has been shown elsewhere¹ and shall not be repeated here, that in this conception, by a hysteron proteron, the harmony of the appearance, [p. 108] which is the effect of the inner ends, has been made the ground, and that moreover the individual ideas suffer from particular difficulties. Should anyone, determined by Herbart, come to believe that even the nobler ethics can dispense with the inner end and the ideal destination that proceeds from it, we refer to earlier discussions.¹

(1) Cf. historische Beiträge zur Philosophie. III. 1867. "Herbarts praktische Philosophie und die Ethik der Alten" p. 122ff. and especially p. 161.

On our conception, the transition from nature to mind lies in the organic; for mind is properly already right in the midst of the organic; and through the end nature is bound up with the ethical world.

5. Out of the organic as what is common, the ethical proceeds through the specific difference of the human.

In organic nature desire is blind, an expression of the inner end that is a stranger to itself, and is at most sensed in pleasure or displeasure. In man the ends come to consciousness; man thinks what he desires.

Further, in organic nature the unity of the ends is preserved of itself; but in man a discord enters, and in the midst of this discord the ethical task is born.

Man, himself a life of his own and in himself a whole, whose drive is the preservation and increase of his own being, is to become a member of a higher whole and to seek and increase it; in this destination there springs up a conflict of the life of the self against the ends of the whole or the ends of others who belong to it.

Further, a discord arises within man by himself. In the life of the self the individual ends, e.g. the stimuli of [p. 109] sensuous nature, can break loose, and the ends as parts can assert themselves against the higher and against the whole. Since irrational life, in order to become the foundation of rational life, develops before the rational, the lively pleasure of the sensuous drives desire to remain in the ground of nature and resists the labour which lies in every development toward the higher. The ends of individual tendencies, the ends as parts, fall into conflict with the ends of the whole.

(1) See the author's treatise just cited in the historische Beiträge. vol. III. p. 122ff. and Naturrecht auf dem Grunde der Ethik. 2nd ed. 1868. §. 32.

On this twofold path there arises in man a hostile, factious power which does not let him become man, the selfishness of the part, an "unbridled will to power." In this discord there results the ethical task of raising the resisting natural man rather into the spiritual one, and not merely to think the ends in their subordination to the ultimate end, but to will it.

The will is desire which thought has pervaded. Its consistency stems from thinking, and its firmness against fear and hope, against pleasure and displeasure, in general against the selfishness of the part, would not be possible without the cohesive thought of the conscious end.

It is the inner freedom of man, the right power over himself, when he brings it about that his desire agrees with his knowledge.

The inner end, whether in the part or in the whole, which becomes the thought-out task of action or of life, is called the ethical idea, as in this sense the idea of the judge, the idea of the scholar, express the centre from which their activities go out like radii.

The thought which underlies the things of the world is known and willed; in order to realise itself it produces new thoughts which, subordinated to the first, become anew a centre of willing and acting. The end [p. 110] which in the formations of nature appears only objectively becomes subjective in man, indeed in the will, as it were, personal; it moves inventive knowledge and drives in new deeds toward ever more perfect realisation; it extends its organs and fashions things to itself as instruments; it drives toward deepening consciousness and enriching knowledge. The organic falls prey to the obstructions of nature; but in the realm of the ethical, common knowledge succeeds in freeing the inner end more and more from hindrances. Thus the power and dominion of reason over the earth grows, and the ethical world, in opposition to the sameness of nature and of the organic, has development and history. Where it forms, it forms organically and forms organisms themselves. But the moral organisms, even where, like the family, they still stand close to nature, have the drive to become conscious of themselves. Their ultimate elements are not, as in the organisms of nature, selfless parts, but individuals grounded in the centre of their own ends. Hence their essence is articulation in a still higher sense than is already the essence of the organic in nature. In the ethical community there is nothing that could not and should not be at once part and whole.

In all these directions the ethical shows itself, insofar as the organic in nature is still blind and bound, as the organic heightened and made free through knowledge and will. It would be a misunderstanding to recognise in the ethical only the external form of the organic, and in the attempted determination only something formally organic. The content is the human essence grasped in the idea in the midst of real psychology; it necessarily lives itself out organically, if indeed it is the essence of thinking that, directed to the whole and universal, it subordinates the parts and the particular to the whole and universal. The ethical is an organic of a higher order.

[p. 111] The development of the principle whose origin has been indicated here does not belong in this place but in ethics.¹

6. Meanwhile the concept of the will, in which the centre of gravity of the ethical falls, still demands closer consideration.

The representation on whose impulse desire acts is called motive, and our animal desire follows sensuous representations as motives. If there is to be a will in the sense we have described, it must be capable of acting on the impulse of thought. For the ultimate end of man, which subordinates all others to itself, contending with the power of the sensuous ones and lacking the intuition of sensuous stimuli, and the ends which proceed from the ultimate one as demands, are only an object of thought. The will is will in the full sense only when it is capable of acting on the motive of this thought. When it does so, when therefore the idea of the human essence drives it, it is the good will.

This capacity, in contradiction with the desires and independently of sensuous motives, to have as its motive the good grasped only in thought, we call the freedom of the will.

If such a freedom of the will could not be assumed, what is peculiar to everything ethical would come to nothing. For the inner end, which constitutes the destination of man, gathers itself as the ultimate end into a command of an unconditional kind. For man there is no remission of the command to be man at every moment and to fulfil the peculiar human essence. If such a [p. 112] command is not to be vain, like an impossible goal, then man must be able to become master over the inner hindrances to fulfilling it. Every demand of the command is a demand of freedom. As the freedom of the will is known from the command, so it conditions the command as an actual one. The command presupposes freedom, or, expressed otherwise, in the consciousness of its truth the inner end, in order to prevail, must demand freedom.

(1) Cf. the determination of the ethical principle in critical investigation and in a development agreeing with the above considerations in the author's "Naturrecht auf dem Grunde der Ethik." 2nd ed. 1868. §§. 16-44.

This necessary presupposition is confirmed in the fact of conscience, and namely of the bad conscience, which, as has been shown elsewhere in a brief psychological discussion,¹ active in the sense of the human idea, is, in the representations and in the sensations of displeasure that proceed from them, the reaction of the whole man against the selfish part, thus of the whole end against the ends of individual desires that have broken loose. The unrest of the bad conscience would be a feeble folly if it had been impossible for man to will otherwise and to act otherwise than he did, if it had been impossible for him to cast down the tempting selfish part and to remain true to the whole.

In these respects ethics demands no indeterminate freedom going beyond the human being, dependent on all sides, but the possibility of being able to do what it ought; it demands of man that he be able to be man, because he ought to be man. The inner end, which wills the individual and the community of men as a concordant whole, prevails only when the will becomes so strong that it is master of the enemy in its own realm.

How desire is so far weaned from the selfish that, acting on the impulse of universal thinking, it becomes will, is a psychological question [p. 113] which we here exclude. As thinking only gradually ripens, so too free will is not born complete but is acquired in development. The demand for free will, which universally the one makes of the other and the law of the community makes of all, itself helps to make the will free; for it stretches toward its goal.

(1) Naturrecht auf dem Grunde der Ethik. 2nd ed. 1868. §. 39.

7. This faith of man in the demanded free will is confronted by the view which strictly and tautly continues the causal law out of nature into mind. According to it, the chain of causes and effects so ensnares and binds man that in the thoroughgoing necessity of efficient causes he is only something done and not a doer. For what he does has its sufficient cause in something else, and he cannot do otherwise. Since man plays out an alien causality, or is only the channel through which it passes, concepts such as guilt become empty semblance. The consciousness that we could also do otherwise if we willed is then only an illusion of deliberating thought that sketches proposals; in reality we can will only the one thing that we happen to will; we suppose otherwise only because the cause that tips the wavering balance remains unknown to us.

To rescue the will from this constraint of determinism, and thereby to make morality possible, Kant,¹ who acknowledged the causal law for the whole world of appearance, but only for this, devised intelligible freedom, freedom beyond and as it were behind appearance.

Kant's deepest motives lie in ethics. As surely as the essence of reason in general is universality and necessity, so surely must the rational practical law [p. 114] be universal and necessary. But such a law would be vain if the human will, dependent on the natural law of appearance, succumbed to the force of the desires. Without freedom, therefore, no unconditional law is possible, and freedom is to that extent a real ground of the law. Conversely, the unconditional law is the guarantee of freedom, a ground of knowledge of its actuality. Freedom and the unconditional law of practical reason point to each other.

(1) Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2nd ed. p. 566ff. Werke in Rosenkranz's edition. vol. II. p. 422ff., cf. Kritik der prakt. Vernunft. p. 169 ff. in the Werke VIII. p. 225ff. Metaphysik der Sitten, in the Werke VIII. p. 88.

Thus reason, determining but not determinable, and therefore lifted out of the connection of appearances, comes forth as causal in the ought, which occurs nowhere in the whole of nature and, if one has merely the course of nature before one's eyes, is altogether without meaning; it is present and the same in all the actions of man in all circumstances of time, but is not itself in time and does not fall into a new state in which it was not before. The thing in itself is indeed veiled by time and space and the categories, purely subjective forms, and is for us an unknown region; but we nevertheless think it as independent of time and space and causality, and the essence of man as thing in itself is therefore suited to be that reason which comes forth plainly in the ought. Accordingly Kant distinguishes between man as phainomenon, who has an empirical character, and man as noumenon, whose character is intelligible and therefore free from the conditions of time. The moral ought is his own necessary willing as a member of an intelligible world, and is thought by him as an ought only insofar as he at the same time regards himself as a member of the world of sense. The empirical character is accordingly the sensuous schema of the intelligible, and every empirical action, regardless of the temporal relation in which it stands with other appearances, is "the immediate effect of the intelligible character of pure reason, which consequently acts freely, without being dynamically determined in the chain of natural causes by external or internal grounds preceding it in time, [p. 115] and this its freedom one can not only regard negatively as independence from empirical conditions (for thereby the faculty of reason would cease to be a cause of appearances), but also designate positively as a faculty of beginning a series of events of itself, in such a way that in it itself nothing begins, but that it, as the unconditioned condition of every voluntary action, admits above itself no conditions preceding in time, while yet its effect begins in the series of appearances, but can never therein make an absolutely first beginning."

In the purest ethical interest, and using the advantage which the consistency of his transcendental idealism offered him in the strict separation of the world as appearance from the thing in itself, Kant devised intelligible freedom in order to ground the possibility that every individual action, notwithstanding all empirical conditions, is to be regarded as free and according to reason as a cause which, regardless of all empirical conditions, could have determined the conduct of man otherwise.¹

Two difficulties stand in the way of this view, indeed make it impossible.

First, it belongs to the general contradiction in which Kant's idealism entangles itself that, according to the result of the doctrine of categories, causality belongs solely to appearance and, applicable only to appearance, has no meaning beyond appearance; and yet in this doctrine, much as in the impulse which the thing in itself gives to sensibility for the apprehension of things in space and time, the thing in itself, though itself not determinable, becomes causal as determining reason.

This contradiction of the system with itself reveals itself still more glaringly in the second difficulty. On the one hand [p. 116] human action and character are to be explained according to causality in appearance, and then again the same action is ascribed to intelligible freedom, which, though itself not determinable, has nevertheless determined the individual action. In the first respect Kant says:¹ "Every man has an empirical character of his power of choice, which is nothing other than a certain causality of his reason, insofar as this shows in its effects in appearance a rule according to which one may gather the grounds of reason and its actions according to their kind and their degrees, and judge the subjective principles of his power of choice. Because this empirical character must itself be drawn from appearances as effect, and from the rule of these which experience furnishes, all the actions of man in appearance are determined from his empirical character and the other co-operating causes according to the order of nature; and if we could investigate all the appearances of his power of choice to the ground, there would be no single human action which we could not predict with certainty and know as necessary from its preceding conditions. In respect of this empirical character, therefore, there is no freedom, and yet it is only according to this that we can consider man, if we merely wish to observe and, as happens in anthropology, to investigate physiologically the moving causes of his actions." In this passage and in the whole connection the question is not, as it might at first seem, how we know the intelligible character, say the maxim of freedom, from its sensuous expression, the empirical character; for then necessity would fall only in our knowing; rather, as the conclusion clearly shows, it is a matter of moving real causes which are investigated physiologically, and it is [p. 117] said expressly: "in respect of this empirical character there is no freedom." By contrast, in the second respect Kant says of the intelligible character:¹ "The blame of a lie is grounded on a law of reason, whereby one regards reason as a cause which, regardless of all empirical conditions, could and should have determined the conduct of the man otherwise. And indeed one regards the causality of reason not merely as concurrence, but as complete in itself, even if the sensuous incentives were not at all for it but even quite against it; the action is ascribed to his intelligible character; he is now, at the moment when he lies, entirely to blame; consequently reason, notwithstanding all empirical conditions of the deed, was wholly free, and the deed is to be ascribed entirely to its omission." "One easily sees in this imputing judgment that one has it in mind that reason is not at all affected by all that sensibility, that it does not change (even though its appearances, namely the way in which it shows itself in its effects, change), that in it no state precedes that would determine the following one, and consequently that it does not belong at all to the series of sensuous conditions which make appearance necessary according to laws of nature." Apart from the question whether Kant, consistently with his view, was entitled to posit the thing in itself as causal, and thus as reaching over into time, which after all is only a subjective form, it is hard to comprehend how the free and the unfree fit into each other and work together in the same action, which is to be regarded now empirically as necessary, now intelligibly as free; how freedom "begins its effect in the series of appearances," and thus cannot be taken into account therein, and yet the series of appearances is necessary. No clear imputation results from this consideration wavering between the empirical and the intelligible. [p. 118] Either the intelligible can break through the empirical causal connection, and then the causal law in appearance is not satisfied; or the empirical character is necessary, and then the ought of reason succumbs.

(1) Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2nd ed. p. 583. Werke II. p. 435.

(1) Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2nd ed. p. 577 ff. Werke. II. p. 431.

(1) Kritik der reinen Vernunft. 2nd ed. p. 583. Werke II. p. 435.

Accordingly Kant's distinction does not accomplish what it means to accomplish. It does not settle the conflict between freedom and necessity. If theologians, attracted by Kant, who does not shrink even from an intelligible deed leading to radical evil (a rational deed leading to what is contrary to reason), have adopted Kant's intelligible freedom and woven it into dogmatics, then they may not take this one thing out of Kant and reject the substructure, the subjective doctrine of space and time and of the categories, which is harder to reconcile with the dogma of creation. The two stand and fall together.

8. Schelling¹ already borrows intelligible freedom from Kant under other presuppositions, but brings it nearer to its origin and archetype in Plato.²

The general possibility of evil, he says in the sense of Christian theologians, consists in this, that man can strive, instead of making his selfhood the basis and the organ, rather to raise it into what rules and into the all-will, and on the other hand to make the spiritual in itself into a means. Free, he continues with Spinoza, is what acts only in accordance with the laws of its own essence and is determined by nothing else either in or outside it. Freedom is not indeterminacy and chance. The essence of man, he adds in Platonic fashion, is his own deed, a primal and fundamental willing which makes itself into what it is. The life of man is determined by an intelligible deed which itself belongs to eternity, but which does not precede life in time, but passes through time. [p. 119] Freedom and determinacy are united thus and only thus. True freedom is in harmony with a holy necessity, such as we feel in essential knowledge, when mind and heart, bound only by their own law, freely affirm what is necessary.

(1) Abhandlung über die Freiheit. 1807. Werke. I. 7. 1860. p. 331 ff.

(2) In the myth of the Republic. X. p. 614 ff.

The cleverly joined elements are beautifully expressed in Schelling's treatise. We pass over the theosophical connection in which, echoing Jacob Böhme, God is described as becoming and in the timeless history of his unfolding. For human freedom is only apparently designed out of and after God's essence. We take out only what belongs to our theme. Were that fundamental deed which itself belongs to eternity but passes through time, were the eternal in the temporal to be taken as it is elsewhere in Schelling, then it would be the idea—but then this intelligible deed could be no freedom for evil. The primal and fundamental willing is a universal deed of which we know nothing, a pre-temporal one, yet passing through time. What, then, determined this fundamental deed? We do not know. A ground would, as in temporal succession, determine it and make the fundamental willing a grounded one; and again, groundlessness is equivalent to chance. According to this intelligible deed we would, further, be free in another world, but not in time, not in the world which is the soil and stage of the ethical. Here we would only be onlookers; temporal life would fall under necessity. Betterment and worsening would be mere semblance, and the determinism of an education, e.g., could not be reconciled with that self-determining fundamental deed,¹ nor at all, as theologians have overlooked, that call to a change of heart with which the Gospel begins.

(1) On further elaboration something incompatible would follow in a similar way as in Plato; cf. "Nothwendigkeit und Freiheit in der griechischen Philosophie" in the author's historische Beiträge zur Philosophie. II. p. 148 f.

[p. 120] Schelling does not draw this deterministic consequence from his conception of intelligible freedom; we draw it; and that we draw it rightly is proved by Schopenhauer. In him intelligible freedom, the theory of which had its ethical origin in Kant in opposition to determinism, turns over into determinism.

9. Schopenhauer's whole doctrine, whose principle is the will to existence, comes into play here, and we must weigh its fundamental points; he himself sums them up in these words:¹ the "kernel and chief point of my doctrine, its proper metaphysics," is the "paradoxical fundamental truth that what Kant opposed as the thing in itself to mere appearance, called more decisively by me representation, and held to be absolutely unknowable, that, I say, this thing in itself, this substrate of all appearances, and hence of the whole of nature, is nothing other than that which is immediately known and very familiar to us, which we find in the interior of our own self as will; that accordingly this will, far from being, as all previous philosophers assumed, inseparable from knowledge and even a mere result of it, is fundamentally different from and wholly independent of knowledge, which is entirely secondary and of later origin, and consequently can also exist and express itself without it, which is actually the case in the whole of nature from the animal downwards; indeed, that this will, as the sole thing in itself, the alone truly real, alone original and metaphysical, in a world where everything else is only appearance, i.e. mere representation, lends to every thing, whatever it may be, the force by virtue of which it can exist and act; that accordingly not only the voluntary actions [p. 121] of animal beings, but also the organic workings of their animated body, even its shape and constitution, further also the vegetation of plants, and finally even in the inorganic realm crystallisation and in general every original force that manifests itself in physical and chemical phenomena, indeed gravity itself, are in themselves and outside appearance, which merely means outside our head and its representation, directly identical with what we find in ourselves as will, of which will we have the most immediate and intimate acquaintance that is possible at all; that further the individual expressions of this will are set in motion in knowing, i.e. animal, beings by motives, but no less in the organic life of the animal and the plant by stimuli, and finally in the inorganic by mere causes in the narrowest sense of the word; which difference concerns merely the appearance; that, on the other hand, knowledge and its substrate, the intellect, is a phenomenon wholly different from the will, merely secondary, accompanying only the higher stages of the objectivation of the will, inessential to the will itself, dependent on its appearance in the animal organism, therefore physical, not metaphysical like the will itself; that consequently one can never infer from the absence of knowledge to the absence of will; rather, the will can be demonstrated in all the phenomena of nature devoid of knowledge, the vegetable as well as the inorganic; thus that will is not, as was hitherto assumed without exception, conditioned by knowledge, though knowledge is conditioned by will." If in this way the world is the objectivation or the image of the will, this view turns as follows for the ethical. Man is, like everything else in the world, a being decided once for all by his very constitution, which, like every other thing in nature, has its determinate, persistent properties, from which its reactions to an arising external occasion necessarily [p. 122] proceed, which accordingly bear their character, unalterable from this side, and consequently, in whatever in them may be modifiable, are wholly given over to determination by the occasions from outside. We must therefore seek freedom not, as the common view does, in the individual actions, but in the whole being and essence (existentia et essentia) of man himself, which must be thought as his free deed, which presents itself in a multiplicity and diversity of actions only for the faculty of knowledge bound up in time and space and causality, but which actions, precisely because of the original unity of what presents itself in them, must all bear exactly the same character and therefore appear strictly necessitated by the motives of the moment by which they are called forth and determined in particular. Accordingly, for the world of appearance the old scholastic proposition that acting follows being (operari sequitur esse) holds without exception. Every thing acts in accordance with its constitution, and its action, following upon causes, makes this constitution known. Every man acts according to what he is, and the action each time necessary accordingly is determined in the individual case solely by the motives. Freedom, which therefore cannot be met with in the operari, must lie in the esse. In it all the expressions of the man are already contained potentia, and they enter actu when external causes call them forth. The constitution that reveals itself therein is the empirical character, whereas its inner ultimate ground, inaccessible to experience, is the intelligible character, i.e. the essence in itself of this man. As a man is, so he must act. Natures are as they are; they are in their actions like the seal in a thousand impressions. In the given individual, in every given particular case, absolutely only *one* action is possible. Freedom belongs not to the empirical but solely to the intelligible character. The operari of a [p. 123] given man is necessarily determined from outside by the motives, from within by his character; hence everything he does occurs necessarily. But in his esse, there lies freedom. He could have been another; and in what he is lie guilt and merit. For everything he does follows from it as a mere corollary. One can correct the representations which present themselves to man as motives; but man always only applies his essence to them. The head is set right, but the heart is not bettered. One can thereby reshape action, but not the proper willing, to which alone moral worth belongs. One cannot change the goal toward which the will strives, but only the way it takes to it. Instruction can change the choice of means, but not that of the ultimate universal ends; these every will sets itself in accordance with its original nature. One can show the egoist that by giving up small advantages he will obtain greater ones; the malicious man, that causing the sufferings of others will bring greater ones upon himself. But egoism itself, malice itself, one will talk no one out of.¹

(1) Ueber den Willen in der Natur. Second ed. 1854. p. 2 f. cf. die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung. Third ed. 1859. I., especially p. 131 ff. Die beiden Grundprobleme der Ethik. Second ed. 1860. p. 132. p. 240. Ueber die vierfache Wurzel des Satzes vom zureichenden Grunde. Second ed. 1847. §. 42. §. 43.

We carry Schopenhauer's ethical view a few steps further, in order to be able to consider his solution of the problem before us in the connection of the whole.

In the closest connection with the above stands his explanation of conscience. "The moral responsibility of man concerns first and ostensibly what he does, but at bottom what he is, since, this being presupposed, his doing, upon the entry of the motives, could never have turned out otherwise [p. 124] than it has turned out. But however strict the necessity may be with which, given the character, the deeds are called forth by the motives, it will nevertheless never occur to anyone, not even to him who is convinced of this, to wish thereby to exculpate himself and to roll the guilt onto the motives; for he clearly recognises that here, as regards the matter and the occasions, and so objectively, an entirely different, even an opposite action was quite possible, indeed would have taken place, if only He had been another.
