It is apprehended in its relation to an other, a result of comparing thought (e.g. useful, dangerous, weight, acidity, elasticity, etc.). In the same way the subject has stepped out of immediacy. Hence the following forms develop.

1) In the singular judgment the individual as individual is a universal, e.g. this metal is heavy. 2) In this relation it is raised above its individuality. Insofar as this metal is heavy, it stands in relation to an other. This extension is an external one. The singular judgment runs: a this is a universal. But considered more closely, a this is not an essentially universal. Such an in-itself has a more universal existence than merely in a this. Hence the next form runs: not a this is a universal; therefore some individuals are a universal¹ – the form of the particular judgment. 3) In the particular judgment the this is extended to particularity. Some this is universal. But this generalisation is not commensurate with the this. The this is something perfectly determinate; [p. 297] but some this is indeterminate. The extension is supposed to belong to the this, and thus, corresponding to it, to be perfectly determinate; such an extension is totality, or first of all universality in general, a comprehension, a commonness, which belongs to the individuals only in comparison.¹ Or, according to another turn: some are the universal (in the particular judgment); thus particularity is extended to universality; or this universality, determined by the individuality of the subject, is allness. In this way the universal judgment arises.

(1) Logik III. p. 93.

c. The judgment of allness (the universal judgment) leads immediately to the judgment of necessity. Until then the predicate was determined as the universal being in itself over against its subject; according to its content it could be taken as an essential determination of relation or also as a mark. But the subject, developed into objective universality, ceases to be externally subsumed. What belongs to all the individuals of a genus belongs to the genus through its nature. This connection, being in and for itself, constitutes the basis of the judgment of necessity.

This is first 1) the categorical judgment, inasmuch as it contains in the predicate the substance or immanent nature of the subject, the concrete universal (the genus). Hence it is sharply distinguished from the qualitative judgment, which has only a contingent content. Compare the judgments: this ring is yellow (qualitative), it is gold (categorical). The copula therefore has in the categorical judgment the meaning of necessity, in the qualitative only that of abstractly immediate being. When 2) the objectively universal determines itself, posits itself into the judgment, the two sides, in accordance with the substantial difference, receive the shape of independent [p. 298] actuality, whose identity is therefore an inner one, so that the actuality of the one is at the same time not its own, but the being of the other. The essence remains identical with the determinateness repelled from it. Thus arises the hypothetical judgment (if A is, then B is). 3) These determinatenesses are immediate, but through the unity which constitutes their relation the particularity is also the totality of them. The concept is concretely identical with itself, so that its determinations have no subsistence for themselves, but are only particularities posited in it. Since in the self-externalisation of the concept the inner identity is posited, the universal is the genus, which is identical with itself in its excluding individuality, once as simple determinateness, the other time this very determinateness as developed into its difference, the particularity of the species.¹ Thus the disjunctive judgment is formed (A is either B or C).

(1) Logik III. p. 96.

(2) Encyklopaedie § 175.

(3) Logik III. p. 101. 102.

d. The copula of the judgment of necessity, the unity into which, in the disjunctive judgment, the extremes have gone together through their identity, is the concept itself. Hence the judgment of the concept has for its content totality in simple form, the universal with its complete determinateness.

1) First, the subject is a concrete individual in general. The predicate relates it to its concept, as to whether it agrees with it or not. Hence the predicates good, true, right, etc., e.g. this house is bad. Only such a judgment is assertoric. 2) The assertoric judgment lacks the concept as the unity which would relate the extremes (house, bad) to one another. Hence its warrant is only a subjective assurance. That something is good or bad, right, suitable or not, and so on, has its connection in an external third. This judgment is therefore only [p. 299] a subjective particularity, and the opposite assurance stands over against it with equal right, or rather wrong. It is therefore at once a problematic judgment. The house is good, according as it is constituted. But 3) the objective particularity posited in the subject of the judgment – its particularity as the constitution of its existence – expresses the subject according to the relation of that constitution to its determination, its genus (this – the immediate individuality – house – genus – so and so constituted – particularity – is good or bad). Thus this apodictic judgment is the fulfilment of the copula.²

(1) Logik III. p. 105.

In this way and in these forms the judgment, which is at first abandoned to chance, is supposed, according to Hegel's development, to condense itself out of indeterminateness into necessity and to fulfil itself into the concept.

What, then, has been achieved in this dialectical derivation?

First, something must be remarked about the names of the forms of judgment, which, however, at once touches the thing itself. The terms have remained the same as in the old logic. One believes one has the same thing, but for the most part has an entirely different one. This has already been mentioned of the infinite judgment; of others it must be specially remarked, in order to remove the ambiguity that follows from such arbitrariness.

Hegel leaves the positive judgment to the stage of contingent, immediate quality, and distinguishes from this qualitative judgment the categorical (properly the substantial) as a judgment of necessity, e.g. the ring is yellow (positive and qualitative), the ring is gold (categorical). Affirmation, for the expression of which the positive judgment served, was otherwise regarded only as *one* side of judgments; it combined as well with quantity as with relation and modality. With Hegel the positive judgment is relegated to [p. 300] the lowest stage of sensuous existence (the rose is red).

(1) Logik III. p. 113.

(2) ibid. p. 116 ff.

The categorical judgment¹ has been restricted to expressing the immanent nature, the kind, as the substance of the subject. According to previous usage the judgment "the ring is yellow" is just as much a categorical one as the judgment "the ring is gold." The new distinction has no full ground. If the judgment "the ring is gold" is called categorical, then in fairness its consequence too, "the ring is yellow," must fall under the same determination. Does not the immediate belong just as much to the immanent nature of the thing? The separation is arbitrary and therefore cancels itself in application. If one declares it a character of the qualitative judgment that its content of immediate existence has been picked up contingently, then such a subjective relation has no right in a doctrine that starts from the premise that things are the judgment. Such a subjective criterion is properly none; for a criterion must lie in the thing.

Assertoric, further, was the name for every judgment that claimed to correspond to an actuality. This view, which touches only *one* side of the judgment, fused with the quality, quantity and relation of the judgment. Hegel, however, makes the assertoric judgment into a peculiar, narrowly bounded kind, in that the mere assertion is supposed to have the value of a judicial verdict. Compare the judgments: the house is high (qualitative), the house is a dwelling (categorical), the house is bad (assertoric). Since here only in the last judgment is the thing measured by the concept, according to Hegel only this one is called assertoric. According to the old, well-grounded determination all three judgments are assertoric, [p. 301] without what they otherwise are being thereby impaired; they all assert something as actual. In accordance with the transformation just discussed, the problematic and the apodictic judgment too have received another sense. They are no longer referred to the possible or necessary combination of subject and predicate, as in this meaning they could otherwise unite, as closer determinations, with all the remaining forms of judgment. The problematic judgment is rather supposed, like the judgment of the concept in general, to pass sentence, only in such a way that it makes the verdict dependent on a third in which subject and predicate (house, good) have their connection: the house is good, according as it is constituted. The apodictic judgment has the same end, only it grounds the pronouncement in the particularity of the concept that forms the subject, so that now, in the last and completed kind of judgment, the three moments of the concept come forward and thereby pave the transition to the syllogism. How, then, does the essence of the old name relate to the new meanings? In the name of the problematic judgment the doubtful outcome of a disputed question is indicated, in the apodictic the necessity of proof. Assertion, question, proof extend over the whole domain of knowledge, and there is no right whatever to claim these names, stamped in the wider sense of modality, solely for the restricted use of a judgment passing sentence according to the concept. The stamp and content of these words have another value. Is language so poor, then, that one can take the designations of new concepts only from the unlawful spoils of well-grounded names? The other sciences watch more carefully that no confusion of language arise. Logic, which cannot, as the natural sciences perhaps can, at once find its bearings in the intuition of a fixed and finished object, philosophy, which must place everything in the inner and self-active generation of concepts and has in [p. 302] names its only external support, ought to hold the property of scientific language all the more sacred. Is it, then, by names that one should and will understand one another, or misunderstand?

(1) On the change of meaning from Aristotle to formal logic see on el. log. Arist. §. 8.

We ask further about the immanent necessity which the development claims. In linking the forms, the dialectic essentially ties the following knots.

It starts from the immediate and frees itself through mediation into the self-determined whole; it therefore begins with the judgment of contingent sensuous quality and completes itself in the apodictic judgment, which, directed to the whole of the concept, presents a necessary bond of subject and predicate. This course from the immediate and contingent to the self-determined and necessary whole, from the external to its own freedom, is the general progress of the dialectic whenever the concept of a thing develops in a determinate domain.

The immediate – a thoroughly logical word – conceals intuition, which the logic of pure thought cannot yet know, and lends the logical semblance where in fact perception is meant. The immediate has its logical content only in the negation of logical mediation. But if, in this determination of the dialectic, one presses for the affirmative concept, there at once emerges from the background of a presupposed mass of thought a representation which must otherwise be foreign to the logic of pure thinking. This is not a consequence foisted upon the dialectic, but comes clearly forward in tacitly inserted explanations. Thus it is said expressly: "The immediate judgment is the judgment of existence; the subject posited in a universality as its predicate, which is an immediate (hence sensuous) [p. 303] quality." Whence, then, the sensuous in a logical development which has promised to move, without presuppositions, only in thought freed from the sensuous? In the concept of the immediate, pushed forward here, lies, as in so many places, the illusion of the pure presuppositionless dialectic. Whoever calmly resolves it will find that it is only a negative concept ("not mediate"). But such a concept has support only insofar as it knows how to fuse with a foreign but solid mass.¹

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 172.

Let the starting-point, however, be granted, the unlogical but broad basis of the sensuous. The rose is red. The individual is universal. How does this first state of the matter lead further? Rather, it is said, such an immediate individual is not universal. The subject, immediately being for itself, is the opposite of abstract universality. Consequently the negative follows at once upon the positive as the higher truth. First it must be remarked that in the individual case no negative judgment arises in the way it is here derived in general. Otherwise from the judgment "the rose is red" the judgment "the rose is not red" would have to come forth. The negative judgment has its backing precisely in another, positive one. Insofar as one positive determination raises objection against another positive one that was tried, the negative judgment arises as the defence which the positive judgment performs.³ So the negative judgment is grounded in all the sciences. Compare only its extensive use in indirect proof, where a firm proposition or the concatenation of the whole repels an attempted positive assertion in a negative judgment. Because precisely a [p. 304] determinate generalisation is acknowledged (the rose is red), another must be negated (the rose is not white). If now no individual case of a negative judgment as it arises corresponds to the universal dialectical development, then the universal has thereby ceased to be, in the same sense in which number ceases when it no longer comprehends units under itself. The universal now only hovers, like a relationless process, high above the individual.

(1) Cf. above vol. I. p. 6S ff.

(2) In the Encyklopaedie §. 172, rather, the expression of this positive judgment runs: the individual is a particular. Whence this divergence of the Encyklopaedie from the Logik? The difference is remarkable, but without influence for our purpose.

(3) Cf. above, section XII, negation.

But we must follow the universal even into this height. The rose is red. The individual is universal. So runs the premise from which the opposite at once springs forth: the concrete is not abstract, the individual is not universal, therefore the rose is not red. But what does the comprehensive expression of the positive judgment mean: "the individual is universal"? The sense can be twofold. First, the individual is universal insofar as it develops activities, properties, which other individuals also develop. In this sense of the common the universal does not contradict the individual. In being active the thing steps out of isolation into the common world and must to that extent be universal. Secondly, the individual can also be called universal because the determination of the predicate goes back to that community of thinking and being which underlies the concept in general. In this sense too, that the individual is rooted in a thought concept, the universal does not contradict the individual. But at this stage of the immediate and sensuous this meaning will have to be set aside. On what, then, does the dialectical advance still rest? "The individual is universal. But the individual is not universal; more precisely, such an individual quality does not correspond to the concrete nature of the subject." The whole motion lies in an arbitrary change of representation. The individual has revealed itself according to the content of the positive judgment. We express it: the individual is [p. 305] universal. But at once the individual is drawn back into itself and the concept of the individual is forcibly shut up within itself, so that its revelation of the universal must now appear as a contradiction driving further. The stress betrays this interplay. First it is said: the individual is universal; then: but the individual is not universal. One should least of all expect such a contrived difficulty in the course of a development which started precisely from the premise that all things are a judgment, i.e. "individuals which are a universality within themselves."¹

The negative judgment intensifies itself into the negation of the judgment itself. In the identical judgment the relation of subject and predicate is empty, in the infinite absurd. Thus the judgment of existence falls apart; it has sublated itself, and the determinations of the judgment are reflected into themselves. Hence arise the judgments of reflection, the singular, particular, universal judgment.

This transition from the judgment of existence to the judgment of comprehension is peculiar. We know of no counterpart to it in the whole range of the rest of the dialectic. Elsewhere the third moment reconciles thesis and antithesis, and it can at least be understood in general how a new sphere of concepts is supposed to spring forth from this positive mediation. It can be conceived, for instance, how from becoming, which fuses being and not-being, existence is born. Elsewhere a living germ is always left behind in the third moment, which shoots up and ripens in the next concepts. Has this happened in our case? The identical judgment is hollow; the infinite has denied the sense of all judging. The previous cycle therefore does not close in the third moment, but "falls apart" in itself. Where is there here even the rudiment of a germ, even the beginning of a new start, even the possibility of a [p. 306] rebirth? On the ruins of the judgment of existence the judgment of reflection is supposed to rise. When it is said that the judgment of existence has sublated itself, this sublation is admittedly a "falling apart," so that here one can by no means, as is otherwise asserted, see in sublation something that still preserves. There is *one* thing more. In the natural life of concepts linking and loosening themselves, such infinite judgments as, e.g., spirit is not sour, is not a table, etc., occur as good as never. In ordinary thinking there would therefore be no transition from the judgment of existence to the judgment of reflection. The second form would sprout without roots. However, we are content. The original dialectic will not concern itself with the sauntering gait of vulgar thinking.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 167.

We grant this transition for the time being, although we do not understand it, and consider the further advance. The singular judgment runs: a this is a universal. But a this is not an existence commensurate with a universal. Hence rather not a this is a universal; and there arises the particular judgment: some thises are a universal. In this form too subject and predicate are still incommensurate. Particularity (some) therefore extends itself to universality – and indeed first to allness in the universal judgment. The dialectical impulse of this motion comes from the fact that the subject is not commensurate with the universal predicate of comprehension (useful, heavy, sour, elastic), and it aims at equalising the two. The heightened predicate of more universal relativity, in contrast to immediate quality, is indeed not grounded in what precedes, but we accept it without conceding it.

Does the advance, then, follow? In the individual case never. E.g. "this solution is acid" is a correct judgment. But not a this is universal. Therefore some solutions are acid. However, since now some (solutions) are the universal, particularity has extended itself to universality. [p. 307] Consequently all solutions are acid. As little as this argumentation is correct in this case, so little is it correct in any. What extension a judgment has must be carefully observed or proved from the nature of the individual thing, and cannot be settled by a universality hovering above it. Thus the conception refutes itself in application.

But the theory too falls apart in itself. The advance takes place in order that the external individualities which the subject presents may become equal to the universality of the predicate. Before this happens, subject and predicate are not commensurate. But it is only a semblance that the judgment of allness reaches this goal. The predicate always remains more universal and still comprehends various species under itself. If, e.g., one had gained as the end-point of the motion the judgment: all metals are heavy, usable, etc., the predicates nevertheless go far beyond the allness of this *one* genus.

With the words "Some are the universal; thus particularity is extended to universality"¹ the advance is introduced. What we remarked above, at the transition of the positive into the negative judgment, about the concept of the universal holds here too. "Some are universal" is the formula of the particular judgment; but the concept "universal" does not here have the meaning of number (some are all), nor can one admit the expression "some are the universal," a designation, as it seems, substituted for the sake of an easier transition. "Some this is universal." This extension into the particular judgment is supposed to contradict the this; for some is indeterminate, this determinate; hence the judgment must pass over into determinate allness in order to be commensurate with the this. This proof refutes itself. If "some thises," i.e. some substances, some things, contained a contradiction that wanted to be resolved, [p. 308] then it would also be a contradiction to count things. Moreover, the particular judgment for the most part designates nothing indeterminate, but a determinate part of the sphere, a species.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 175.

Numerical allness attests the essence of the kind. Hence the universal judgment passes over into a judgment of necessity, first into the categorical, which expresses the genus. But since the concept of the subject differentiates itself within itself without forfeiting its identity, since it therefore repels itself from itself into actuality, the hypothetical judgment arises. If in this self-externalisation of the concept the inner identity is posited, the universal is the genus, which is identical with itself in its excluding individuality. This third form, the disjunctive judgment, therefore gathers the differences of the second into the unity of the first.

This whole development has the greatest similarity with the development of substantiality, causality and reciprocity. But then similar misgivings remain as with Kant. If the disjunctive judgment were to present the unity of the hypothetical and the categorical, the concept, in repelling itself from itself in the hypothetical judgment, would have to generate species. For it is said expressly: "in this self-externalisation of the concept (which the hypothetical judgment contains) the inner identity posited," and the disjunctive judgment comes forth. One can at once form a hypothetical judgment from a disjunctive one, grounded on the exclusion of the species; but not, conversely, a disjunctive from a hypothetical. A is either B or C, therefore if A is B, it is not C. But from the proposition: if A is B, it is not C, that coordination of disjunct concepts standing on the same line does not follow; the proposition presents a much more universal relation.

The disjunctive judgment completes the striven-for equalisation of subject and predicate, in that once the universal as such, the other time the circle of its mutually [p. 309] exclusive particularisation, is posited. Hence there now appears the judgment of totality. In the assertoric, problematic and apodictic judgment the concept in its totality is the measure by which to pronounce whether the subject agrees with it or not. Since Hegel sought the concepts of the possible and the necessary purely in the thing,¹ he also had to place these forms differently from before.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 150.

We pass over the fact that such an apodictic judgment is properly already a formal syllogism, whereas it is supposed only to pave the transition to the syllogism.

*One* thing must be especially striking. According to the express declaration, the judgment is not to be taken in a subjective sense, as an operation and form occurring merely in self-conscious thinking. "Since this distinction is not yet present at all in the logical, the judgment is quite universal, and all things are a judgment." Accordingly the real judgment, which is the soul of things, ought to be unfolded. Whence, then, on this straight path, such side-leaps as the identical judgment, which has no content, the infinite judgment, which is absurd and therefore cannot be a judgment of the thing, and the problematic judgment, which is nevertheless literally designated as mere assurance, as subjective particularity? One may seek for the infinite judgment an actuality in the sphere of freedom (in crime); this hardly gives it a right to a place in the development of the forms of judgment of immediate, "hence sensuous," quality.

The fundamental defect of this whole derivation seems to lie in this, that the forms are not developed from their peculiar end and content, but are supposed to generate one another for themselves, as forms. It is not the content that is to form the form of the judgment, as content and form are otherwise one, [p. 310] but the earlier form is supposed to put the later out of itself, e.g. the positive judgment is supposed immediately to bring forth the negative, the particular the universal, and so on. A life is ascribed to mere forms which they nowhere have. Such a dialectic of the forms of judgment is not much better than if one were to arrange and present the organs of local motion, the instruments of swimming, flying, walking, creeping, in such a way that the one was supposed to spring from the other. One could, in comparing them, devise kinships and transitions. But the forms would nevertheless have another origin. They do not descend from one another in a progressive course, and one will comprehend them only by looking to the element for which they are destined, to the body which they are to move, and so on. Such organs, generated by the end of the content, are the judgments too, and in vain does one implant in dependent forms, with a violent fancy that is called dialectic, an independent development.

(1) Cf. above: the modal categories. vol. II. p. 219 ff.

(2) Encyklopaedie § 167.

(3) ibid. § 179.

(4) Rechtsphilosophie § 95.

Let one try, following the direction of the dialectical intermediate links, to raise any example from the lowest stage through the continuum of all the forms to the highest stage of the apodictic judgment. Let one keep strictly to the prescription of the dialectical turns of thought, so that, according to the indications, not only the universal form of the judgment changes, but likewise the content of the predicate rises from sensuous existence to concepts of reflection, from these to the substance of the thing, and finally to the judicial verdict of the concept. Were the general development correct, this attempt would have to succeed in the individual case. But why, then, has it nowhere been carried out? If one begins it, one soon feels the impossibility. Here the apparently tenable thoughts of transition collapse when one sets one's foot on them; there the connection is cut off from the outset. The whole difficult derivation offers the peculiar spectacle of a universal that comprehends no individual under itself.

[p. 311] In Hegel's exposition psychological elements cross the objective dialectic. If one wishes to pursue the psychological development, one will indeed see the judgments that rest on experience reach the stage of the concept from the stage of perception only by passing through reflection, but the positive as well as the negative, the singular as well as the particular, the categorical as well as the conjunctive. These three stages are the ones which present themselves predominantly in modality. But then the whole division will turn out otherwise than with Hegel, and one will be able to assign neither the positive and negative judgment to immediacy alone, nor the universal to reflection alone, nor the categorical and hypothetical to necessity alone, and one will be compelled to let fall the kinds which Hegel placed under the concept, in the sense in which he took them. The judgments of immediacy (unsuitably called judgments of quality), of reflection and of the concept thereby receive another meaning and their connection in the subjective mind: Hegel has, in his system of the judgment, welded together the logical and the psychological.

[p. 312]

## XVII. DIE BEGRÜNDUNG. — XVII. GROUNDING.

1. The individual judgment springs from the concept like a single ray. Since it represents a living activity, it excites other judgments in the measure in which one activity excites another. The judgment acts, like activity, generatively, groundingly, and on this side it itself cancels its isolation.

The judgment ripens as it passes through the modal stages. The problematic and the apodictic judgment, resting on conditions, already indicate in their form that they presuppose a grounding. The activity of the substance is excited and conditioned by an external cause; the judgment by an external ground.

Thus the judgment is given back into the grounding connection, and it seeks the higher whole in which it has its subsistence as a member.

The judgment becomes clear by isolating itself, but it becomes firm by linking itself into a chain.

2. Necessary grounding takes place from a universal, as became evident above; for only from the living universal, in which thinking and being touch and interpenetrate, does the necessary proceed.

Even the individual judgment which merely expresses the given [p. 313] fact as a result of perception already stands, in the midst of the individual, upon the universal, before it seeks any grounding at all. For the senses, which are the organ of the individual, behave universally, inasmuch as their power spans a whole domain of objects, and they themselves carry within them the element of motion through which they are accessible to universal thought. If the individual judgment of sense perception, which still carries within it the whole changeableness of the subjective, is to be verified, this takes place through means that are designed from the universal. The observational sciences, which establish individual judgments, have developed, out of a scepticism of exactness, a peculiar logic of the senses. Thus, for example, the knowledge of heat is not left to wavering feeling, but is referred to the thermometer or pyrometer. The decisive observation now falls not to the indeterminate vital feeling, but to the sharper sense of sight. The possibility of such a translation from the subjective into the objective stems from the thought of the universal. When the senses are armed in order to determine indeterminate perception, this takes place out of the universal. The microscope and the telescope are grounded on an insight into the universal nature of sight and of the ray of light. Science becomes so objective out of the universal that it makes even illusion its object, for example the double image of the single object in the double refraction of certain crystals. Time falls only within inner sense; but since it is the number of motion, the mind forces it, out of this universal thought, into the realm of outer observation, as happens in the ingenious clock, and so on. When in history or in the transmission of literature the individual wavers, criticism [p. 314] steps in with its universal judgment. In these few examples the fact of science sufficiently presents itself, that the verification of the individual judgment as individual rests on a universal. Subjective perception is objectified through the dexterity of universal thought. Thus the universal nature reveals itself in the individual. The universal in general does not let the individual go, but leads it back to itself.

(1) Cf. above vol. I. p. 241 ff.

If, now, grounding stems from the universal, whence, then, is the universal grounded?

An ultimate principle lies in the universal itself. We appeal to the whole preceding investigation of principles and of the ground. But for human knowledge something else must not be overlooked. Necessity includes within itself the universality of the actual. The necessary is universally actual. The power of the ground presents itself outwardly in the universal appearance, and this cannot be comprehended without that. If, therefore, the universal is an exclusive property of the necessary, one can infer back from the universal fact to the ground. In this case the universal flows from observation.

3. It has already been shown above that the universal [p. 315] as ground and as fact must be distinguished. According as the method has the one or the other for its goal or for its beginning, it will be different.

(1) See above section XIII. modal categories. vol. II. p. 201 ff. There the misunderstanding (Ueberweg's Logik. 1857. §. 101. p. 263 ff.) has already been forestalled, as though the universal of fact were meant to signify that it is, like facts otherwise, always drawn from experience. Kant extended the usage of the word (Kr. d. Urtheilskraft p. 451. 1st ed. 1790). The mathematical proposition that all plane triangles have the sum of their angles equal to two right angles expresses, although proved, a universal of fact (of the actual) just as much as the empirical one: all men are mortal. The mathematical proposition, in this its form, states only what is, and only as such a universal of the genus. In opposition to a universal which, together with others, creates as ground, it has been called, as a resting universal that merely states how all individuals of a genus behave in actuality, a universal of fact. In this connection the expression is meant to designate only that a universal is asserted as actual.

Induction sums up from the individual the fact of the universal; the syllogism infers from the fact of the universal the individual. The analytic procedure seeks from the given appearance the universal ground; the synthetic constructs from the universal ground the appearances as consequence.

4. Let the following serve provisionally to elucidate these four modes of grounding.

The opposition which in the first place governs the division, so that the path is taken now from the individual to the universal, now from the universal to the individual, is none other than the old opposition in which the highest difference of thinking and being has been more closely determined, and which, with slight alteration of the thought, is called now law and appearance, now content and extension, now concept and intuition. Grounding, which is to penetrate both, starts from the one and proceeds to the other, or conversely.

5. The analytic and the inductive procedure, which both start from the given appearance, do not simply coincide. While the analytic procedure takes the appearance apart or works it through in order to seize in the appearance the producing ground, induction leaves the individual as it is and merely gathers it together in what it has in common, in order to sketch the universality of the appearance. When, for example, empirical grammar collects the rule from individual cases (say, that ut, "in order that," governs the subjunctive), it proceeds inductively; but when it seeks the ground of this universal appearance (say, in the agreement of the concept of the conjunction and the concept of the mood, since both in the first instance designate the possibility of the thought), it proceeds analytically. [p. 316] Induction prepares analysis, since the universal fact is an expression of the necessary ground.

6. The logical value of induction is not to be discussed at length here. Certainly it cannot close itself off into a whole by itself, and it remains open to the chance of a contradicting experience, and its universality is therefore incomplete, properly nothing but the greater or smaller sum of the observed appearances. Certainly induction already presupposes a universal under whose guidance it stands and for whose ends it works; and it is therefore helpless by itself. But notwithstanding this it is of far-reaching significance. Though its result may not be absolutely grounded, it nevertheless grounds other judgments dependent on it, even if on no surer footing than it has itself. Its result is provisional, but it is a transition to a firm possession. External universality takes the place of the universality that is thought and seen through; and it so governs thinking that many remarkable inventions of experience rest upon it, while insight into the process follows only late upon the skilfully used fact. Induction is, as for example in statistics, the collector of experience, which sets research its task. The a priori sciences know no induction proper; where they employ it, a deduction, a synthetic procedure, is interwoven with it. But the [p. 317] empirical sciences owe to it the whole firm and full content of which they are proud.

(1) Cf. among others Heinrich Ritter Abriss der philosophischen Logik. 2nd ed. 1829. p. 102 ff. E. F. Apelt's Theorie der Induction 1854 is instructive through its examples from the history of the sciences, even if the presuppositions of the theory are doubtful on many points.

(2) Thus, for example, in the so-called complete induction of the binomial theorem. The completeness, which is foreign to the nature of induction, stems there from the universal law of the number series, and hence not from induction. Cf. Drobisch neue Darstellung der Logik. Second ed. p. 222 ff. Kästner on the geometrical axioms in Kästner's and Klügel's philosophisch-mathematische Abhandlungen. p. 57 f.

7. The syllogism is more than a mere inversion of induction, although it otherwise stands opposed to it in its direction. The difference lies in this, that the universal fact is indeed striven for by induction but never reached, whereas the syllogism must assert its major premise as absolutely universal if it does not wish to founder entirely. But is it then right to designate the basis of the syllogism as a mere universal fact? By this expression it is by no means meant that the fact from which the syllogism starts has merely been gathered up into a collective universality (see p. 314 note). A law is expressed which is there. Whence it stems remains undecided. To be sure, it will be the brief result of an inner grounding if it is to have the right to reach out over the individual; but for subsumption only the universal fact comes into consideration. In the syllogism, for example, that in all triangles, and hence also in the right-angled one, the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, the major premise, in all triangles the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, is expressed merely as a universal fact. Since, however, the law is derived from the genesis of the triangle itself, it has a quite different significance from the universal fact of induction. The latter rests on limited observation, the former on unlimited insight into the essence and becoming of the triangle. The next section is to treat of the syllogism in particular.

8. Syllogism and synthetic method agree in this, that they both start from the universal, and they are therefore very frequently declared to be the same mode of procedure. The difference, however, soon becomes evident if one distinguishes the universal as fact and as ground.¹ The former [p. 318] procedure has merely the power of an external subsumption, the latter the force of a progressively forming generation. The syllogism moves within the same genus; synthesis can generate new ones for thought. The syllogism contains in the universal law of the major premise the whole ground of the subsumption; synthesis at first brings forward only *one* condition, which it must combine with others in order to produce, as ground, something new. The major premise of the syllogism cannot be grounded on and on by a syllogism; otherwise we fall into an infinite series of prosyllogisms and episyllogisms and find a determinate hold nowhere. The first generating activity, which is certain in itself, precedes the resting, self-enclosed law of the major premise. The transition to the concept of a new genus, the activity which, according to an inner connection, carries the genera over into new shapes, lies beyond the syllogism, whose power is only formal, not real, like that of synthesis.

(1) See above section XIII. modal categories. vol. II. p. 201 ff.

When the syllogism is worked out: in all triangles the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, the right-angled triangle is a triangle, therefore in the right-angled triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, the universal acts only in its dominion over what is given and finished. When, on the other hand, the same proposition is applied to calculate the magnitude of the angle of a regular polygon, it acts productively (synthetically), in that it fuses with the original construction, conditioned by no syllogism, which divides the polygon into regular triangles and composes it again out of them. In the first case the procedure remains within the sphere of the same concept; in the other it generates something new. Geometry is famous for its strictly syllogistic proofs. It transforms the elements of space-generating motion into universal propositions and then gives every advance the appearance of a purely syllogistic subsumption. One easily notices, however, the [p. 319] synthetic determinations which run alongside the syllogism. Drobisch¹ has, for example, analysed in an instructive way the proof of the theorem that parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal to one another in area, and has resolved the intricate chain of syllogisms into its simple subordination. Syllogism follows upon syllogism. But the synthetic elements act through all the syllogisms; they are, first, the first principles of construction, then the division of the parallelogram into triangles and its composition out of the triangles, finally the superposition for the cognition of congruence, which rests on a free transference of the figure in indifferent space. The difference between the subordinating syllogism and generating synthesis can be shown in many examples. When the conditions of the similarity of triangles are applied to the smaller triangles which arise in the right-angled triangle through the perpendicular dropped from the vertex, the similarity of these among themselves and with the enclosing triangle proceeds purely through the syllogism. When, on the other hand, the same law of similarity is used in order to derive from it, with the help of proportions and equations and through substitution of equivalent values, trigonometrical formulae, and again by means of these to determine new triangles or to solve higher equations, or when the same law of similarity is used to prove on the cone the fundamental property of the parabola, that the abscissae are to one another as the squares of the corresponding ordinates, then the same universal acts as a member of a development; and in the individual cases it will be easy to find the construction or combination [p. 320] that intervenes creatively in the syllogisms. The further the object removes itself from the simple, a priori element of mathematical consideration, the more the determinations grow together empirically, the more the synthetic procedure outweighs the syllogism. Only try the syllogistic form when one wishes to comprehend an individual fact of history (and we certainly do comprehend it from the universal). In another way the end, which is universal in itself, acts not immediately syllogistically, but synthetically.

(1) Neue Darstellung der Logik, appendix. 2nd ed. 1851. p. 209 ff.

(2) If two triangles have equal angles with one another, the triangles are similar; the three triangles in question have equal angles among themselves; therefore they are similar.

Since the universal of the ground has its outward expression in the universal of fact, and the latter springs forth from the former as extension from content, the syllogistic procedure goes protectively alongside the synthetic as its outward exposition. From the broad base of the universal the thoughts taper to a point until with the point of the apex they reach the individual point that is to be grounded. The universal mind thereby itself becomes the matter. Thought is itself conscious of its strictness and therein, for itself, initially secure. But if it wishes to present what it has grasped to itself or to others, the binding, subordinating syllogisms serve to present visibly the invisible course of thought and to grasp the final point from the same breadth of the first universality. The individual glance of synthesis is related to the syllogistic unwinding as judgment by eye to the surveyor's chain. That immediate connection is, as it were, the community of thinking and being continued creatively from the principles, the deed of genius; but for its own certainty and for recognition by others it must submit itself to mediation. Only thus does the secure common possession of science arise.

9. The analytic and the synthetic procedure are, in the point from which they start and in the direction which they pursue, as clearly distinguished as oppositions in general. But the separation is more difficult if one observes them in their progress. Are they separated there too, [p. 321] and can they both, each alone by itself, the one without the other, continue their way and reach their goal?

The analytic procedure seeks from the given appearances the shaping ground; the synthetic designs the appearances from the ground it has grasped. We shall therefore have to regard as an analytic element what can be understood only from the appearance, as a synthetic element what can be understood only from the ground.

Mathematics, with methodical acumen, first distinguished analysis and synthesis and lent to the other sciences, for kindred relations, the names which in the first instance apply to the outer intuition of spatial magnitude. Arithmetic, which derives all the laws of the operations from the genesis of number through combination and is active out of the ground of the matter, is rightly designated as synthetic. Algebra behaves analytically in its direction, since it posits the equation as possible, like something given, and seeks its roots, that is, the grounds which satisfy the equation. Euclid's Elements, starting from the simplest grounds and advancing through construction to the developed figures, proceed synthetically, his Data analytically. The course of the empirical sciences is analytic, that of the speculative ones synthetic. Thus the relation presents itself in general if one has in view the beginning and the direction of these disciplines.

10. We first follow the analytic path, in order to see whether by itself it leads to the goal.

What compels the mind to go beyond the appearances? What gives it everywhere the direction toward the ground from which they derive? In fact a synthetic element reveals itself in the direction of the analytic. Only because [p. 322] the nature of the mind is itself creative, only because it produces appearances of a similar essence, does it seek the producing ground. Otherwise, as the animal grazes the meadow, it would calmly accept the present and seek nothing further.

(1) Cf., however, Hegel Logik III. p. 282, who restricts the meaning of the analytic to the identical and calls arithmetic, despite the laws which it generates with the matter itself, an analytic science.

Even perception itself, which does not passively receive what is given but re-creates in response to the stimulus received, might from one side be called synthetic; for the appearances are united into a whole. Observation is synthetic in its innermost nature; for it is observation only in so far as, guided by the universal, it is directed to what is essential. Perception would glide along as over the wide undifferentiated surface of the water, and nothing would stand out above it, if observation did not divine and pursue what is more essential in the matter. Analysis dissects the appearances; but in order to hit upon the members, it must guess their significance and in turn distinguish according to the essence. Thus the first step of the analytic procedure is already synthetic; for what is essential is measured only by the determinations of the ground.

If perception is to verify itself, it does so through universal considerations that are added to it. Illusion of the senses already induces the ordinary man to practise on a small scale what on a large scale science calls hypothesis. What meets the eye is confirmed or refuted through its harmony or disharmony with the whole of perception and with the other marks.

The given material of the senses is worked up in analysis and transformed into concepts. The contingent is stripped off; what remains and persists is grasped. That what is essential appears in the latter is a synthetic presupposition of the mind.

The analytic concept is completed only when it takes the ground up into itself. But the ground is grasped only when a possibility proves so fruitful that it is able to generate the [p. 323] appearances which form the task of analysis. The mind must provisionally exploit a point and, as it were, foresee its logical yield before it introduces it even as a problematic ground of the given appearances. This intervention of synthesis in analysis, or properly this supplementing of analysis by synthesis, appears most clearly where the ground runs out into an end, for example in the analysis of the organic. Since here the continuous connection of the efficient cause breaks off, which otherwise gives the appearance of an exclusive, solely active analysis, different directions must be linked into a unity of thought which can be accessible only to the mind that looks ahead.¹ Thus the analytic procedure ends with a synthetic moment.

If the ground is to verify itself, it must unfold synthetically on all sides and measure itself against the appearances which it is to satisfy. This final comparison is again analytic; but it is possible only after the completed process of synthesis. In hypothesis, which is peculiar to the analytic procedure, analysis and synthesis touch one another most intimately and strive to regulate and balance each other. Analysis, in proud possession of the facts, asks synthesis whether it is able to generate and exhaust them. Where the task of analysis is not yet reached by synthesis, the latter, with the preponderance of the intellectual ground, asks in turn, backwards, whether observation and dissection, and accordingly the task, have been correctly determined by analysis. Thus the two procedures sharpen each other.

It always remains the essence of the analytic procedure that it draws the firm line of the appearances and thereby affords fixed points to inquiry into grounds. What gives it value is not merely the external force of what exists and [p. 324] is actual; for such barriers the mind would break, but would not be willing to recognise. In the facts which the analytic procedure investigates, the re-creating synthesis beholds the signals by which it has to direct itself in its motions. The more securely the points of that line are determined, the more sharply can the line running through them be drawn, the more easily and certainly is the formula found which satisfies it and contains the generating ground.

(1) See above section IX. End.

The analytic sciences attest in detail what has just been presented in general. Analysis advances only with the help of synthesis; but synthesis is here always determined by the beginning and the direction of analysis.

In the analytic problem of geometry, what is required is provisionally sketched, and it is asked under what conditions such a sketch becomes possible out of what is given. The resolution of the sketch leads to the means of execution. The provisional construction, the discovery of the mutual relations, the linking with the means are synthetic elements in it. If the direction of equations is analytic, in that the roots (the possible grounds) are to be sought, then the operations for this end, and indeed not merely the application of foreign trigonometrical formulae but even the simplest transpositions and eliminations, are synthetic combinations. One detaches the terms one after another, to be sure, in order to isolate the value of the unknown; but the means of this analytic procedure are synthetic, taken from the universal law of the genesis of numbers.

Physics has become great through induction and analysis. But only mathematical synthesis completes its theories; and that its dissection ends in the most creative concept is proved by its results. When we hear, say in optics, that 458 billion vibrations of the ether in one second, and waves of which 37640 go to an inch, [p. 325] produce the sensation of a red colour, or indeed that 727 billion vibrations produce the extreme violet, no one will any longer divine in these enormous numbers the dissection of simple red or violet. And yet they have been calculated from the phenomena of interference. So they have been found by analysis? Rather, the presupposition of wave motion, and the appearance that is necessary if such waves should meet, form the synthesis of such an analysis. Astronomy, in the Copernican system, has inverted the appearances of analysis through the boldest synthesis. Physiology stands on analytic anatomy and on the sharp observation of the phenomena of life; but the ingenious construction of the living process out of the individual data, the organic interaction of the parts toward the whole, are its synthesis.

The experiment is peculiar to the natural sciences. Grown out of the mystical alchemy of the Middle Ages, it now serves as the most significant organ of lucid physics and is the mightiest vehicle of its progress. Bacon of Verulam demanded above all, for his induction and analysis, the service and the warrant of the experiment. Is the experiment still analytic? In the experiment a question is put to nature, and the outcome gives the answer. The end of the experiment is synthetic. The arrangement of the experiment is its proper soul, observation only its passive side. Hence the execution of the experiment is synthetic too.

Within this universal determination we can distinguish a twofold direction of the experiment. The experiment presents outwardly the essential directions of mental activity; it is either abstraction become external, in order to isolate the intertwined activities and to relate them, as in their essence, as it were to themselves (the experiments with the air pump may serve as an example), or it is combination become external, so that the isolated activities, in meeting with others, may reveal their [p. 326] hidden essence, as for example in the experiments of electromagnetism. The experiment is nothing other than the activity of the mind become objective, the mind which has the things carry out the abstraction or combination that it cannot carry through to the result by itself. In this respect one can say that in these kinds of experiments analysis and synthesis again present themselves. But just as abstraction is directed to what is essential, and to that extent is guided by an anticipating synthesis in order to reach its end, so too the analytic experiment is essentially synthetic. The question which the mind puts to nature, the means which it employs in order to compel nature to a pure answer, evidently stem from the divined or already known ground of things; they are synthetic.

There are sciences which admit of no experiment and whose object is accessible only to calm consideration. The more individual the object is, and the more, therefore, it realises its own thought, the less does it permit the intervention of an external arrangement. Consideration must investigate it as it is. But in these sciences too synthesis at once meets analysis. Grammar dissects the forms and finds through analytic comparison the transitions of sounds; its path is not purely analytic, but the analogy which it follows in the significance of the forms, the insight into the possibility of articulated sounds, into the linking of sound and concept, the understanding which always takes place from the whole, and so on, are synthetic elements with which it is equipped in the dissection of the appearances. In history, criticism proceeds analytically when it collects and compares the testimonies, but synthetically in deciding their value and determining the doubtful fact accordingly. Historical exposition may be called analytic so long as it follows chronology; but when it marks what is essential with stronger strokes, or even wishes to comprehend the ages out of the course of the whole, out of the natural elements of the [p. 327] geographical and the national, out of the development of what is human, it becomes synthetic. Matters stand in a similar way in the other sciences which, starting from the observation of the actual and working only for it, have in the first instance an analytic character.

Common to all the sciences is the indirect proof. As they seek the ground, various possibilities offer themselves. Only from the consequences of the possible grounds can it be recognised which agrees with the appearances and which does not. The struggle of hypotheses presents this side of the indirect proof on a large scale. The possibilities are exploited, and there appears therein even a synthesis of what does not take place, a synthesis of what is false for the question at hand, so that it may make itself known as impossible. This synthesis of the false must serve to limit the possibilities until they contract to the *one* actual ground.

Because the possibility of error lies close to the self-activity of synthesis, the analytic sciences would gladly confine all knowledge to bound observation. But despite this ban, the creative mind tacitly does the best in them. Synthesis, turned toward the whole and toward the ground, is the nobility of the sciences. But it is admittedly arbitrariness if it does not submit itself to the strict discipline of the analytic method.

11. The analytic method, accordingly, builds no science without the synthetic. We therefore ask further how the synthetic procedure fares without the analytic.

Pure thinking would be purely synthetic; since it would be imageless and without intuition, it would also not have a remnant of appearance which it could dissect. But in accordance with our investigations we have had to deny entirely such a pure thinking, for us human beings a non-entity. [p. 328] Rather, the first activity of thinking at once generates an intuition. Once it is generated, the fixed image acts back on the invisible thought, and in the analysis of the product synthesis has its verification. In this way the generating force flows back multiplied from the counter-image.

What results here from universal relations is confirmed in the factual state of the sciences. The geometry of Euclid is synthetic; for it knows by generating. It proceeds with the elements of the matter itself. But its proofs are in part analytic. It demonstrates, for example, the Pythagorean theorem by dividing up the constructed squares, hence by dissecting the appearance.

The synthetic procedure of the end is at the same time an analytic one, in that the means are found from the execution as thought. This analytic procedure appears most purely in the treatment of the geometrical problem, which is synthetic in its demand.

The most external appearance of synthesis is combination. Taken by itself alone, it becomes a contingent throwing together, and the glance matured in the dissection of the matter stands far higher than the formal completeness of the synthetic calculus of combinations, which some here and there wish to take as the basis of logic as the proper principle of thinking.

12. The yield of all these considerations is simple. The analytic and the synthetic procedure are determined only by the starting point and the direction; in execution the one demands the other. Analysis without synthesis remains on the surface of the appearances, in the infinity of the individual; synthesis without analysis remains in groundless thought. In grounding, analysis draws the firm boundaries; synthesis gives the motion within them.

[p. 329] Thus the mind acts wholly in every single direction and in every part of its activity; it invents while it dissects, and dissects when it invents. "Analysis and synthesis, both together like breathing out and breathing in, make the life of science."

13. In agreement with the preceding considerations, we attempt in addition a survey in the following way.

If in knowing thinking and what is at first stand opposed to one another, then what is is an activity from itself, and thinking an activity after it. Such an activity as the latter is possible only in that what is, as activity, is connected with activities of whose causality we have consciousness. Our own conscious causality opens up to us the causality of others, conscious and unconscious.

This conscious causality we exercise, first through constructive motion, purely and determined only through itself, in the mathematical domain, and pure mathematics is an expansion of this conscious causality and of its great consequence in all knowledge. With similar power a conscious causality recurs in the ethical domain and, from our own conscious end, casts a light backwards on the blind end in nature. In the end that first relation is reversed, and thinking is now the activity from itself which what is must follow. Only in a conditioned sense and in part by detours do we have consciousness of causality in the domain of material forces. We ourselves are, in the great causal connection of the world, effect and cause at once, and exercise certain effects with consciousness, for example when the hand presses. From these few, with the help of observation, of experiment and of the mathematical element, knowledge spreads with ever greater sharpness and in ever greater [p. 330] extent. Thus the ground of all science is set upon consciousness and self-activity.

(1) Goethe Werke vol. 50. (1833) p. 198.

Universality springs from this source. Since we are conscious of causal activity, we are able to measure and to delimit its validity. The contact between constructive (causal) and subsuming (inferring) thinking becomes evident in this consideration.

[p. 331]

## XVIII. DER SCHLUSS. — XVIII. THE SYLLOGISM.

1. Syllogisms are distinguished into mediate and immediate. The latter need no new concept in order to produce a new judgment from a judgment, but ground another judgment from the mere form of one judgment. In this way no properly new content of the judgment is gained, but only a more determinate relation for a given purpose. The only question here is what is expressed together with the judgment that has been passed.

Formal logic, which is entirely in its place in this question, since what matters here is the exploitation of the form, brings together several modes of such immediate inferences: subalternation, opposition, equipollence, conversion and contraposition. If one asks about the means, the consideration is confined to two simple points of view: to the relation of the more universal to the particular, and to the nature of negation.

On the relation of the more universal to the particular rests subalternation, in that the degree of the quantity of the subject is taken into account, and conversion, in that the extension of subject and predicate is weighed in order to determine their reciprocal relation.

[p. 332] On the nature of negation rests opposition, in that it is weighed how far the determinations of contradictory, contrary and subcontrary judgments depend on one another, and equipollence, in that an equivalent negative expression is put in place of the positive, and conversely.

Finally, on both points of view together rests contraposition, in that a negation is taken up into the conversion.

If the immediate inferences — with the exception of the transformation of the disjunctive judgment into a hypothetical one with a negative antecedent or consequent, which follows from the relation of extension to content — come back to the two concepts of the universal and of negation as the sole determining ones, then this progression confirms the exposition of the judgment, since, as we saw, these same concepts alone condition the development of the judgment.

We pass over the sufficiently explored particulars which would have to be considered in the immediate inferences, and refer to Twesten's logic, which discusses them most exactly.¹

Conversion is the most important of these relations and finds its application, for example, in the converse propositions of the geometrical system. Yet the consideration of the form of the judgment, on which the doctrine of conversion is grounded, proves to be an insufficient ground except in the universal negative judgment, and formal logic does not suffice for this task either.

Universal affirmative judgments, it is shown, can be converted only with limitation of the quantity (per accidens). From the form of the judgment no more can be inferred. But in point of the matter itself the most significant exception is found. For if the predicate belongs to the subject [p. 333] peculiarly and exclusively, then unlimited conversion is certainly admissible, and is precisely a sign of the indissoluble connection of subject and predicate.¹ But only the content decides this, and the form determines nothing about this relation. Hence the geometer proves the so-called converse propositions with strict exactness, and through the conversion separates the specific difference of a concept and its consequences from the mass of what the concept has in common with others. Thus conversion gives some theorems significance before others and interrupts their uniform series by a noticeable elevation. The convertible theorems, expressing the exclusive peculiarity of a concept, are throughout the fruitful ones for the further development of the science. But what would happen if one stopped at the rule of formal logic, to convert the universal affirmative judgment only per accidens? An example may give us the answer. The Pythagorean theorem states that all right-angled triangles have a side whose square is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides. According to the prescription of conversion this judgment would take the shape: some triangles in which the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides are right-angled. Formal logic is right when it cautiously teaches that no more follows from the form; but here too little follows.

(1) Die Logik, insbesondere die Analytik. 1825. §. 77 ff.

(1) It is an external proof that the property is specific. Cf. Aristot. analyt. prior. I. 27. 28. II. 23., and indeed in the last passage unlimited conversion is the condition and mark of a complete induction.

The particular affirmative judgment can, according to the logical rule, be converted simply. Certainly. But there is nevertheless a great difference here whether the predicate expresses a mere accident or the substantial species of the subject. An example of the latter case is the proposition: some [p. 334] parallelograms are squares; an example of the former the proposition: some parallelograms serve as mechanical instruments. Here one will approve the conversion: some mechanical instruments form parallelograms; but hardly the conversion carried out by the same prescription: some squares are parallelograms; for obviously all are. The result of logical conversion says too little, and logic, which means to be a canon against what is false, itself produces the semblance of error. The grammatical expression does not distinguish what logical consideration ought to distinguish. Since formal logic has no other support than the grammatical expression, it takes up into itself the whole indeterminacy of that expression. The essence of the difference in question can be made intuitive by the schema of one circle enclosed by another and of two intersecting circles. Let the whole surrounding circle be called a, the enclosed one b. Or let one of the intersecting circles be called a, the other b. Fig. 1 represents the case in which the predicate designates the essential species of the subject, e.g. some parallelograms are squares; Fig. 2, on the other hand, the case in which the predicate states a specific difference or an external determination of the subject, e.g. some parallelograms are right-angled; some parallelograms serve as mechanical instruments. In this last figure it lies before one's eyes that a part of the one circle always includes one part of the other and excludes the other part. The determination "some" therefore has its full sense forwards and backwards, wherever the predicate may stand. But in the first case, although only a part of the larger circle coincides with the enclosed one (some a are b), the smaller always falls wholly within the larger (all b are a). Hence only an expanding conversion (the opposite of the limiting one per accidens) would satisfy the [p. 335] truth; the conversion which the logical rule demands (some b are a) throws a false light on the matter, as though only some b were a.

The universal negative judgment is converted simply; for since the concepts of subject and predicate have nothing in common with each other and fall entirely outside each other, they always repel each other, whichever of the two concepts one chooses as subject. Hence the conversion of a negative proposition does not first need to be proved.

The particular negative judgment, it is finally shown, cannot be converted; but notwithstanding this it holds true when converted if the predicate does not compare the narrower and subordinate concept with the wider concept of the subject, but contains only an accident. For example, the proposition "some parallelograms are not squares" cannot be converted, for all squares are parallelograms. The first figure above represents this intuitively. A part of the circle a (the ring) is not the circle b; but the whole circle b falls within a. The judgments "some parallelograms have no right angles" and "some parallelograms do not serve as mechanical instruments", however, can be turned round. Some right-angled figures are not parallelograms, e.g. the right-angled triangle. Some mechanical instruments do not form a parallelogram. In the second figure above it is clearly shown that parts of the two circles always mutually exclude each other, and that therefore, however one may relate these parts to each other, particular negative judgments must be formed.

Thus, then, with the exception of the universal negative judgment, the whole doctrine of conversion becomes doubtful. Conversion with limitation of quantity (per accidens) is a makeshift and in essential cases gives too little, and thereby, strictly speaking, something incorrect.

The natural origin of the judgment is always turned upside down in conversion; for the concept of the [p. 336] subject does not produce the predicate from within; rather, one experiments with the form.

If in the predicate of the original judgment an accident is asserted, which in itself is no substance and therefore also cannot become a concept, as the subject requires, then in conversion the accident is tacitly raised to a substance, and therein lies a surreptitious assumption which must be well heeded. For example: all triangles have the sum of their angles equal to two right angles. According to the rule of conversion this proposition will run: something that has the sum of its angles equal to two right angles is a triangle. Apart from the defect (something, etc.), one tacitly adds in thought: some figures. If one wishes to say that this subject lies necessarily in the concept "having an angle-sum", then one enters upon a development which is foreign to the formal consideration of conversion. The concept of substance is arbitrarily borrowed from the subject that is to be converted.

Thus conversion, apart from that case of the universal negative judgment, appears only as a trick of formal logic. And if one does wish to convert a judgment, one has to consider the content and not the form. Otherwise one obtains only a blunted, not a sharp, judgment of the matter.¹

Contraposition (A is B; no A is a not-B; the not-B is not A) might seem to be an application of the infinite judgment rejected [p. 337] above; the ὄνομα ἀόριστον of Aristotle would even stand in the subject. But considered more closely, the transformation takes place only through a negative judgment.

(1) Acute representatives of formal logic have well recognised the limitations and ambiguities of conversion set out above. Cf. e.g. Drobisch §. 71 ff. in the 2nd ed. We part company only in the view formed from them. They hold the consideration to be significant that no more follows from the universal form of the judgment, even if the content of the concepts should yield more. We believe we see in the insufficiency of the whole result an indication that the whole standpoint of the science, on which the form is detached from the content, is insufficient. The undertaking of conversion is altogether violent. Cf. Friedrich Fischer Lehrbuch der Logik für akademische Vorlesungen und Gymnasialvorträge. 1838. p. 108.

2. Sir William Hamilton, under the name of the "quantification of the predicate", has devised a new theory for conversion and carried it through into syllogistic.¹ Since he considers the extension of the predicate as well as of the subject, and regards the judgment in its logical significance as an equation of the two, he demands that the extension of the subject be thought strictly in relation to the predicate, and that both be stated as equal in the affirmative judgment and as unequal in the negative. If the quantity of the predicate is stated, there is, he holds, only a conversio simplex. It will suffice to make this doctrine intuitive in the most important case, the universal affirmative judgment. Compare the examples: all men are imperfect, and all men are responsible. In the former we think only a part of the extension of the predicate; for besides man there are other imperfect beings. In the second example we think the whole extension of the predicate; for besides man we know of no responsible beings. The former example represents the equation: "all men are some imperfect beings"; the latter the equation "all men are all responsible beings". As this is thought implicite in those judgments, so, he holds, it must be [p. 338] expressed explicite. Through this quantification of the predicate conversion becomes a simple interchange of subject and predicate, the ground for which lies in the equation.

(1) "New analytic of logical forms" 1846 as an appendix to Reid's works, then in Sir William Hamilton's lectures on logic 1860 vol. II appendix. p. 249 ff. in the discussions 1852. p. 614 ff. cf. William Thomson's an outline of the necessary laws of thought 1853. p. 177 ff. William Spalding an introduction to logical science 1857. p. 83 ff. cf., as a counter-treatise from the mathematical standpoint, De Morgan on the symbols of logic, the theory of the syllogism 1850 in the Transactions of the Cambridge philosophical society vol. IX. 1856, further the Athenaeum Nov. 1860. p. 705, and some critical remarks in Charles Waddington essais de logique. Paris 1857. p. 117 ff.

Against this theory essential objections arise. The judgment is psychologically no equation and has no tendency at all to be an equation. The mathematical invention of an equation and the natural formation of a judgment lie far apart. The judgment of content (the categorical judgment) does not aim at comparing the extension of two concepts (subject and predicate). It is, as has been shown, the counter-image of something real that stimulates thought. What the thing does, that the judgment means to assert of the subject. Whether the thing or its kind (all) alone among all others does this, or others do it too — whether, therefore, the subject is exclusively the predicate or not — is a further investigation of knowledge, but is not thought along with it in the judgment at all. It does not lie implicite in it at all, so that explicite it could take, e.g., the form "all men are some imperfect beings, or all men are all responsible beings". The forced, artificial, scarcely intelligible form of these propositions shows clearly that natural thought has not clothed itself in it. What language can scarcely express, the mind has also not thought in the simple form of the judgment. Psychology and grammar alike contradict this conception of the judgment.

To the judgment: all men are imperfect, the judgment: all men are some imperfect beings, does not correspond. For this contorted form has welded two judgments into *one* expression, namely the judgment: all men are imperfect, and other beings besides men are imperfect too. To the other example: all men are responsible, the judgment: all men are all responsible beings, corresponds just as little; for [p. 339] this expression forces two judgments into *one* form, the judgment: all men are responsible; and besides men no beings are responsible. In the former case a judgment of experience is added, in the latter a judgment of exclusive knowledge. The right of exclusion is grounded in the specific nature of man, his moral essence. One sees, then, that in that so-called quantification of the predicate one takes out of the judgment what the thought did not put into it.

It is the peculiarity of conversion to be an immediate inference, i.e. to ground a new judgment from what follows from the mere form of a judgment (from the signs of quantity, quality, modality). But whether a judgment, to use Hamilton's expression, is a toto-total one (all men are all responsible beings) or a toto-partial one (all men are some imperfect beings, all men are some mortals), cannot be seen at all from the identical form (all men are responsible, all men are imperfect). It may be that it is easily determined how the extension of the subject is related to the extension of the predicate; but in the most important cases a deeper investigation, a concatenated proof, is required. Whoever, for example, learns the proposition that in a plane triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles, or whoever first grasps the Pythagorean theorem, does not yet know at all whether the judgments in which these propositions are presented are toto-total or toto-partial; he knows it only when the converse propositions have been proved.
