Consequently he has not at all thought implicite what is expressed explicite in that quantification of the predicate. The mathematician proves the converse propositions, and only now can he state that the predicate belongs exclusively to the subject (thus, in Hamilton's language, that the judgment is a toto-total one). Whoever therefore already knows this distinction no longer needs conversion and has long since gone beyond the immediate inference, which [p. 340] concerns solely the form of the judgment. In short, this theory of conversion contradicts formal logic, on whose ground all conversion keeps.

And yet it is precisely the author of this "quantification of the predicate" who appeals to the formal.¹ It is not to be denied that it belongs to the formal element of the judgment, and that on this foundation one can build a formal system, as its acute inventor did. But this formal system is of a peculiar kind. Taken by itself the distinction is formal, but one arrives at it only through knowledge of the matter, and in the most important cases only by a path which presupposes the application of the whole of syllogistic. The system is formal as long as it calculates in the abstract notation of the equation. For if a judgment is toto-total, it can be converted simply. But in order to apply the system one must go far beyond the form of the judgment. Whether the judgment is toto-total cannot be recognised from the form. The point of view of the whole doctrine is therefore unsuitable, and a falling away from the formal consideration. If it is applied to syllogistic, an artificially contrived substitution takes the place of natural subsumption.

Sir William Hamilton gives his theory the heading: new analytic of logical forms, and to that extent offers it as a correction or completion of the Aristotelian Analytics. Is this name justified? Analytic seeks to resolve the composite operations of thinking, e.g. the syllogism, into the simple constituents that ground them, and to comprehend them from these. But the new analytic does not resolve; it composes; it forces two judgments into one, e.g. man is responsible and besides him no other being, into the form: all men are all [p. 341] responsible beings. It does not ground the composite through the simple, but grounds through what is more composite. To that extent the new analytic does not correspond to the sense of its name.

(1) Sir William Hamilton lectures on logic. vol. II. appendix. p. 289 ff.

3. From the immediate inferences are distinguished the mediate ones, which take place through the intermediate link of a concept of their own. They form the syllogism in the narrower sense.

Aristotle examined the forms of syllogisms with admirable acuteness. What he had sketched, commentators and scholastics spun out into the fine and the small. Kant censured the false subtlety of the syllogistic figures, and, while asserting the basic features of the principal form (the first figure), he rejected the "useless lumber" of the others in order to make room for things more worth knowing. The trump that Kant played on this did no good. Hegel, on the contrary, declared the syllogism to be the absolute form of everything rational. Everything rational, he asserts, is a syllogism, e.g. the planetary system, the state, God himself, and these present a firm living whole by virtue of the fact that the three figures of the syllogism interpenetrate in them. In this state of affairs it is necessary to enter more closely into some essential points.

4. According to Aristotle, the subordination of concepts underlies the syllogism as its common principle, which comes out most clearly in the first figure. Because the concept C (terminus minor) stands under the concept B (terminus medius), and B under the concept A (terminus maior), C stands under A.

All B are A.

All C are B.

Therefore all C are A.

(1) In the cogent essay on the false subtlety of the four syllogistic figures, written as early as 1762, see Kant's Werke. ed. Rosenkranz I. p. 55 ff.

[p. 342] Three circles, of which the outer encloses the middle one and the middle one the innermost, represent this relation pictorially. Since Aristotle reduced the cases of the other figures to the first, they too follow the law of subordination. In general he drew up three figures, according as the terminus medius occupies the middle place in the series of subordinated concepts (first figure), or the highest (second figure), or forms the lowest concept (third figure). On this view of the subordination of the three concepts necessary to a syllogism, three figures result. When later four figures were counted, one followed another principle of division, namely the possibility of the different positions which the middle concept can have in the two premisses. Aristotle looked to the inner relation of the three terms occurring in the syllogism; later one considered externally whether the middle concept holds the place of subject or of predicate in the two premisses.

Four figures of the syllogism are drawn up according to the following schema, in which M is understood as the middle concept, S as the subject and P as the predicate of the conclusion.

1. M. P. / S. M. / S. P. — 2. P. M. / S. M. / S. P. — 3. M. P. / M. S. / S. P. — 4. P. M. / M. S. / S. P.

If one wishes to keep these designations, the three Aristotelian figures are to be determined as follows:

1. P. M. S. 2. M. P. S. 3. P. S. M.

Here, however, the transposition of P and S must be permitted. Otherwise, on the Aristotelian principle, six figures of the syllogism would arise. The designation of the premisses by the subject and predicate of the conclusion also contains, properly speaking, a hysteron proteron. For the conclusion first proceeds from the premisses, and not conversely; and one orders what is earlier (the premisses) according to what is later (the conclusion), of which one properly as yet knows nothing, and which in [p. 343] natural thinking only follows. One must already deliberately abandon the simple progress of thought and dissolve the interlacing judgments into bare concepts, in order to put the question for the syllogism, say, thus: what formal conditions must be fulfilled in order to attribute to a concept (S) as subject another concept (P) as predicate, or to deny it of it, through the mediation of some third concept (M) which already stands in a determinate relation to both? Then one does not follow the free pull of the indication given in the premisses for the production of a new judgment, but already knows, as it were, what is to come about, or asks, testing, after the warrant of what has come about. The disadvantage of such an arbitrary fixing will show itself further below.

That Aristotle held fast to this inner principle of the subordination of concepts in the division is very clearly evident from the definition of the individual figures, and especially from the reduction of the second and third to the first, in which subordination presents itself most clearly. Only in a later passage, where he takes the three figures together and compares them, is the other view found, since he there derives these same figures from the different ways in which the three concepts can be predicated of one another.

But even in this passage Aristotle has left no considerable gap. "If the middle concept is the concept which is both itself affirmatively predicated and has something affirmatively predicated of it, or which is both itself affirmatively predicated and has something denied of it, then the first figure is present; but if it is both affirmatively predicated of something else and denied of it, the second; but if different things are affirmatively predicated of it, or partly denied of it, partly affirmatively predicated, the third."

(1) Analyt. priora I. 4. 5. 6.

(2) Analyt. pr. I. 32. p. 47a 39.

[p. 344] In the wording of this passage the later fourth figure falls under the definition of the first; for in the fourth figure too the same concept is once predicate ("it is affirmatively predicated"), once subject ("something is affirmed or denied of it"). Only two cases of the fourth figure escape the definition of the first figure given in the words cited, namely fesapo and fresison, since in their premisses the mediating concept is not affirmatively predicated (forms no affirmative predicate). But precisely these cases suffer from particular defects.

If we bring the forms of the fourth figure under the first, it must not be overlooked that Aristotle leaves the order of the premisses free. In the more recent view this order is bound, in that the concept which becomes subject in the conclusion is always assigned to the minor premiss. This arrangement, however, is, as was remarked, an arbitrary contrivance and an inversion of the natural relations, since the conclusion that follows from the premisses cannot react in any determination upon its grounds (the premisses).¹

If we follow this hint and let the premisses freely interchange with one another, the syllogism becomes more significant than it otherwise is according to the formulas of the fourth figure.

One need only consider the familiar rules of this whole group. 1. Calemes, after transposition of the premisses, concludes in celarent. If one wishes to insist that the conclusion [p. 345] receive as its subject the concept which the minor premiss had in the arrangement of the fourth figure, then the unlimited conversion of the universal negative conclusion easily helps out. Free thought breaks through such contrived obstacles of its own accord. An example of premisses in calemes runs, say: All squares are parallelograms. No parallelogram has converging opposite sides. Obviously the natural conclusion will be: No square has converging opposite sides. But the technical obstinacy of formal logic forms the clumsy conclusion: Nothing that has converging opposite sides is a square. 2. Bamalip, after transposition of the premisses, concludes in barbara. Then the yield for knowledge is more significant than in the particular affirmative conclusion which the formula calculates out merely in order to bring the subject of the minor premiss back as subject into the conclusion. For example: all triangles in which the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides are right-angled triangles. All right-angled triangles are so constituted that a semicircle can be drawn about them. The natural conclusion would run: All triangles in which the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides are so constituted that a semicircle can be drawn through their vertices. But formal logic brings to light only the indeterminate judgment: Something about which a semicircle can be drawn has that Pythagorean property. If with the representation "something" one stays within the triangle, as the predicate requires, which presupposes a three-sided plane figure, then too little is asserted. 3. Dimatis, after transposition of the premisses, concludes in darii. For example: some parallelograms are squares; all squares have four equal sides and four equal angles. The syllogism, put into the first figure, will yield: some parallelograms have four equal sides and four equal angles. According to dimatis there results what proceeds from the conversion of the conclusion just [p. 346] obtained: Something that has four equal sides and four equal angles is a parallelogram. Here again the old ambiguity arising through conversion prevails; for not some, but all plane figures that have four equal sides and four equal angles are parallelograms.

(1) Against the above view of Aristotle's system of the figures of the syllogism Ueberweg, System der Logik und Geschichte der logischen Lehren 1857. §. 103. p. 273 ff., has raised objections. His own conception is not free of difficulties, some of which he himself points out. It will be necessary to return to this point elsewhere in a special investigation, which for the present purpose would bring with it too much Aristotelian detail. Cf. meanwhile Christ. Aug. Brandis Geschichte der griechisch-römischen Philosophie II. 2. a. p. 184. III. 1. p. 23. Prantl Geschichte der Logik I. 271 f. Zeller Philosophie der Griechen II. 2. 1862. p. 164.

Fesapo and fresison can indeed be reduced to the first figure by the guidance of the characteristic letters; but they do not fall under the designation of the first figure that is given in the above passage of Aristotle. Fesapo and fresison both have an adversative direction and are therefore much more easily reduced, through conversion of the minor premiss, to festino of the second figure than, through the double conversion of both premisses, to ferio of the first figure. But to them too, as to the cases in bamalip and dimatis, there clings the whole ambiguity that was censured in the doctrine of conversion. It is therefore a question whether Aristotle would acknowledge them, although in the third figure he presents moods that are not much better.

Thus of all 5 moods of the fourth figure only calemes stands the test; but it coincides completely with celarent of the first figure. The moods bamalip and dimatis have become ambiguous without need, because they have squeezed themselves into the stiff garment of the fourth figure. If, in agreement with that passage of Aristotle, they are given back to the first figure, they are sound forms.

The whole fourth figure is accordingly an artificial and doubtful construction, and Aristotle's view proves to be the more correct.

The derivation of the syllogism from subordination, attempted and carried through by Aristotle, flattened out into the so-called dictum de omni et nullo, in which there is no longer [p. 347] thinking but only counting;¹ and the view was put forward that the syllogism is properly nothing but an extended subalternation. Subordination moves solely within the extension of concepts. This view, however, when examined more closely, does not suffice.

(1) Quidquid de omnibus valet, valet etiam de quibusdam et singulis; quidquid de nullo valet, nec de quibusdam et singulis valet.

If in the principal mood of the first figure the major premiss expresses the exclusively peculiar mark or the exhaustive law of the middle concept, and the minor premiss subjects the species contained under the middle concept to the property or the law — a case which presents the syllogism in its full power — then there is properly no complete series of subordination; for in this case the predicate of the major premiss is neither wider nor narrower than the subject, but covers it.¹ Then it is not the middle concept that is subordinated to the higher, but only, one-sidedly, the lower to the middle. If, further, one of the premisses is negative, one of the terms is posited simply outside the others, and the relation of subordination ceases. Hence already in the second figure, which concludes only negatively, there can no longer strictly be talk of a complete series of subordination; and that in the second figure the middle concept is the highest is more an assumption by analogy, since as a rule the predicate is more universal than the subject, than strictly true, since the negation, which must lie in one of the premisses of the second figure and mostly even lies there in simply universal form, tears apart the bond of subordination. Obviously, therefore, the syllogism cannot be comprehended from the relations of extension [p. 348] alone. A similar objection arises in those moods of the first and third figures which have a negative premiss.

(1) Let the major premiss be, for example: in every right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides; further, the minor premiss: every triangle in a semicircle is right-angled; then this last is indeed subordinated to the universality; but the subordination goes no further; the extension of the terminus maior is rather equal and similar to the extension of the medius, since it expresses a relation that obtains only in the right-angled triangle and always in it.

Kant, in the process of the syllogism, grasped precisely the opposite view, the view of content. For him the first and universal rule of all affirmative syllogisms is: a mark of a mark is a mark of the thing itself; of all negative ones: what contradicts the mark of a thing contradicts the thing itself.¹ Since content determines extension and extension develops out of content, this view of Kant's comes nearer to what is original. Those difficulties which arise when one asserts extension alone do not come up here at all. Nevertheless it may be striking in this formula that the genus sinks to a mere mark of the thing and subsumption is translated into a relation of content.²

Perhaps the nature of the syllogism can be presented more simply and brought into closer agreement with the development of the concept and the judgment. The syllogism, namely, proceeds from the mutual relation of the content and the extension of concepts. If the content (the positive or negative law) of a concept is applied to its extension, the categorical syllogism arises. The content (terminus maior) of a concept (medius) governs its extension (the species, terminus minor). If, conversely, the same law of all the species is expressed, and from this content of the extension the content of the comprehending universal is drawn [p. 349] together, the disjunctive syllogism arises. The species form the middle concept, whose content becomes the content of the genus.

(1) Von der falschen Spitzfindigkeit der vier syllogistischen Figuren. Werke. I. p. 59 f. Nota notae est etiam nota rei ipsius; repugnans notae repugnat rei ipsi.

(2) For Herbart's peculiar treatment, which hangs together consistently with his view of the judgment, see the Hauptpunkte der Metaphysik. 1808. p. 120. Einleitung §. 64.

Examples readily elucidate what has been said. The essence of the categorical syllogism becomes clearest in universal affirmative judgments. For example: all parallelograms are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles. The square is a parallelogram. Therefore the square is divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles. The major premiss expresses the property (the content) of the middle concept (parallelogram). The minor premiss subjects to this content the species (square) which belongs to the extension of the middle concept.

There are, to be sure, cases of the syllogism in which, on closer investigation, the matter can also be taken in such a way that content is related to content. This will occur when the concepts in the premisses contain only what is mutually specific. For example: all right-angled triangles are so constituted that their vertices determine a semicircle. All triangles in which the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides are right-angled. Therefore all triangles in which the designated relation obtains are so constituted that their vertices determine a semicircle. Here one can decline subsumption (the relation of a law to the extension) insofar as the subject of the minor premiss coincides completely with the middle concept and the latter has no wider sphere. This consideration, however, lies beyond the form of the syllogism and becomes evident only from investigations of another kind. It was remarked above that in the judgment of content the predicate at the same time contains the relation to the — mostly higher — extension, and nowhere can the predicate have a narrower extension than the subject, even if it can equal it, as in the definition. Hence the categorical syllogism can [p. 350] be regarded as a relation of content to extension.¹

The procedure of the disjunctive syllogism is the reverse. For example, the proposition: in every circle the angle at the centre is twice as great as the angle at the circumference when both stand on the same arc, is proved by a disjunctive syllogism.² The centre of the circle falls either within the arms of the angle at the circumference, or on *one* of them, or outside them. In all these cases the angle at the centre is twice as great (according to the proof); therefore in general. Here, as everywhere in the syllogism of complete induction, the law of the individual cases or of the species forms the middle concept, in order, as it were, to draw together the content of the universal out of the extension. In a corresponding manner the negative disjunctive syllogism drives the negation through all the species of a concept, in order to compress it into a universal negation of the genus.³

In this way the categorical syllogism is related to the disjunctive as the judgment of content to the judgment of extension, and one could also call the former the syllogism of content, the latter the syllogism of extension.

Content and extension, in the relation of law and appearance, constitute the essential sides of the concept, and their reciprocal relation its life. The understanding is educated to govern freely this interaction of content and extension, and its formation is completed when in the direction of thought neither content nor extension one-sidedly predominates, but the [p. 351] manifoldness of appearances is always compressed into the determining, pervading simplicity, and the simplicity proves itself in the outflowing manifoldness. The syllogism is nothing but this easy motion of thought from content to extension and from extension to content; and therefore the indication of the moments suffices, and the working out becomes tedious. This original process is demonstrated especially by the cases designated by logic as irreducible. In these, thought, measuring content and extension against each other, draws the conclusion without effort; but logic provides only an indirect proof of its correctness.

(1) Herbart too has designated the syllogisms of the first and second figures as syllogisms of subsumption (Einleitung §. 68).

(2) Euclid's Elements III. 20.

(3) As an example let there serve, from Aristotle On the Soul (III. 3), the proof that imagination is no judging taking-for-true (no ὑπόληψις); for it is, he argues, no species of such a thing: not perception, not science, not reason, not opinion.

These cases are, in the second figure, baroco, e.g. all squares are parallelograms; some regular rectilinear figures are not parallelograms. With easy survey one concludes: some regular rectilinear figures are not squares. This simple case is proved with long circumlocution, since, on the view of the subordination of concepts, it will not fit into the first figure, at least not directly. Already Aristotle¹ treats it apagogically. From the third figure bocardo belongs here, a case which is less simple, as is the third figure in general, but which is nevertheless more easily comprehended if one weighs the content and the extension of the given terms against each other than if one makes trials with it by the detour of indirect proof. In an example the task presents itself thus: Unite the premisses: some parallelograms have no right angles; all parallelograms are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles, into a conclusion. Here, to be sure, one will not be able to substitute the law of the parallelogram directly in place of the concept itself, but at all events one can do so with the limitation of the part. Some figures which are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles have no right angles.

(1) Analyt. pr. I. 5. p. 26 a 36.

[p. 352] From the view that the syllogism mediates the relation of content to extension and conversely, the familiar syllogistic rules follow of themselves. Ex mere particularibus nihil sequitur; for the right to relate the content to the extension lies solely in the at least relative universality of the content. Ex mere negativis nihil sequitur. The law can be negative, but then the subsumption must be positive. Mere negations separate, but give the law no domain of rule. Conclusio sequitur partem debiliorem; for the conclusion will have to acknowledge the limitation of the law or of its application that is given in the premisses.

The first and second figures of the categorical syllogism present this application of content to extension most clearly. Since in the first figure the minor premiss introduces the species which submit to the (positive or negative) law of the genus, it is, in this act of subsumption, always positive.¹ Were it negative, and thus to reject the possible assumption of a species, then nothing would follow for this concept excluded from the extension; for possibly it might still have the same mark as the concept of which it is not a species, since the law expressed in the mark can also hold for other genera. But if, conversely, a concept excludes itself from the law of another, it also excludes itself from the extension of that other; for the content determines the extension. This the second figure presents. It has an adversative character, and major and minor premiss therefore necessarily alternate in affirmation and negation. It is just as original as the first figure and forms its opposition.²

To these two original ways of relating content to [p. 353] extension correspond two ways of the disjunctive syllogism, in which the content of a concept is determined from its extension. For the positive form, which is to be compared with the first figure of the categorical syllogism, the proposition of Euclid cited above¹ can serve as an example. For the negative, which corresponds to the second figure of the categorical syllogism, the following example, say, can be formed. Parallels, when cut by a third line, are recognised either from the equality of the interior and exterior angle, or from the equality of the alternate angles, or from the sum of the interior angles being equal to two right angles. The sides of a pentagon have none of these properties. Therefore they are not parallel.²

(1) Hence in the formulas the minor premiss is determined only by a or i. Cf. the second syllable in barbara, celarent, darii, ferio.

(2) Cf. Herbart Lehrbuch zur Einleitung in die Philosophie §. 67.

In this way the syllogisms of content and of extension are related symmetrically.

The third figure of the categorical and hypothetical syllogism has not the same value nor the same degree of clarity as the first and second. Two concepts meet in the same subject. What follows from this? The concepts of the predicate are either the substantial genus or else a species-forming or accidental difference. If one of the two premisses is universal affirmative and has a [p. 354] predicate of the first kind, the syllogism can most simply be regarded as the genus being more closely determined in one of its species. For example: all squares are parallelograms, all squares have right angles; some parallelograms have right angles.¹ But if in both premisses the concept predicated of the same subject is a dependent mark, then the syllogism gives rise to an artificial and, in several cases, a thoroughly ambiguous formation. The artificiality consists in this, that the dependent mark must first be made independent in order to become subject of the conclusion. Conversion suffers from this defect, as was shown above, and transplants it to the syllogism of the third as of the fourth figure.

(1) Elements III. 20. See above vol. II. p. 350 f.

(2) Drobisch (Logik 1836. §. 92) lists two forms of the disjunctive syllogism in the second figure: 1) P is either A or B or C / S is neither A nor B nor C / Therefore S is not P. / 2) P is neither A nor B nor C / S is either A or B or C / Therefore S is not P. Both forms differ indeed in expression, but not in substance. The premisses of the first form say: the species of S are not the species of P; those of the second: the species of P are not the species of S. Both therefore coincide as regards the mediation of the conclusion.

The moods darapti and felapton require a conversion of a universal affirmative proposition with limitation. In individual cases this gives too little. Datisi and ferison suffer from the whole ambiguity which the conversion of a particular affirmative judgment brings with it. All these cases are to be applied only with the caution that, although no more can be concluded from the grammatical expression, perhaps more follows from the content.

The moods disamis and bocardo are the only cases that involve no danger of error. But since they give only a particular result, they are of no scientific significance.

The conclusion is always artificial when dependent marks which formed the predicate of the premisses are raised to an indeterminate substance in order to be fit to serve as subject. The conclusion always yields only an external connection of subject and predicate.

Whoever wishes for evidence of what has been said may consider the following examples. 1. According to the rule of darapti one concludes from the [p. 355] premisses: All parallelograms are four-sided; all parallelograms are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles. Therefore something (only something, and what is this something?), something which is divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles is four-sided. 2. Felapton. No right-angled triangle has an obtuse angle. All right-angled triangles have the property expressed in the Pythagorean theorem. Therefore something (!) that has this property has no obtuse angle. 3. Datisi. All parallelograms are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles; some parallelograms are squares. Therefore some (!) squares are divided by the diagonal into two equal and similar triangles. 4. Ferison. No parallelogram is a trapezium; some parallelograms are squares. Therefore some (!) squares are not trapezia. If in the examples given of datisi and ferison the indeterminate expression of the minor premiss is explained, according to the content of the matter, to mean that all squares are parallelograms, then a full syllogism of the first figure results, one which really has content.

(1) This can take place in all cases except in ferison.

Thus this figure, apart from two moods of little significance, is properly obtuse, since in conversion it cannot distinguish what absolutely must be distinguished; and it is unsafe, since it easily misleads one into taking for true only an indeterminate part instead of the warranted universality.

Herbart¹ sought the essence of the third figure in substitution. Such an equating can be derived from the premisses as judgments only with essential limitation, and the conversion, which cannot be avoided here, again yields something artificial. Whether the mathematical substitution to which Herbart refers can be counted as a syllogism of the third figure is doubtful. For example, n = b; n = g + h; [p. 356] therefore g + h = b. In such a case it is completely undetermined what is subject and what predicate. Hence the syllogism can just as well proceed in the first figure. Such a mathematical substitution proceeds from the consideration of equality, but not from the essence of the syllogism. Euclid laid down as an axiom: if two magnitudes are equal to a third, they are equal to each other; and in such cases of substitution one usually subsumes under this major premiss.

(1) Hauptpunkte. 1808. p. 124. Einleitung §. 68 (3rd ed.).

After all this, the third figure cannot stand on the same line as the first two. If it is to yield anything sound, its premisses first require closer determination from the nature of the matter. Thereby it passes over into the two earlier figures. Nor does any form of the disjunctive syllogism correspond to the third figure of the categorical.

Already Laurentius Valla rejects the third figure of the syllogism as a mode of inferring which is contrary to nature and is heard in no man's mouth.¹

The hypothetical syllogism has no special modes and is to be attached to the categorical syllogism in a way similar to that in which the hypothetical judgment was united with the categorical. Herbart has shown simply that the so-called positing and cancelling modes of the hypothetical syllogism belong with the same right to the categorical syllogism.

But what, then, guarantees the completeness of the forms of the syllogism? Content is related to extension, and content is determined from extension, and indeed in both ways positively and negatively. This simple survey affords the insight that the relations are exhausted.

If, however, one wishes to insist on a complete knowledge of the forms of judgment in the premisses and in the conclusion, [p. 357] then the path of combination, taken more than once, leads to the goal. The elements are a, e, i, o.¹ There result 64 possibilities of different premisses; from these the impossible and unfruitful ones are to be eliminated. But according to what rule? First, two relations present themselves which prevent any conclusion from the premisses. If the premisses are only negative or only particular, [p. 358] nothing can follow from them. This flowed, as we saw, from the essence of the syllogism itself. In 16 cases among those 64 the premisses will present themselves as purely negative, and these thereby drop out. In another 12 cases the premisses will present themselves as purely particular, and these too drop out of themselves. In several cases, however, the premisses will outwardly contain a universal determination, but in the mutual relation of content and extension have only a particular value. Then too no syllogism will be possible. For if in both premisses the middle concept occurs only as a species,¹ the law of its content operates only partially, and there is no right to a conclusion. Of such cases there will be 8 besides the above. If, further, a species of a concept is denied of another, it remains undetermined whether the concept itself is to be denied or attributed to it. For where the particular is excluded, the universal may obtain and may also not obtain. Of such cases there are 9 besides the previous ones. In this way the familiar 19 cases of the categorical syllogism remain, which, however, are to be comprehended from 3, and not as the remainder of the possible after deduction of the impossible. In order to remove the unfruitful possibilities, only the relations following from the nature of the syllogism were applied here as the standard. However, [p. 359] several of the 19 cases again remain undetermined on closer investigation, as has just been shown.

(1) Dialecticae disputationes III. c. 9. Opp. ed. Basil. 1543. p. 738 sq.

(2) Lehrbuch zur Einleitung in die Philosophie §. 64.

(1) On the use of a, e, i, o the following may be remarked in passing. Since in quantity we count three kinds of judgments, the universal, the particular and the singular, and possess signs in those letters only for the universal and the particular, whether affirmative or negative, the subsumption of the singular affirmative and negative judgment under them wavers. Should the singular judgment (e.g. Caius is a man, a man invented that) fall under the sign of the universal (a) or of the particular (i)? Opinion differs. Aristotle leads to the view (analyt. pr. I. 1) that one regards the individual, without distinction, as part of a sphere, and therefore opposes the singular judgment to the universal and places it under the particular. On the other hand, already before Kant (see Kritik der reinen Vernunft §. 9. ed. Rosenkranz p. 72) logicians remarked that in syllogisms of reason it is to be treated like the universal (thus a, e), because it has no extension at all, and Kant concurs in this view. Herbart, however (Lehrbuch zur Einleitung in die Philosophie §. 62), demands a more exact distinction. That equating, he holds, is valid with a determinate subject, e.g. Vesuvius spews fire; but it is not valid when, with the help of the indefinite article, the meaning of a universal expression is restricted to some individual or other, e.g. a man invented that. Cf. Ueberweg Logik §. 70. p. 159. and §. 107 p. 296. Accordingly there is dispute whether, in that old example of a syllogism which holds before us the necessity of dying, Caius dies in barbara or in darii. It will be all the same to him. But the mode of consideration is different. As long as one represents Caius as one of many and indeterminately as a part of all, darii applies; but if in Caius one thinks only the *one*, and not individuals in general, then barbara is certainly more correct. It is inconvenient that the application of those letters first requires a preliminary investigation into the meaning of the singular judgment; yet for an exact determination it is in accordance with the matter. Thus it is more correct to take the syllogism of the Stoic who ensouls the world — Nothing unconscious has conscious parts; the world has conscious parts (man); therefore the world is not unconscious — not according to festino, for in the sense of the Stoics the world is only *one*, but according to cesare.

(2) Cf. the careful treatment in Drobisch, Logik §. 71.

(1) E.g. some parallelograms are squares: all rectangles are parallelograms. The concept parallelogram is the terminus medius. But in the minor premiss too it operates only particularly; for it designates only: some parallelograms are rectangles.

(2) E.g. all squares are parallelograms; no rectangle is a square. The middle concept here would be square.

(3) Anyone will easily demonstrate the particulars following this indication.

(4) The derivation given by Beneke (syllogismorum analyticorum origines et ordo naturalis. Berlin 1839) rests on a division of the extension and of the marks. After what we remarked above about the organic bond of the marks, we cannot assent to such a view of a mechanical division of them, nor therefore to the whole development. The marks are the deeply intertwined features of a whole, but not the joined-on stones of a mosaic.

If the disjunctive syllogism shows no such manifoldness of forms within its figures, the ground of this lies in the boundness of the disjunctive judgment, which we set out above;¹ for it is in itself universal and affirmative, never particular and negative.

Aristotle proceeds combinatorially in determining the forms of the syllogism; in particular, all 16 possibilities of premisses within the first figure are recorded by him.² The admissible ones he proves directly, by reducing them to the principle of subordination; the inadmissible ones he refutes indirectly. He shows the contradiction in individual cases, in that, with the relation of the premisses otherwise the same, two examples would have to yield opposite conclusions. Since one false consequence suffices to overthrow a hypothesis, Aristotle gives no further refutation. This procedure of finding individual cases that raise an objection may be called empirical; it is nevertheless cogent and sufficient, even if it does not rise to the ultimate grounds.

In the foregoing, the syllogism in all its manifoldness has been set out in consistent agreement with the concept. Syllogisms reveal the community and intercourse of concepts among themselves. In linking themselves together they support one another and, through their interaction, exclude what is absolutely contradictory. Concepts by themselves are merely determinations at rest. In weaving themselves together, they present the world of thoughts, in which the bodily world is born again out of the spiritual depth.

The universal law of a concept, to which its extension submits, is the fundamental view of the syllogism. The [p. 360] universal law, however, is the quantitative expression of that qualitative universality which rests on the community of thinking and being. From this side an insight into the real significance of the syllogism readily opens up. Before this is developed, however, we must cast a glance at Hegel's comprehensive treatment.

(1) See vol. II. p. 292ff.

(2) Analyt. priora. I. 4.

5. According to Hegel's peculiar exposition, the copula of the judgment in general was fulfilled in the apodictic form. Through this fulfilment the concept, particularised and divided in the judgment, was restored in its unity. The unity of the concept and the judgment is therefore the syllogism, since in it the determinations of the concept, the extremes of the judgment, are contained, and at the same time their determinate unity is posited.

The universal nature of the concept gives itself external reality through particularity (in the judgment) and thereby, and as negative reflection into itself, makes itself into the individual. The syllogism presents the circuit of these self-mediating moments of the concept (the universal, the particular and the individual).

At first, then, the syllogism, like the judgment, is immediate. This syllogism of immediacy is called the qualitative syllogism. Through its own dialectic it makes itself into the syllogism of reflection, just as the judgments of reflection formed the second stage of judgments. The syllogisms of reflection are finally completed in the syllogism of necessity, in which the objective nature of the matter is what mediates.

In this way syllogisms are graded just as judgments are, and the forms run parallel with one another. Since the syllogism is determined as the unity of the concept and the judg[p. 361]ment, this conception seems to be necessary.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 181ff. Logik III. p. 118ff. Cf. with this the exposition founded upon it by J. H. Fichte, Grundzüge zum Systeme der Philosophie I. p. 139 ff. §. 107 ff.

(2) See above vol. II. p. 298 f.

The qualitative syllogism, or the syllogism of existence, is also called the formal syllogism. In its first figure particularity mediates individuality with universality (I-P-U). A subject, as individual, is joined together through a quality with a more universal determinateness. The middle is some property or other of the subject; since the subject has many properties, termini medii can also be found in it which allow the opposite to be inferred. The isolated middle concept is one-sided in this contingent relation. The premises demand proofs, and so a series of prosyllogisms opens up into infinity. From these defects arises the necessity of the next figures.

In the second figure the mediation takes place through individuality. The particular joins itself together with the universal through the individual. Since in this figure the terminus medius is a contingency and the syllogism yields only a particular judgment, this second figure is the truth of the first; for, while the first was contingent in itself, in the second the contingency is posited and brought to light. It mediates the major premise of the first figure (P-U). Since the second figure admits only a particular conclusion, it sublates the determinateness of the particular, and hence the terminus medius will become merely abstract universality.

The third figure therefore mediates the individual with the particular through the universal and grounds the minor premise of the first figure. It is the truth of the formal syllogism in general, since it expresses that the mediation of the latter is the abstractly universal one. Its conclusion is necessarily negative.

Since each moment has thus passed through the place of the middle and of the extremes, their determinate difference [p. 362] from one another has been sublated, and the syllogism now, since its moments have become undifferentiated, has equality for its relation (the external identity of the understanding). Thus arises the fourth figure, or the mathematical syllogism. If two things are equal to a third, they are equal to each other.

Since in this course each moment has received the determination and position of the middle, and so of the whole in general, it is thereby freed from one-sidedness and immediacy. The first figure, it is true, pointed out into infinity for the grounding of its premises. But the mediation is completed, since the figures presuppose one another and the conditions close themselves into a circle. In the first figure I - P - U the premises P - U and I - P are still unmediated; but the former is mediated in the second figure, the latter in the third. Each of these two figures likewise presupposes its two others for the mediation of its premises.¹

In the qualitative syllogism the middle is abstract particularity, by itself a simple determinateness, and the middle only externally and relatively to the self-subsistent extremes. Now it is posited as the totality of the determinations; thus it is the posited unity of the extremes; at first, however, the unity of reflection which comprehends them within itself² (the syllogism of comprehension). Individuality is at the same time determined as universality.

In the syllogism of reflection the middle is not merely an abstract particular determinateness of the subject, but concrete, since it comprehends all the individuals to which, among others, that determinateness also belongs. Thus the syllogism of allness is formed under the form of the first figure. But since the major premise comprises all the individuals, it presupposes the conclusion, which it ought rather to ground.

(1) Cf. Encyklopaedie §. 188. 189.

(2) Logik III. p. 148.

[p. 363] This defect is first remedied in induction, which corresponds to the second figure. The complete individuals as such (a, b, c, d and so on) form the middle. It is the syllogism of experience, whereas the second figure of the qualitative syllogism is only a syllogism of perception.

Individuality can be the middle only as immediately identical with universality. This is presupposed in induction, which never reaches the genus. Universality is external to the determination of individuality which underlies induction, but essential to it. The truth of the syllogism of induction is therefore a syllogism which has for its middle an individuality that is immediately in itself universality. Thus arises analogy, whose middle is an individual, but in the sense of its essential universality, while another individual is the extreme, which has the same universal nature as the former. This syllogism has the third figure of the immediate syllogism for its abstract schema.

In the syllogism of analogy universality is still encumbered with individuality as the immediate. When the mediation frees itself from this, in the syllogism of necessity the universal that is in and for itself becomes the middle.

The first syllogism of necessity is the categorical syllogism, in which a subject is joined together with its predicate through its substance. Substance raised into the concept is the universal in and for itself, whose essential difference is the specific difference. In the syllogism that has such a foundation the subsumption is no longer contingent, and the conclusion is no longer presupposed in order that the major premise may be true.

When the solid positive identity, which in the [p. 364] categorical syllogism forms the universality of the middle, opens itself out into the negativity of the extremes, there arises the hypothetical syllogism, in which the individual appears in the significance of immediate being, such that it is as much mediating as mediated. In it externality and its unity that has gone into itself are posited.

(1) Logik III. p. 155.

The mediation of the syllogism is accordingly the identity that differentiates and draws itself together into itself out of the difference. The syllogism in this determination is the disjunctive syllogism. The middle is the universality filled with form. The mediating universal is posited as the totality of its particularisations and as an individual particular, so that one and the same universal is, in these determinations, only in forms of difference.

In this completion of the syllogism the difference between the mediating and the mediated has fallen away. The result is therefore an immediacy that has emerged through the sublating of mediation, a being that is just as much identical with mediation, and the concept that has restored itself out of and in its otherness. This being is therefore a thing that is in and for itself, objectivity.

In these determinations Hegel develops the forms of the syllogism and, through their own process, purifies them of the admixture of the contingent and immediate into a content solid in itself.

The difference between this conception and the usual treatment strikes one even externally in the three times three syllogisms. The qualitative syllogism and the syllogism of allness are otherwise grown together with the categorical syllogism. Since, however, the categorical judgment received from Hegel the higher concept of a substantial and essential judgment, the significance of the categorical [p. 365] syllogism has, in agreement with this, also been heightened; and the separation of the syllogism of allness from the categorical may be granted. But can there be a syllogism of immediacy, as there is a judgment of existence?

(1) Logik III p. 171.

The judgments of existence, which grasp an "immediate, hence sensuous quality", are not yet universal.¹ Only at the later stage of the judgment of reflection does allness come forward, only in the judgment of necessity the concrete universal. But if the universal is an essential element of every syllogism, then a syllogism is not possible from premises which apprehend only what is immediately sensuous and therefore do not even so much as divine the universal. All syllogisms from such premises are mere semblance; but deceptive semblance is surely not to be acknowledged as the first stage and the foundation of truth. The sophism is no syllogism. How, in general, is the major premise in a syllogism of existence to run, so as to distinguish itself from the syllogism of allness? Unfortunately examples and applications are lacking which would have led us out of indeterminate assertions of the universal into the determinate confirmation of the individual. We do, however, find some information under the syllogism of allness.⁴ A syllogism of existence would run, for example: the green is pleasant; the painting is green; therefore the painting is pleasant. The major premise of the syllogism of allness, on the other hand, would not content itself with the abstraction of green, but would comprehend all the actual concrete objects that are green, and would therefore run: everything green is pleasant. On closer consideration, however, the boundary drawn here dissolves like a furrow in water. For in the syllogism of existence cited, the expression "the green" means everything green [p. 366] and has the significance of allness. Perhaps the allness has been closed too hastily; perhaps the proposition was meant to say only: some green (what has been perceived) is pleasant. But in this shape it would remain on its own and would never become a major premise. If it is to introduce a syllogism, if it is to have the power of taking the minor premise up into itself, then that expression is the expression of allness and tacitly ascribes this power to itself. It must therefore be maintained that the qualitative syllogism, as a syllogism, is a syllogism of allness; the syllogism, stemming from universality, has naked immediacy behind it in its procedure, and the syllogism of immediacy is an idle, strictly speaking an impossible, formation.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 172.

(2) Encyklopaedie §. 175. 177, cf. above vol. II. p. 296ff.

(3) Hegel himself gives I-P-U as the schema of the qualitative syllogism (individual, particular, universal).

(4) Logik III. p. 150.

If we follow the qualitative syllogism further, then according to the account the premises of the first figure (P - U and I - P) are to demand a grounding and to receive it through the second and third figures. The major premise (the particular is universal) is mediated by the second figure in individuality, the minor premise (the individual is particular) by the third figure in universality.¹ In this way the second and third figures are supposed to arise necessarily from the need of the first.

At first glance this development seems to correspond to the nature of the matter. But it only seems to. The contradiction would have announced itself at once if anyone had ever attempted the application and had not kept this dialectic merely in the unresisting "aether of pure thought". According to Hegel's own account, which agrees with the relation demonstrated by Aristotle, the second [p. 367] figure yields only a particular conclusion, and the third only a negative one. But was a particular major premise and a negative minor premise to be grounded in the first figure? Whoever thinks that the form P-U signifies a particular major premise need only try to draw an inference when, in the example above, the major premise runs: some green is pleasant. More than this is not gained from the second figure; more than this it does not ground. With such a mediation the syllogism is at once null and void. The form P-U designates the relation of subject to predicate as that of a particular species to the universal genus, but not, as would have to be the case, that only a part of the species is to be taken. Where is there a particular major premise in the first figure? - Likewise the syllogism ceases if the minor premise of the first figure becomes negative, and yet the third figure, which is summoned to ground that premise, yields only a negative result. Even if the subsumption of a concept under the middle concept were denied in the minor premise, the concept could nevertheless carry within itself the property of the more universal predicate. Hence the minor premise of the first figure must be positive. Thus it comes about that in fact the dialectical mediations of the first figure do not support it but tear it down completely. The whole connection dissolves into discord.

(1) Logik III. p. 131. Encyklopaedie §. 189. These figures agree with the Aristotelian ones; except that Aristotle's second and third figures are with Hegel the third and second. Logik III. p. 135. The second figure is listed as the third from old habit without further reason.

(2) Logik III. p. 135.

Besides the general connection just examined, a particular transition is further paved from the first figure to the second³ and from the second to the third.⁴ It could easily be shown that these connections are just as little genetic.

Another point seems more instructive for the standing of the dialectic. How, then, does Hegel prove that the second [p. 368] figure concludes only particularly, the third only negatively? In the second figure¹ the proof proceeds, as usual, by reduction to the first figure, the minor premise being converted under the necessary limitation. This, it seems, is how the passage in question is to be understood. With regard to the third figure it is said: "the middle, as the universal, is subsuming or predicate with respect to both its extremes, and not also, on the one occasion, subsumed or subject. Insofar, therefore, as the syllogism, as a species of syllogism (of the qualitative syllogism in general), is to correspond to the latter, this can only happen in such a way that, since the one relation I - U already has the proper relation, the other U - P also obtains the same. This happens in a judgment in which the relation of subject and predicate is indifferent, in a negative judgment. Thus the syllogism becomes legitimate, but the conclusion necessarily negative." In this passage too a reduction is set in train; but how it is to be carried out, how in particular an indifferent judgment is to result and how this is to be the same as the negative one, we must leave to others to understand.

(4) ibid. p. 136.

(4) ibid. p. 136.

In the three figures, it is said further in the qualitative syllogism, the particular, the individual and the universal have alternately become the middle and have likewise taken the place of the extremes. Thereby the determinate difference of the moments from one another is sublated, and equality now becomes the relation of the syllogism. Thus results the quantitative or mathematical syllogism. If two things are equal to a third, they are equal to each other. A third in general is what mediates; but it has no determination whatever relative to its extremes. Each of the three can therefore with equal right be the third, the mediating term.

This position of a fourth figure is surprising, since Hegel [p. 369] rightly rejects the so-called Galenic figure. According to the exposition, the quantitative syllogism of geometry appears as the completion of the immediate syllogism, and yet the syllogism of difference evidently has a higher significance. If each moment has passed through the place of the middle and of the extremes, this means nothing other than that each has in itself a part of the grounding force. But do they thereby become undifferentiated? Is there in this any reference to the indifferent relation of a quantitative equality? Euclid's axiom: if two things are equal to a third, they are equal to one another, arises from the concept of equality, from the nature of the identical quantum. The relation concerns the content of the terms, but has nothing to do with the form of the syllogism. The concepts of the universal, the particular and the individual are not levelled out against one another by the fact that something can be inferred from all of them. Identical in this one respect, they otherwise remain wholly different. Finally, does the dialectic of the concept cover the genesis of the matter? At least nowhere within mathematics does the quantitative syllogism arise from such a process as is described in the course of the qualitative syllogism.

(1) Logik III. p. 135.

(2) ibid. p. 138.

When the qualitative form-determinations, so the account continues,¹ are extinguished in the merely quantitative, mathematical syllogism, only the negative result has been reached. But what is truly present is the positive result, that the mediation does not take place through a single qualitative form-determinateness, but through their concrete identity, the totality of the determinations. Thus the qualitative syllogism passes over into the syllogism of reflection, and the syllogism of allness is the next form, which grounds itself through induction and analogy.

We cannot grant that the syllogism of allness [p. 370] springs from the procedure of the qualitative syllogism, since, as we have shown, there is no such syllogism at all. The syllogism begins only with the gathering together of the universal, with reflection.

(1) Logik III. p. 141.

We now ask about a subsidiary determination. The syllogism of allness is the syllogism of the first figure. But can it be said that induction concludes in the second figure, analogy in the third? We recall here that, although Hegel's second figure is the third Aristotelian one and Aristotle's second figure is Hegel's third, Hegel otherwise, like Aristotle, articulates the three figures according to the particular, the individual and the universal, which form the middle concept one after another.

Induction agrees at one point with the third Aristotelian figure. Induction infers from the individual, the third figure from the lowest concept of a series; but the essence of induction remains number, and only if the middle concept splits into its individuals or species and thereby becomes manifold can induction be brought under the schema of the third figure. This collection of the same subjects in both premises, this multiplication of the middle concept, already contains the essence of induction. Further, induction aims at universality, and indeed by means of the individuals and species; the third figure, however, always yields only a particular judgment. Let it not be said that induction too remains incomplete and therefore has precisely in the particular judgment the expression of this defect. The particular judgment is indeterminate; the comparative universality which induction must at any rate claim is determinate. This essential relation drops out in the third figure. Hence Aristotle, where he treats the third figure, makes no mention of induction; and while he binds the third figure to the law of a merely partial validity, [p. 371] he demands universality of induction. Later, to be sure, Aristotle does compare induction to the procedure of the third figure.¹ But besides that peculiar dissection of the minor concept into its individual species, a particular condition is added which at once goes beyond the third figure and transforms its particular result into a universal one. The minor premise, namely, is to be so constituted that it can be converted simply. If this is [p. 372] the case, the particular which enters the syllogism through the limited conversion of the minor premise is thereby avoided. Subject and predicate are now identical; but this can only be the case if the species have been completely enumerated. Evidently this condition of Aristotle's conceals the disjunctive major premise which lawful induction demands. Through the third figure alone, therefore, induction does not come about, and we may not assert that Aristotle regarded it as a species of the third figure.

(1) Analyt. pr. I. 6.

(1) Analyt. pr. II. 23. We explain the passage in a few words. Aristotle has the following example: if it is to be proved by induction that those animals which have no gall-bladder are long-lived, the members of the induction are, say: man, horse, mule. The syllogism would be arranged according to the third figure thus: man, horse, mule are long-lived. Man, horse, mule have no gall-bladder. The conclusion would run: some animals which have no gall-bladder are long-lived. But in this induction has not reached its goal. The allness that is striven for follows only if the minor premise can be converted simply. For only in this lies the guarantee that all the species have been found for the universality (animals that have no gall-bladder), and unlimited conversion is the surety of the completely exhausted sphere. In conjunctive form there is then, in essence, a disjunctive judgment present. Once the conversion has taken place, a universal syllogism follows according to the first figure. This is the sense of the demand added by Aristotle, that b and c (middle concept and minor concept) must be interchangeable with one another and the middle concept must not be wider than the minor concept. Since the possibility of that unlimited conversion requires a special proof (mostly a syllogism of the first figure), induction according to Aristotle is evidently an interweaving of the syllogism of the third figure with another. The complete division of the genus into its species and the subsumption of all the species under this law is what is peculiar to the disjunctive syllogism. It alone unites Aristotle's two conditions into a unity. On the natural-historical representation underlying the example cf. Aristot. on the parts of animals IV. 2. p. 676b 16 ff. especially IV. 2. p. 677a 30. It is at the same time clear from this passage that Aristotle strives to lead induction back into the knowledge of causal connection; where this really succeeds, the ground with its necessity gives the universality which in induction cannot spring from the enumeration of cases. In such an analytical treatment lies the deeper complement of induction.

With analogy the matter stands still more doubtfully. Since it infers indeed from the individual, but in the sense of its universal nature, it is supposed to follow the schema of the second Aristotelian figure. The second figure, however, concludes only negatively, whereas analogy seeks to extend knowledge positively into an unknown region. Since, further, the middle concept must be taken in a double significance, once as individual, then as universal, since therefore there are properly four terms present,¹ analogy cannot be accommodated under any of the figures of the strict three-membered syllogism. In creative analogy, as it reveals itself for example in Newton's discoveries, the universal genus from which the inference is drawn must first be projected out of the individuals which the analogy apprehends. The ancients meaningfully regarded analogy as proportion. The force of analogy lies in the formation and introduction of a universal which comprises in common the minor concept, for which the inference is made, and the compared individual, which would like to appear as middle concept but cannot. This new universal, however, is not the highest concept among the three terms of the syllogism, but the middle one, and it becomes nothing other than the terminus medius of the first figure.

(1) Hegel himself has instructively drawn attention to this difficulty. Logik III. p. 157. What he adduces to remove it, however, rests only on the example of induction, which, according to the above, we may not acknowledge in this respect.

[p. 373] That the predicate of the compared individual is ascribed to the newly formed universal is the doubtful side of analogy. For what entitles us to do so? Rather the possibility remains open that the individual has that property or determination, which in analogy is hastily attributed to the newly formed universal and through it to the minor concept, only as such and not as subject to the universal; that the compared individual has it by virtue of its species-forming difference or of its contingent particularity, and hence precisely in opposition to the comprehending universal. But if this universal is posited in this determination, the syllogism is a syllogism of the first figure.

The history of the sciences has preserved for us many futile analogies. Theories which proved false rested for the most part on unsuccessful analogies. A universal was formed from compared phenomena, and the determinations recognised only in the individual phenomena were predicated of the universal. The error concerns either the formation of the universal or the extension of the individual determination to the universal, or both points at once. The analogies of the grammarians and of the natural scientists can serve equally as examples.

Gravitation in its pervasive action had disclosed itself to the mind of Newton. The masses of the solar system, the regular motions and the so-called perturbations, the ebb and flow of the sea and the oscillations of the pendulum were subject to the law of attraction. Newton compared the phenomena of the diffraction of light, when it passes close by bodies, to deflections through attraction. Thus arose that view of attractive and repulsive forces in optics. Light, as it were a particle of the sun, falls into the sphere of action of the body past which it would hasten, and is thereby deflected. This long-maintained analogy proved untenable on closer investigation. What has happened here, and wherein lay [p. 374] the error? The members of the analogy are attraction, the solid bodies which exhibit this phenomenon, and light. The syllogism would run thus: the solid bodies, planets, pendulums etc., are attracted to one another; light is such a solid body; therefore light is attracted and bent aside. The error lies in the minor premise. What entitles us to bring light together with the planets, the pendulum etc. under the *one* concept of solid bodies? Once this has been done, however, the syllogism is a syllogism of the first figure. Were it to be a syllogism of the second figure, the terminus medius would have to form the more universal concept (the predicate) in both premises.

The same can be shown in Hegel's example. The earth has inhabitants; the moon is an earth; therefore the moon has inhabitants. Tacitly, earth and moon are placed under *one* genus (heavenly bodies). The concept of the earth is widened, and the determination of the narrower concept has been left to the widened concept (heavenly body); for only the earth was known to be inhabited. There is immediately no right to this extension; for it may be that the earth has inhabitants as such, but not because it is a heavenly body in general, not insofar as it stands on one line with the moon.¹ If, however, this extension has been admitted, the syllogism proceeds in the first figure. Were it to belong to the second, it would have to rest - which is not the case - on the most universal concept of the three terms (thus here on habitability) as the connecting middle concept. The external arrangement, too, of the syllogism of analogy submits to the first figure.²

(1) Cf. Logik III. p. 158.

(2) In Aristotle analogy will fall under the example. Analyt. pr. II. 24. In the example we read a universal, and in what has befallen the example we divine the fate of the universal. In arousing this activity the example has a stimulating effect, and the universal consideration is always mirrored in the intuition of the individual case. Aristotle has the example: the war of the Athenians with the Thebans is an evil, for the war of the Thebans with the Phocians was an evil. Brought into the strict form of analogy, the syllogism would run: the war of the Thebans with the Phocians is an evil. A war of the Athenians with the Thebans is such a war as the war of the Thebans with the Phocians. Therefore etc. The example is widened into the middle concept: war with neighbours. This middle concept, put into the syllogism, yields the first figure. The question now is this: was the war of the Thebans with the Phocians a misfortune because it was in general a war with border neighbours, or rather only in its peculiar course and context? In the former case the analogy is correct, in the latter mistaken. Aristotle therefore treats the example as a grounding of the major premise (all wars with border neighbours are a misfortune) by means of a case that is similar to the subject of the minor premise. Accordingly he is far from placing analogy under the second figure. In his writings (e.g. in the natural-historical ones) he usually takes analogy as a proportion.

[p. 375] The yield of this investigation stands out readily. The significance of the syllogistic figures is regarded only roughly and wholesale if induction is simply assigned to the third figure, and it is completely abolished if analogy is assigned to the second (Aristotelian) figure of the syllogism.

With analogy the syllogism of reflection has run its course. The universal nature of the matter, the genus, has now become what mediates. Thus, according to Hegel, arise the syllogisms of necessity, and first the categorical syllogism, whose middle is objective universality. Since the substantial content stands "in identical relation, as a relation that is in and for itself" to the subject, this syllogism no longer presupposes its conclusion for its premises, as a syllogism of reflection does. The syllogism of existence and the syllogism of allness still suffered from this defect. But by what is it overcome? The intermediate members are solely induction and analogy, so that the great advance must have taken place in these. But induction remains incomplete in the face of the infinite fullness of phenomena. Analogy is indeterminate, since it is properly experimenting with the universal. Induction and analogy, both beginning with the individual, therefore cannot give that substantial content, [p. 376] that necessary determination, which, being in and for itself, reaches over the minor premise as a law without needing the conclusion itself. They still leave a great gap for grounding by themselves a judgment of necessity. Have the necessary judgments of geometry, which form the basis of chains of syllogisms, become what they are out of induction or analogy? Rather, these two forms do not come into play at all. Or have the categorical propositions of ethics arisen in this way? The genesis of the categorical syllogism in the unconditioned significance in which it is taken here is not comprehended in this dialectical development. A leap suddenly transports us into this form so rich in content. The immanent connection is broken off. What came earlier does not suffice for understanding this shape. What, then, is the use of this dialectic?

According to the dialectical view, the categorical syllogism develops further into the hypothetical, in that the inner substantial identity becomes negative and, without giving itself up, displays an external diversity of existence. The hypothetical syllogism presents the necessary relation as connection through the form or negative unity. This shape already contains what constitutes the essence of the disjunctive syllogism, the unity of the mediating and the mediated. In the disjunctive syllogism what mediates is the universal sphere of its particularisation and something determined as individual. What is mediated is itself an essential moment of what mediates it, and each moment is as the totality of the mediated. Thus the syllogism is supposed to complete itself into objectivity.

The hypothetical syllogism runs: if A is, then B is; now A is; therefore B is. In this form it is expressed most abstractly that the individual is subject to the universal. No new content is connected with the middle concept, as otherwise happens in the categorical syllogism, but only the pure existence of the middle concept (A) is pronounced, without any connection. [p. 377] Hence also only the existence of the predicate (B), bare and detached, is inferred. If one counts three terms in the syllogism, only two are present here at first, and existence, this most abstract result of intuition, the mere foundation of the individual, appears colourlessly as the third. Whereas in the categorical syllogism (according to its universal significance) existence is presupposed, because the individual that rests on its basis appears in the minor premise, whereas therefore the categorical syllogism offers, on the presupposition of existence, a richer relation of content: the hypothetical syllogism presents only this isolation, the relationless existence of the predicate (B), and is in this respect poorer than the categorical syllogism. It has also been pointed out above that the categorical syllogism admits of the same form. We therefore cannot regard the hypothetical syllogism, which has for its content nothing but the fact of subsumption, without anything else, as a fuller unfolding of the categorical syllogism, but only as a shape that has stripped off the blossom and left behind only the supporting stem.

The disjunctive judgment is, as was shown above, the ripe fruit of an important development and a fully formed form. The disjunctive syllogism, however, does not stand higher in the significance of its form than the categorical, with which it runs parallel. In the sciences it is essentially applied in a twofold way, first for the grounding of a complete induction and then for the methodical laying-out of indirect proof. Neither procedure can be described as the completion of the syllogism.

If the hypothetical and the disjunctive syllogism are placed as high as they are with Hegel, and regarded as the apex of the pyramid which builds itself up from broad immediacy to clear height, then such a view may fairly be met with [p. 378] the demand to demonstrate this great significance in actual application. The sciences, with their quiet acuteness, are the sole guarantee of logical theories. Where, anywhere in their wide compass, does the hypothetical and disjunctive syllogism appear with such an all-completing power?

(1) See above vol. II. p. 356.

If the dialectic, from the contingent syllogism of existence up to the disjunctive syllogism, in which the mediating and the mediated are supposed to be one, presented not merely an artificial chain but the natural development, then it would have to be possible to show in a continuum of examples how knowledge ripens from one form to the other. But for such a confirmation of the dialectic nothing has yet been done, and we doubt its possibility.

If we sum up the misgivings that have pressed themselves upon us, then the qualitative syllogism set up, with its variations, falls away, since the syllogism as such begins from the universal and is therefore already removed from immediacy; the qualitative syllogism flows over into that of allness, and the latter into the categorical syllogism, since allness is only the outer expression of inner universality. Induction and analogy cannot be conceived as figures of the syllogism of allness, and in the hypothetical and disjunctive syllogisms as such there lies no greater completion. Moreover, the transitions are empty.

Syllogisms move within delimited concepts and relate to one another. But how do concepts come to be? This question points to the formation of the universal, which takes place beyond the formal syllogism, whether in outer experience or in synthetic construction. The forms do not arise out of one another, but jointly out of the mutually related sides of the concept.

But the syllogism is supposed to accomplish still more. Not merely is one form to produce the other, but the last is even to produce the world of objectivity.

[p. 379] "The syllogism," it is said, "is mediation, the complete concept in its positedness. Its motion is the sublating of this mediation, in which nothing is in and for itself, but each is only by means of another. The result is therefore an immediacy that has emerged through the sublating of mediation, a being that is just as much identical with mediation, and the concept that has restored itself out of and in its otherness. This being is therefore a thing that is in and for itself, objectivity." Through the development of the syllogism, accordingly, since each moment became the mediation of the whole, a self-subsistent, self-sufficient being has formed itself. This is objectivity.

Hegel puts this transition from the subjective concept and its unfolding to objectivity alongside the ontological proof, in which the existence of God is inferred from the concept of God. The comparison can hold only in a remote respect.

In the ontological proof existence is supposed to follow from our concept of God. But this difficulty, if the course of Hegel's logic is correct, is not present at all at the present point. For thinking determines itself to being throughout, and with every moment of thinking, according to the fundamental view, a determination of being has been gained. The concept has never come out of the objective at all and therefore has no difficult transition to the objective to make. The concept, as the truth of substance, has always remained in the objective. The judgment, according to Hegel, presents the immanent nature of things, and the syllogism is the unity of the concept and the judgment. This point of view is carried through by Hegel, and only singly and inadvertently do contradictory determinations escape him, e.g. in the infinite and the problematic judgment, in the subjective [p. 380] syllogism of analogy. Here, therefore, there can be no talk at all of a transition into the object.

(1) Logik III. p. 170. 171.

The matter could be taken differently. How does God (the subjective concept) externalise himself into the world? All those systems which begin with the absolute as subjective have to withstand this difficult question. Can the transition under discussion be an answer to this question? If one examines the nature of the concept as it has produced itself, one must deny it. Since substance is identical with itself in interaction, it remains with itself and is free concept.
