But the identity is nothing but a logical relation, a repetition of the same form of substance and effect.¹ It does not touch the content of the matter, and still less does it produce such a centre of subjectivity as is surely posited where the question how God externalises himself into the world is raised at all.

The system therefore needs at the present place no transition to objectivity at all, neither from our subjective concept nor from God's subjective determination. It is mere semblance that one is entering a new world. One remains on the ground of the old.

But if a transition were nevertheless to be made, as is asserted, by what would it take place? Mediation has sublated itself; for the moments of the concept interpenetrate to form a whole. This sublation of mediation is immediacy, and immediacy is objectivity. But the immediacy which is otherwise assigned to the sensuous world must not here bribe us and sweep us along into the same representation. This immediacy here, the self-supporting whole, would always remain within inner subjectivity, like a spaceless and timeless metaphysical system. But that external world, as objectivity is nevertheless understood forthwith in [p. 381] mechanism, chemism and end, is in this transition indicated by nothing, represented by nothing.

(1) See above vol. I. p. 75 ff.

Nevertheless, let us take the leap with Hegel from this self-mediating and therefore immediate, self-subsistent thing of thought into the world of the object, as though the latter had really been derived. It now follows necessarily that objectivity is a system of syllogisms, and Hegel seeks to comprehend mechanism, chemism and teleology as such a system. The nature of the thing itself has the form of the syllogism and is thereby rational.

We first single out individual examples. Mechanism, in which only pressure and impact relate the objects, self-subsistent for themselves, to one another, runs its process as an objective syllogism. The product of the formal mechanical process is the heap. Its determination is given thus: "It is the conclusion in which the communicated universal is joined together through the particularity of the object with individuality." The heap, the very counterpart of logical order and interpenetration, may be hard to trace back to the syllogism. Here, however, it is done, and the following might be the sense of the obscure words. The communicated universal is the relation into which the things, in themselves self-subsistent and individual, are placed with respect to one another. Their particularity is the reaction which they exert and by which the form is determined. Thus the individual has externally become universal, just as the conclusion of the first figure pronounces the individual as universal.

The chemical process, it is said further, has for its product the neutral of its tensed extremes. The concept, the universal, joins itself together through the difference of the objects, the particularisation, with individuality, the product, and therein only with itself. Equally, the other syllogisms are also contained in this [p. 382] process; individuality as activity is likewise what mediates, as is the universal, the essence of the tensed extremes, which comes to existence in the product.

(1) Logik III. p. 189.

(2) Cf. Encyklopaedie §. 201.

In the neutral product the tension of the opposition and the negative unity as activity of the process are extinguished.¹ Something alien, which contains the negative unity outside the object, kindles it anew. The neutral is thereby sundered. "This determination belongs to the immediate relation of the differentiating principle to the middle, in which this principle gives itself its immediate reality; it is the determinateness which, in the disjunctive syllogism, the middle has at the same time, besides being the universal nature of the object, whereby the latter is just as much objective universality as determinate particularity. The other extreme of the syllogism stands over against the external self-subsistent extreme of individuality; it is therefore the equally self-subsistent extreme of universality; the sundering which the real neutrality of the middle therefore undergoes in it is that it is broken up into moments that are not different but indifferent towards one another. These moments are accordingly, on the one hand, the abstract indifferent basis, and on the other, its animating principle, which through its separation from the basis likewise attains the form of indifferent objectivity. This disjunctive syllogism is the totality of chemism, in which the same objective whole is presented, as well as the self-subsistent negative unity, then in the middle as real unity, but finally the chemical reality dissolved into its abstract moments."

The teleological relation, finally,² is the syllogism in which the subjective end joins itself together with the objectivity external to it through a middle. This middle (the means) is the unity of the subjective end and [p. 383] objectivity, objectivity posited under the end. The means is the formal middle of a formal syllogism; it is something external relative to the extreme of the subjective end, and hence also relative to the extreme of the objective end.

(1) Logik III. p. 204 f. cf. p. 207.

(2) Encyklopaedie §. 206, cf. Logik III. p. 222.

In this way the syllogism has become real and actuality logical.

Attention has already been drawn above to the consistent character of the view just indicated. The only question is whether the consistency of the view is the truth of the matter, or whether, conversely, the consistency of the matter rather makes the truth of the view doubtful.

In the first place it is questionable that the system of the three syllogistic figures repeats itself in mechanism and chemism entirely, and in end essentially, in the same way. It cannot be said that they differ, say, as the stages of the qualitative, the reflecting and the necessary syllogism do. For in chemism the mode of the disjunctive syllogism, that is, of the syllogism completed at the last stage of necessity, has been expressly brought out. The heap (in mechanism) now stands logically under the same form as the product of the end. Both are a conclusion of the first figure. It is more than questionable that what is externally thrown together and what is spiritually shaped should bear the same logical signature. Even if the stage is higher, the logical relation nevertheless recurs.

The difficulty grows when one examines the terms of the supposed syllogisms. In the subjective syllogism they were related, in Hegel's treatment too, as the universal, the particular and the individual, and indeed in the sense of subordination. The particular appeared as the species of the universal, as a part of its conceptual sphere, the individual as comprised by the species. Are, then, in the objective syllogism too the major term and the minor term related as genus and individual, and the major term and the middle term as genus and species? Is the minor term logically subsumed under the [p. 384] middle term? Let us compare mechanism first. If one sought to regard the given reciprocal relation in the heap of stones as the universal genus or the universal property of the stones themselves, one would be wrong; and one will hardly even attempt to set the reacting particularity of the stones, which is supposed to form the middle term, in such a relation to the major term as the concepts man and mortal have to one another in the usual example of the syllogism; and yet this would have to be the case if more than a vague analogy is to remain. In chemism, further, neither can the neutral be regarded as a conclusion from the difference of the tensed substances, nor the sundering of the neutral as a disjunctive syllogism. Or would one declare the formation of gypsum, to keep the example given above from Goethe's Wahlverwandtschaften, to be a conclusion from sulphuric acid and lime? According to the view Hegel has indicated, sulphuric acid and lime would be the terminus medius through which the concept (gypsum?) joined itself together with individuality (gypsum). Is the terminus medius here to be a duality? and if it is, can one say that gypsum is a species of sulphuric acid and lime? What, properly, is the universal in this process? The concept, which is designated as the universal, hides itself here and seems to mean only the chemical process in general. But even then the proper subsumption is lacking. Conversely, when the neutral is sundered, new compounds arise; but we surely do not have before us a disjunctive syllogism that exhausts the universal in its species. In end, finally, the means is supposed to form the terminus medius through which the subjective representation joins itself together with objectivity. The three terms of the syllogism would be, in a simple example: wanting to see distinctly, the one extreme; the optical glass, the middle term; the actual distinct image, the other extreme. One may here say by way of comparison that the [p. 385] subject joins itself together with the objective world, from which it wins or into which it imagines its end: this alliance is not yet a logical syllogism. How, among the three terms named, will one subordinate seeing distinctly to the optical glass as extension to intension? or even subsume the actual distinct image under wanting to see distinctly in the way that the minor term otherwise falls within the logical extension of the major term? One surely cannot regard the actual execution as a species of the one represented. If the real syllogism, as Hegel has introduced it into objectivity, really corresponded to the logical one, then it would have to be possible to put it into the complete form of a syllogism. But one will attempt this in vain. In the teleological relation the means is the producing ground; when its law is applied to the extension, the real process initiated by the end can be presented in a syllogism; but the end itself, which appropriates this process to the subject, which makes the effect into the cause and the anticipated conclusion into the impulse of the syllogism, precisely the reconciliation of the subjective and the objective, is not contained in the syllogism and belongs to synthesis, which produces and does not infer. Within the sciences, end appears most simply and most intuitively in the geometrical problem, as was remarked above. The solution and the proof take place through syllogisms, but the problem itself arises through the apprehended requirement of other propositions or through a creative foresight. Its origin lies beyond the syllogism.

If the syllogism is sought in actuality in the way Hegel has done in the application set out, then the three terms are distributed arbitrarily among different realities from the point of view of the universal, the particular and the individual, without holding fast the mutual relation of logical subordination. In the teleological relation the subjective thought of the end is universal in and for itself; but it is not the universal [p. 386] genus of its means and its execution; the means are for themselves the particular and the different, but surely not the species of that thought; they are really subject to it and are governed by it, but surely not logically subordinated to it as its species; the realisation of the end is an individual, but neither the individual of the heterogeneous means nor of the thought that projects the end. If one wishes to say that the means is subordinate to the design, and the execution to both, then one must carefully distinguish this real dependence from the logical one, which arises from the relation of the intension and extension of concepts and alone conditions the syllogism.

If, finally, logical inferring by means of the terminus medius is transformed in reality in such a way that two extremes join together in a third, this already alters the matter, since the determinate syllogistic relation becomes more indeterminate. Every union in a third can now be regarded as a joining together. But how the product can be the conclusion, what in it, corresponding to the extremes, becomes subject and predicate, the individual and the more universal, remains uncertain.

In a similar but still more significant way the power of the syllogism is supposed to present itself in every whole. Through the nature of joining together, through the triad of syllogisms of the same terms, a whole is supposed to be truly understood in its organisation for the first time. In this sense it is said: everything rational is a syllogism, the living body is a syllogism, God (the triune) is a syllogism, and so on. Thus everything real becomes logical.

We insert the clearest explanation of this doctrine.¹ "Like the solar system, so, for example, in the practical sphere the state is a system of three syllogisms. First, the individual (the person) joins himself together through his particularity (the physical [p. 387] and spiritual needs, which, further developed on their own account, give civil society) with the universal (society, right, law, government). Secondly, the will, the activity of individuals, is what mediates, which gives satisfaction to the needs in society, in right and so on, as well as fulfilment and realisation to society, right and so on. Thirdly, however, the universal (state, government, right) is the substantial middle in which the individuals and their satisfaction have and maintain their fulfilled reality, mediation and subsistence. Each of the determinations, in that the mediation joins it together with the other extreme, precisely therein joins itself together with itself, produces itself, and this production is self-preservation."

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 195.

According to this view the whole grows vigorously together through the particular, the individual and the universal becoming alternately and mutually ground and consequence. That the activities of the whole and of the parts intimately interpenetrate does indeed constitute the self-preservation of the organic whole. If one wishes to call the cooperating members the universal, the particular and the individual, this too has a ground in linguistic usage. But one confuses the matter when one forms the analogue of a syllogism; for the needs are not subsumed as a species under the universality of the state, nor the individual citizens as individuals or species of a genus under the needs. With which syllogistic figures, in general, is one to compare this process? The syllogism of allness, in which the particular forms the middle, induction, in which the individuals do, and analogy, in which the universal does, lie nearest. And yet it is evident, especially at first glance, that analogy, which with its admitted indeterminacy is only a human inference, cannot present itself in the real at all. If the doctrine that every living whole bears the typical form of the three syllogistic figures is to be not merely a logical semblance but [p. 388] a real truth, then the agreement, which rests only on the indeterminate and ambiguous use of the universal, the particular and the individual, must be demonstrated more rigorously.

When one says, or repeats after others, that God is in himself a syllogism, one calls this the speculative concept of the Trinity. A syllogism is certainly comprehensible; but not that the persons of the Trinity are related to one another as universal, particular and individual, i.e. as genus, species and individual. Without this God is no syllogism.¹

6. Is the syllogism then, as might appear after this refutation, to remain nothing but a subjective function, without any real counterpart? The whole derivation preserves us from this. The content, presenting the law of the extension, contains the possibility of the syllogism, and in this its objective value is at the same time indicated. To the genetically universal, which is grounded on an original community of thinking and being, the quantitatively universal corresponds. The necessary ground therefore clothes itself in the expression of a universal fact and in this shape becomes the middle term of an objective syllogism. What in the real is the ground, that in the logical is the middle term of the syllogism.

Aristotle already demonstrated this parallelism with acuteness. Formal logic, which wished to have nothing to do with the real, left this profound indication lying unheeded. The producing ground, in unfolding its content, will always form the universal middle term in the major premise; for the necessary converts itself into external [p. 389] universality. The syllogism, whenever it is positive, must fall into the first figure, in which the dominion of the law over the extension expresses itself most purely. All synthetic sciences, which project the phenomena from the ground, can furnish the attentive observer with examples in abundance, and the more apt ones, the more faithfully they reproduce the course of the creative ground.

(1) Already from Abelard the saying is cited: Sicut eadem oratio est propositio, assumtio et conclusio: ita essentia est pater et filius et spiritus. Otto v. Freisingen de gestis Friderici I. (I. c. 47); but the comparison was more intelligible, and moreover did not, like the speculative conception, pass itself off as orthodox.

(2) Analyt. post. II. 2. 11. 12. d. anim. II. 2. cf. elementa log. Arist. §. 60 ff.

Aristotle has already adduced examples enough. Arithmetic and geometry, which demonstrate most strictly, furnish the proof on every page. In order not to have to stretch the chain of syllogisms into several links, we choose a couple of fundamental propositions. For example, in a geometrical proportion the product of the outer terms is equal to the product of the middle terms. The proof is usually drawn up algebraically. a: aeb: be; axbxe = axexb. The syllogism would run: equal factors give equal products; the outer and the middle terms contain mutually equal factors. Therefore, etc. The equal factors are the producing ground of the phenomenon and form the middle term of the syllogism. The proposition that the diagonal in a parallelogram forms two equal and similar triangles is proved genetically from the doctrine of parallel sides, in that the diagonal forms equal alternate angles and becomes the common base of two triangles. The syllogism will proceed in the first figure. All triangles in which one side and the two adjacent angles are equal are equal to one another. The diagonal forms two triangles in which one side and the two adjacent angles are equal, therefore two equal triangles. The conditions of the triangles lying in the parallelogram and in the diagonal are the producing ground of the phenomenon and become the middle term of the syllogism. Universal grammar will derive the necessity of the cases, or of the prepositions that take their place, from the concept of the verb. If one wished to form the complete syllogism from this, it would run roughly: most activities include a direction; [p. 390] verbs express such an activity; therefore verbs include an expression of direction, etc. Aristotle has presented a suitable example in the physical process of the lunar eclipse. When nature spreads out the phenomena before the perceiving sense, it gives the conclusion as a problem for which the terminus medius is to be found. Such a conclusion would be the observed fact, e.g. the moon is eclipsed, language has cases, the transversal of a square forms two equal triangles. Nature has inferred in creating. The result lies before us. The contemplating mind seeks the middle term of this creative syllogism. That is its task in all analytic sciences, a task which it solves only synthetically.

The producing ground stamps itself in a universal fact. Thereby arises the law of the middle term. Where, therefore, the ground is known, a terminus medius is tacitly generated. But conversely, is every middle term of a syllogism the logical expression of a real ground?

We distinguished above the ground of being and the ground of knowing.¹ Where both coincide, as in genetic knowledge, science completes itself. So long as consideration must proceed analytically, the two fall apart. The grounds of knowing, the effects of things, initiate a course opposite to the creative procedure of nature. The empirical sciences have their greatness in establishing such grounds of knowledge through observation. If these now form the middle term, this external relation does not reach the inner producing ground. In this multitude of cases the terminus medius does not present the real ground.

But if the middle term corresponds to the producing ground, the syllogism completes itself. In this [p. 391] significance it is an inference from the essence to the appearance, as induction is an inference from the appearances to the essence. As the essence pours itself out into the appearances and confirms itself in them, so induction is from this side too a counterpart of the syllogism.

(1) See above vol. II. p. 70. and section XV., the grounding.

If in the theory as carried out we placed the second figure of the syllogism on a level with the first, which Aristotle alone held to be the principal one, the question arises whether we can now carry further the Aristotelian thought of the real force of the middle term and recognise a real significance in the second figure as well.

It is the law of the second figure that it admits only negative results. Where it is overhasty and concludes positively, fallacies do not fail to appear.¹ We really have a natural propensity to positive syllogisms of the second figure, in that the association of ideas puts itself in the place of thinking. For this association playfully carries our representations onward according to kinship, that is, according to a common predicate, and, governing the subjective course of our thoughts, follows a connection which corresponds to positive premises of the second figure. The connections of mythology in its symbols, the transition of meanings in the sign of words, show us such combinations, which would be fallacies if they claimed to count as syllogisms. The mighty impression, for example, which raised the eagle to be the bird of Zeus, symbolised, as this explanation has only recently been given, according to what struck it as evident. The lightning of Zeus darts through the air; the eagle darts through the air; therefore the eagle is the lightning of Zeus. Already an interpretation of a myth which Aristotle has preserved for us in the Metaphysics (I. 3. p. 983b 32) proceeds in an affirmative syllogism of the second figure. The aroused representation stops at connection, but thinking begins with subordination. The metaphysician who concludes affirmatively in the second [p. 392] figure steps out of science into the association of ideas. The second figure, with its direction toward negation, serves in particular for the grounding of distinction and acts critically in science.

(1) See above vol. I. p. 105 f. Eth. Nic. II. 4. in Ueberweg in the Logik. 1st ed. p. 317.

Since, then, the second figure may conclude only negatively, it can have a real significance, if at all, only in presenting negation in its real ground, which according to the discussion above was none other than the positive determination of the essence. And indeed, in two moods of the second figure (cesare, festino), if we consider the minor premise, this determination appears to us immediately in the terminus medius. We illustrate this by an example from Aristotle's Ethics: ¹ the affects do not rest on deliberate choice; the virtues rest on deliberate choice; therefore the virtues are not affects. It lies in the essence of virtue that it rests on deliberate choice, which is what the terminus medius of the minor premise states; hence it rejects the predicate imputed to it of the affect that arises blindly and surprises us. In the two other moods (camestres, baroco) the minor premise itself already contains a negation, which by means of the positive major premise leads to a new negation. Let another example from Aristotle's Ethics serve as illustration:² all original faculties are gifts of nature; virtues are not gifts of nature (they are acquired), therefore virtues are not original faculties. The minor premise generates a new negation in that it excludes the subject from the predicate which it first denies. Only mediately does one arrive at the same result, virtues are not original faculties, if one starts from the major premise, which, affirming the middle term, excludes from the original faculties everything that the middle term is not, and so also the concept virtue. Thus it is inferred: original faculties are not virtue, which only by conversion becomes: no virtue is an original faculty. The thought has the concept virtue as its [p. 393] goal and makes straight for it. Hence the roundabout way indicated is hardly the natural course. We may therefore assert of those first moods (cesare, festino) that they present the real ground of negation; of the other two (camestres, baroco), the same only in a derived manner. In any case it is evident from this that the second figure too has a real significance, so far as, being negative, it can have one at all. The third and fourth figures we may not investigate in this direction; for they are artificial or ambiguous.

(2) Ibid.

Against Hegel's crabbedly intertwined theory of the three times three syllogisms, which are supposed to generate and articulate the system of things really, the indicated view of Aristotle on the real significance of the syllogism stands simple and plain. Whereas the former forces an artificial logical formalism upon things, the latter, conversely, gives the formal syllogism support and content in the development of things. The former volatilises the actual into a play of forms; the latter fills the form with the actual.

[p. 394]

## XIX. DIE ABLEITUNG AUS DEM BEGRIFF UND DIE BEGRÜNDUNG DURCH ZUFÄLLIGE ANSICHT. — XIX. DERIVATION FROM THE CONCEPT AND GROUNDING THROUGH CONTINGENT VIEW.

1. The syllogism is not the ultimate form of knowing. The universal major premise already comprises the conclusion which it only means to generate, and, in order to be true, itself presupposes it. Prosyllogisms multiply the difficulty but do not remove it. The syllogism would describe a circle if it did not have an origin that is no syllogism.

A fact proves that the syllogism is not that form of truth into which nothing false can be fitted. For from untrue premises something true can follow. Aristotle already carried this possibility carefully through the three figures. In hypotheses the same phenomenon merely repeats itself on a larger scale. From the false premises of a hypothesis conclusions are drawn which agree with the actual, and this derivation of true propositions carries and supports for a time the untenable presupposition. For example, the phenomenon of the [p. 395] lunar eclipse is derived just as consistently from the hypothesis of the Ptolemaic system of the world as from the Copernican.

(1) Analyt. pr. II. 2-5.

Not seldom a weakness of the syllogism lies where it operates with the indeterminate "some" and runs out into an indeterminate or even ambiguous "some." Only where it is entitled to posit the premises universally and to conclude universally does it have its full strength. And were it really so, as some logicians may imagine, that God thinks in syllogisms, then at least he would not think in the moods burdened with "some."

The quantitative universality which the syllogism demands is the expression of something necessary that rests on the community of thinking and being. This synthetically universal is the higher-lying source. In motion and in the end it appeared like a simple abstraction, yet so original that it presses forward into the concrete and regenerates it. In the original element the mind frees itself from the rigid syllogism. In creating (constructing) the image, it intuits the universal in the individual and is able to translate the necessary, which it grasps creatively, into external universality.

There are domains, such as history, in which the individual so prevails that they withdraw from the detour of the syllogism; and yet one infers in history and is able through inferences to comprehend its development. This is not accomplished by the universalities of experience. The greatest figures of history stand alone in their greatness, grounded in themselves, without their equal; and, arisen as it were from themselves, they give laws to experience without receiving them from it. Whoever comprehends such figures comprehends them from that part of living human development which is in himself, and through the re-creating thought aroused by these elements. Thus the syllogism, a cautious support, gives way to the freer, bolder mind. One goes toward the goal [p. 396] without measuring and counting the pendulum-beats of one's steps.

Here consideration returns to the first grounds discussed above. In motion, whose laws underlie experience, and in the end, which governs it spiritually, thought translates itself into intuition, and intuition remains in faithful union with thought. Through this fundamental relation alone is that glance possible which, like the idea of the artist, is at once individual and universal. Thought generates a pure image of the coming-to-be and intuits the universal law in it. What was said above about knowledge that prefigures in the a priori elements and knowledge that re-figures in experience finds its application here.

In the manner indicated, universal concepts arise and are now the norm of the phenomena that fall within their extension. Since the concept apprehends and preserves what is peculiar and necessary in the coming-to-be of the thing, one can in turn also know from it what is given potentially with the act of coming-to-be and then emerges when the thing enters into further relations. Such a derivation from the concept of the thing is a knowledge necessary in its origin and its progress. With such knowledge chance has vanished, and the mind rejoices in its pure property.

2. But the limits are narrowly set; care is taken that the trees do not grow into the sky. Experience is shot through with chance, and it is the common labour of the sciences, divided among the generations of mankind, as they draw their net ever tighter, to exclude chance and to win fixed points capable of generating the particular in synthetic development. Every age attempts in its own way to comprehend the contingently given as necessary and to gather the individual together into a synthetically universal. In attempting this, the [p. 397] mind, which would otherwise be buried in the contingent, seeks to rise again in victory over the external world. Every science works at this according to its part. From this calling springs, consciously or unconsciously, the enthusiasm of the inquirer. Even in the consideration of the most individual detail this universal striving makes itself known. But it is, as it were, the last day of the sciences when the whole of experience, variously clouded and strictly bound, is freed and transfigured in *one* great glance.

In mathematics, it seems, this goal of letting the individual come to be synthetically from the universal and of comprehending it in its coming-to-be ought to be most attainable, since mathematics proceeds from the element which, as the most original, underlies thinking and being. It does indeed stand at an admirable height, and from Plato to our own day the more ideal direction of knowledge has again and again raised itself up on the grand fact of mathematical science. But nevertheless chance seems still to play into the auxiliary lines of construction and into the methods of calculation to such a degree that Herbart in particular has grounded the doctrine of contingent view on their example.¹

The ground, Herbart teaches, is composite, and the composition produces the consequence. Hence in a derivation the ground at hand must be augmented by a contingent view in order to yield anything. Herbart illustrates this especially by the Pythagorean theorem, the pillar of all analysis. The usual proofs of it rest on a contingent view. It is a lucky stroke that one drops a perpendicular from the vertex of the right angle onto the base. Thereby one gains either, by the doctrine of similar triangles, proportions [p. 398] which by calculation yield the proposition, or a construction, as in Euclid,¹ which, by means of a new contingent view, a decomposition of the squares and parallelograms into triangles half as large, shows that the square of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the two legs. Everything here rests on the perpendicular drawn in, which augmented the figure. This intervention, says Herbart, is one of the artifices which we so often meet in mathematics, and whose effect consists in leading the object at hand into a known and finished series of representations, which then runs off of itself. These artifices enlarge the ground from which the consequence is to proceed. Thus one sees the initial ground first enlarge itself and then contract again. When, to take another example, the mixed quadratic equation becomes soluble by completing the square into a complete binomial, one takes a contingent view of the quantity x² + ax. In this way science advances through a contingent view, as Herbart seeks to illustrate by several examples.

(1) Herbart Metaphysik II. §. 174 ff., cf. Hartenstein die Probleme und Grundlehre der allgemeinen Metaphysik p. 138 ff.

So the glory of science, necessity, seems suddenly to evaporate, or at least to rest on the basis of its opposite, on the happy hit-or-miss of chance.³

(1) Elemente I. 47.

(2) Metaphysik II. 1829. p. 29.

(3) This agrees with what Hegel, in the fine section on the theorem (Logik III. p. 304 ff.), remarks about construction, p. 311: "Afterwards, in the proof, one does indeed see that it was purposive to draw such further lines on the geometrical figure as the construction specifies; but in the construction itself one must obey blindly: taken by itself this operation is therefore without understanding, since the end that guides it is not yet expressed. It is a matter of indifference whether it is a theorem proper or a problem for whose sake it is undertaken; as it first appears before the proof, it is something not derived from the determination given in the theorem or the problem, hence a senseless doing for one who does not yet know the end, but always something directed only by an external end."

[p. 399] Herbart, to be sure, has already sought to reassure us on this point and has shown, by the same Pythagorean theorem, that there are solutions which follow as guides only the concepts already lying in the problem and require only that one develop these concepts in the manner appropriate to them. We leave it undecided, however, whether a contingent view does not nevertheless remain in his proof, conducted by means of differentials, inasmuch as the infinitely small arc is after all set equal to the tangent in order to obtain similar triangles. Otherwise the solution of the problem might recommend itself by its genetic direction. Still we have only *one* happy example and no instruction as to how the proof is indicated by the concepts inherent in the problem. Herbart rather carries the contingent views, in the method of relations, on into metaphysics.

One thing seems certain. If in the mathematical domain, in which, by virtue of the original act of the mind, an insight into the evolution of grounds can be opened, chance cannot be banished but rather remains the unsteady foundation of necessity, then it will be possible in no science; for all are further removed from that first source. As matters stand, the chance of the apt view does indeed hold sway. It emerges clearly in the Euclidean proofs, and we may study this relation in them as in a model. In the auxiliary lines the contingent stroke first appears. Why this or that auxiliary line is to be drawn, whence its necessity, is not explained. The possibility of a straight line, of a circle, is postulated. Draw it now here or there: so runs the unconditional command. What comes of it [p. 400] must turn up. The auxiliary lines are the arbitrariness of the construction.

(1) Kästner indeed says (Anfangsgründe 4th ed. p. 428): "every geometrical textbook possesses the less of the proper value of geometry, clarity and certainty, the further it departs from Euclid's Elements."

We wish to mark out a way that is regulated entirely by the necessity of the concept, and to illustrate it by a couple of salient examples.

The concept of a thing apprehends its peculiarity. This peculiarity must contain, in the whole extent of possibility, the action and reaction of the thing. The point is to set out what lies therein. The concept has as its elements the next higher universal and the species-forming difference. What follows from the universal is determined in the particular by the specific difference. Hence the task is to apprehend the thing, as it were, at the point of contact of the universal and the particular. Where the two interpenetrate in living fashion, there the properties of the thing have their origin. Geometry will therefore have to design the construction so that the universal and the specific difference are presented in interaction. From such a construction the properties spring forth.

We shall make what has been said intuitive by the same example by which the dominion of contingent view in the midst of necessary knowing was just demonstrated, and for this purpose we consider the right-angled triangle.

The concept of the right-angled triangle readily resolves itself into its universal and the species-forming difference. From the universal there follow for the right-angled triangle the necessary properties of every triangle. The proposition that in a triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles contains the fundamental relation of the triangle in general. To this [p. 401] property of the angles the specific difference, right-angled, points. If both determinations are brought into connection, it follows that in the right-angled triangle, and only in it, one angle is equal to the two others. If now this exclusive property is presented in the general image of the right-angled triangle, as indeed the construction proceeding from the concept is what is sought, a twofold case necessarily results, in that the right angle divides itself into the two others; for the two angles at the base can have a twofold position within the right angle. Either the angle at the base on the right will also take the place on the right within the right angle, and the angle on the left the place on the left. Or the angles will exchange places, and the angle at the base on the right will be thrown over to the left side, and the angle at the base on the left to the right side, of the dividing line. Only these two constructions are possible; and precisely they at once yield the two principal theorems of the right-angled triangle.

(1) The old rule, already drawn up by Aristotle, of defining per genus proximum et differentiam specificam is here taken up and developed in its consequences.

In the first case there arise, in accordance with the construction, two isosceles triangles within the right-angled one. One of the equal sides is common to both triangles. The three equal sides thus radiate like radii from one point. Or, what is the same thing, a semicircle lays itself around every right-angled triangle in such a way that the hypotenuse forms the diameter.

In the second case there arise within the enclosing right-angled triangle triangles which are similar to one another and to the enclosing one, since two angles in these three triangles at once present themselves as equal. From this follows, by means of proportions, the Pythagorean theorem. One might suppose that this proof is one and the same as the so-called arithmetical one. The difference lies, however, in the construction. In the arithmetical one a perpendicular is dropped according to contingent view; in the one just [p. 402] attempted, what is demanded and indicated in the concept is constructed. That the line which divides the right angle into the two others is precisely a perpendicular follows only as an after-born property from the original construction and does not concern the consideration at all. Before there can be any talk at all of a square of the hypotenuse or of the legs, the theme of the multiplication of lines, obscure up to that point, must have gone before. The proof therefore presupposes nothing that must not, in a genetic development, be established before the theorem.

The construction was determined by nothing external, but solely by the elements of the concept. What lay tacitly in the nature of the thing has been realised. The universal and the difference (the generic and the specific) entered into interaction; and this projection of the concept, in which the synthetically universal emerged, at once revealed the necessary properties. The yield is surprising in the present case. No proposition expresses so essentially the nature of the right-angled triangle as the proposition that a semicircle can be described about every right-angled triangle, and the Pythagorean one, that the sum of the squares of the two legs is equal to the square of the hypotenuse. From these the remaining properties follow further. Both propositions belong to the most fruitful of the whole of geometry. They spring forth here, as at *one* stroke, from the simple construction of what is given in the concept. If now in the proposed procedure everything is determined by the necessity of the concept, contingent view has thereby become superfluous. What had to be demanded in general, but seemed unattainable, has been achieved in the particular instance.

What follows from the universal and the exclusively peculiar (from the generic and the specific) can belong only [p. 403] to the thing whose concept is taken as the basis, and to no other; for the specific difference, the source of the proof, cuts it off from all others, since it apprehends precisely what other things do not have. Where, therefore, a presentation of the exclusively peculiar, such as has just been attempted in the example, yields determinate propositions, these propositions belong as its own only to the object of the concept taken as the basis, and to no other. A perpendicular can be dropped from the vertex of every triangle. What follows from such an auxiliary line, as in the Euclidean proof of the Pythagorean theorem, therefore possibly follows for triangles other than the right-angled one as well. Hence it is necessary to prove the converse of the theorem. But since among plane triangles only the right-angled one is so constituted that one angle can be divided into the two others, the proposition follows as a specific one from such a specific construction. Or, if we translate this into the logical language of the system: in the case indicated it is superfluous still to seek a proof for the converse of the proposition. The proof of the principal proposition contains at the same time the proof of the converse. If it has been proved from the peculiar concept of the right-angled triangle that the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides, it follows that this relation, which flows from the exclusive nature of the right-angled triangle, always and everywhere indicates the right-angled triangle. That is the content of the converse proposition: if in a triangle the square of one side is equal to the sum of the squares of the two other sides, the triangle is right-angled. Whereas in the system the converse propositions for the most part lead to indirect proofs, on the proposed way one is spared these. So long as the proof of a proposition rests on a contingent view, and consequently on a contingent connection with other propositions, the possibility remains open that the property expressed in the proposition [p. 404] belongs equally to other figures too and is thus to be found more generally. The proof of the converse first removes this possibility, which remained over like a residue from the externally conducted proof, and is therefore unavoidable in this connection in order to establish the exclusive peculiarity.

(1) Cf. above vol. I. p. 291 ff.

The converse of a proposition can, according to the reciprocity of a function, have a still more real significance. The subject of a proposition presents itself as the ground of the predicate. In the formulation of the principal proposition, therefore, the concept of the subject appears as the original ground and the predicate as the derived property. If the proposition is converted, the predicate receives the place of the subject and so the significance of the original ground, and what was just now subject and ground receives the significance of the consequence. If actuality corresponds to this reciprocal relation, the mutual dependence of the members is thereby expressed. Neither has a prior right over the other. Each can be regarded as cause and in turn as effect of the other. Where this is the sense of a converse, a direct proof will be found for it just as for the first formulation, provided that the direct proof imitates the course of coming-to-be. Only then a contrary point of attachment is needed, a derivation from the contrary possibility of origination; and the proof of the converse proposition must renounce leaning merely on the principal proposition already established. Where the converse has the significance just indicated, it ought not to appear even in the system as the logical trick of an inference backwards, but as the expression of the contrary mode of origination.

In Euclid the most important propositions are proved only from the external connection and by means of contingent views, but not under the guidance of the elements necessarily given in the concept of the thing. Yet in some [p. 405] propositions what was just demanded has already been accomplished. Thus in particular the propositions on the parallelogram are established immediately from the specific difference of a figure enclosed by parallels. Compare, for example, the proposition¹ that the parallelogram is divided by the diagonal into two equal triangles. The exclusive property of the parallels and the cutting diagonal are therein solely the factors of the proof, and nothing is taken up from outside. In such models there already lies the impulse toward a higher logical completion of the system.²

When the theorem is sent ahead ready-made and the proof is dispatched after it, the whole looks like a series of rigid assertions which gain a foothold and then entrench themselves. So appear Euclid's Elements, so Spinoza's Ethics, and whatever other writings take the well-fortified way of Euclid. Everywhere there is an artful concatenation, but nowhere a coming-to-be and growing. The proposed way leads further. For it guides us to find what lies in the nature of the thing, not to secure, by a discovered connection, what has been found from elsewhere. The theorem is newly won and not merely externally vouched for.

3. No science has so fortunate a position as mathematics for developing its content from the concept of the thing. Hence analytic geometry too, which derives the properties and relations from the formulae of the figures, as from algebraic definitions of the thing, has reached an admirable height.

In no other science can the coming-to-be and essence of the object be so purely observed and therefore also so purely fixed in the concept. In no other [p. 406] science do the relations which can be given to the object, in order to call its dormant properties into actual life, lie in the same way in the hand of him who wishes to know the object. Nowhere does the element lie before us so purely, and nowhere is it in the same way accessible to the eye of the mind, since it is projected by the mind's own creative hand.

(1) Euklides Elemente I. 34.

(2) As a confirmation of this logical demand, Steiner's great achievements may perhaps be mentioned, on which, however, the author is not competent to judge.

Nevertheless the demand goes beyond mathematics. In the example treated we merely see in its simplest shape that task which must be set everywhere where the mind has taken possession of the origin of the thing and advances from it into the phenomena.

Where the peculiar grows into the universal, where the specific fuses with the generic, there, in every thing as in the geometrical theorem, is the seat of life. From there, as from the source, the phenomena and properties radiate forth. There the brighter image of the thing gathers, as in the focus of the lens.

If science wishes to advance synthetically and to guide its course with the necessity that lies in the nature of the thing, it has no other norm than to penetrate to the point where the universal is determined by the peculiar, the generic of the thing by its specific, and is as it were enlivened and fertilised. The concept of the thing fixes these elements. And a derivation that proceeds in this way is a development from the concept and completes knowledge in the particular. If now the concept, as it ought and as it does at the last stage, grasps those elements genetically, then the derivation from the concept indicated is only a continuation of the genetic procedure, which has first deposited its yield in the concept of the thing.

What in life is called a "glance" is something similar. Whoever, for example, apprehends the physiognomy he encounters in such a way as [p. 407] the particular bent in it, and in general the individual, is as it were interwoven with the universal nature of man, like warp and weft; whoever from this living point divines the bearing and the activity of the mind sketched out in the physiognomy; or whoever knows how to intuit, in a man, the abiding character and the momentary influences in their living relation and to survey them in their consequences; or whoever understands, in a work of art, the idea as it had to become embodied in this or that way in the particular material, or in general grasps the universal motive and the peculiar situation in one another; whoever in this way penetrates the universal with the peculiar and the peculiar with the universal and so judges from the living essence: to him one ascribes a glance. The procedure of science indicated is such a glance, only enlarged and elevated. Yet the difference is easily noticed. If the glance strikes that vital point of the thing with genius, but only in the individual case and without consciousness of the grounds, science does indeed follow this stroke of the mind, but it raises the individual to the universal, the unconscious to conscious necessity. In what we call a glance there is already one element more present, and a twofold motion is intertwined. The glance is fixed on the individual case, reads in it the universal and the peculiar, and from here projects its judgment. But this individual case is not yet present in the derivation from the concept; it is only won there.

The hardest thing always remains to win the basis of the procedure, the concept. Where science possesses it, it is no doubt able to exploit it in a similar way. If, for example, calculation is applied to a physical phenomenon, the concept formed of the latter seems as it were to form the specific difference to the more universal power of the mathematical element. The application is the living relation of the universal and the peculiar. This holds [p. 408] in law as in mathematics. Universal grammar seeks to understand the essential phenomena of language from logical concepts which are peculiarly determined by the condition of their presentation in sound. History comprehends the shapes of the world from the universal task of the age and from the tribal character of a people in conflict with the physical conditions of the land and the other stirring events. In the organism the determinate end appears as such a specific difference, which in interaction with universal life governs the activities and stamps the character. The examples presented above can also bear this out.¹ Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics (I. 6) seeks to determine ethical eudaemonia from the peculiar essence of man. These indications may suffice to show that in all sciences the same elements for a development from the concept are found as in the case of geometry carried through above. The more sharply that point is apprehended where the universal and the peculiar touch, limit and enliven each other, the more fruitful the derivation becomes, and the more the connections of contingent views are excluded.

The seed-grain, in order to germinate and grow, must be given back to the natural conditions out of which it itself came to be. Isolated, it remains shut up in itself. The concept behaves in a similar way. By itself it is indeed capable of formation, but it must be thought in the interaction of the context in order to develop.

A concept by itself alone never sets forth out of itself what lies in it, although it is often so presented, and the matter then appears more wonderful. Development never takes place [p. 409] from the *one* concept alone, progressive motion never from its own elastic force confined to itself. Development presupposes stimulating elements in the external world, motion a resistance against which the force pushes itself onward. It is similar in the mind. Concepts must work together in order to produce something new. It is the creative act of the mind to apprehend this working together and to project the new from it. For example, the concept of the circle, which is simple in itself, does not develop from itself alone into the propositions on the relations of chords and tangents and on the relation of the angles within the circle. The concept of the straight line must be added, and what they generate together is the development of the concept, or properly of both concepts.

(1) Cf. above vol. II. p. 8ff., where Cuvier in natural history proceeds exactly as we illustrated the higher demand by the geometrical example.

With derivation from the concept there results an organic form of knowledge. The form does not stand externally over against the material, so that it would merely be added as the ordering factor. Form and content generate themselves, as it were, together. Every organic development proceeds from a whole (the seed and germ), and since the power of the whole remains the dominant factor, the parts become members which serve the whole and in which the whole is mirrored. In the procedure indicated, the concept is this whole, which carries through the power of its law in manifold knowledge. Hence the derivation from the concept here attempted, and only this, is called development.

4. The procedure indicated is synthetic and presupposes the full knowledge of the concept of a thing as the basis of derivation. But how many concepts then lie so open in their grounds? How many things can then be observed in their coming-to-be, so as to let themselves be gathered synthetically into a concept? What was possible in numerical and spatial magnitudes repeats itself with the same strictness perhaps only in simple ethical relations.

Most concepts must be lifted out of the phenomena by the analytic way, [p. 410] and the question arises whether on this course from the phenomenon to the grounds a necessity is possible similar to that in the synthetic development of the concept.

The analytic procedure first considers the phenomenon and seeks in it the traces which the essence of the generating concept has left behind. What does it hold to in the phenomenon? First, perhaps, to an articulation of the parts. But in order even to find the joints of the parts, one needs a guiding representation of the whole, from which one divines the significance of the parts. Even analytic decomposition is guided by a provisional construction of the causal connection. In order to dissect (analyse) the phenomenon, one needs points of view that stem from the whole or are taken from known cases of coming-to-be. Only through the open or tacit help of this synthetic element is this first step of the analytic procedure taken. Without it we should always remain within the phenomenon. Such a linking of synthetic points of view with the analytic procedure is a contingent view.

Where the analytic procedure advances with certainty, it combines out of a fund of specific causal connections whose possession is already secure.¹ Where it newly invents, it mostly follows the thread of analogy or gives a creative construction its fixed data. In all these cases the analytic procedure goes by the hand of a synthesis.

How known causal connections (synthetic elements) form the supports in the analytic procedure [p. 411] shows itself most simply and purely in the analytic problems of mathematics. To solve the analytic problem of a division, one needs insight into the genesis of the number system, and we make use of the synthetic results of the multiplication table. For the extraction of a root one needs knowledge of the binomial law. Other problems can be solved only by means of logarithms already calculated. Every equation demands operations guided by a supreme end (e.g. to isolate x); the knowledge of what can be done with the equation without cancelling the expression of an equation, the knowledge of the means for this end, is just as synthetic as the guiding point of view itself. In the solution of an equation one easily distinguishes synthetic elements which are subordinated as members to the universal analytic method, e.g. in the usual derivation of Cardano's formula for the reduced cubic equation, the assumption x = y + z, 3yz + p = 0, y = (y³)2 6 etc. The acumen of the method lies in skilfully combining the possible decompositions and compositions for the determinate end. But to know what is possible is only the consequence of an insight opened into the coming-to-be, and therefore a synthetic element. In the analytic problems of geometry the same shows itself, as even the simplest cases prove. If a circle is to be described through three points which do not lie in a straight line, one thinks of the circle as drawn. Then the points form the ends of chords, and the perpendiculars at the midpoints of the two chords pass through the centre. Where the perpendiculars intersect, there the centre must lie. The synthetic element here is in particular the proposition that the perpendiculars erected at the midpoint of a chord pass through the centre. Or if a triangle is to be inscribed in a circle which is equiangular (similar) to a given triangle,¹ then the [p. 412] tangent, which is drawn first in order to lay off at the point of contact a chord making one of the angles of the triangle, is a contingent view, but one that has arisen from knowledge of the causal connection that every angle at the circumference standing on this chord as the base of the required triangle is equal to the angle constructed at the tangent. This construction of the tangent is only an attack upon the matter, or as it were only like a substructure which is broken away again when the vault is finished. If a circle touching the three sides is to be inscribed in a given triangle,¹ the bisection of the angle is the contingent view, the synthetic element of the analysis. What is evident here from examples of that science in which method appears most purely holds equally in others. If a difficult passage in an author is to be explained, an analytic problem lies before us; for the expression, the appearance as it were of the thought, is to be led back to its producing ground. The mind created the word and the sentence as its external form (synthetically); and understanding is this reanimation of the husk with one's own mind. Analysis at once appears here as a synthesis turned backwards. The passage is understood only when the indications of the appearance are sharply grasped and, in accordance with them, the knowledge of words and forms (synthetic elements) is combined. In the domain of law, circumstantial proof is an analytic problem; but it comes about only because one already knows causal connections of intentions and actions, of moods of the soul and their expressions, of instruments and their effects, etc. The fact is dissected, but the dissection is compared with the possibilities arising from these synthetic elements. The analytic way, the way from the broadly poured-out phenomenon to the simple [p. 413] ground, has a wider scope than the synthetic, since with *one* act the phenomenon is produced. With *one* radius the circumference is generated from the *one* centre; but on the circumference there are infinitely many points from which one strives back to the centre in order to find the radius. In the same way the synthetic procedure is more bound, the analytic more manifold and more subject to chance. What Herbart demonstrates concerning the contingent view that cooperates in grounding has its proper place in the analytic procedure and must there be recognised as essential.

(1) On the certain and uncertain in proof from signs (the analytic circumstantial proof) Aristotle already speaks in the Rhetoric (I. 2. p. 1357a 32ff.) and judges it aptly according to the laws of the syllogistic figures. Cf. the author's "Erläuterungen zu den Elementen der aristotelischen Logik." 2nd ed. on §. 37. p. 77ff.

(1) Euklides Elemente IV. 2.

(1) Euklides Elemente IV. 4.

5. Where synthetic points of view leading directly to the ground do not immediately offer themselves to the analytic procedure, there it commonly follows analogy, the most widespread kind of contingent view.

It may at first sight seem as if analogy were initially without objective logical significance and nothing but the psychological association of ideas. When the course of representations shoots onward by itself, without being guided and regulated by the methodical consideration of the matter, this flow is driven and renewed by the similarity of the things represented. One similar representation awakens another, as if according to a physical law of attraction, and the images of things spring up in the mind according to this relation. It may seem as if the analogy of logic rested only on this involuntary connection. The logical course would then be wholly abandoned to chance. For that arousal of representations through an elective affinity depends besides on many influences, in particular on temporal succession, on intervening series, and on the vividness of the first apprehension. It is not to be denied that the improvising association of representations [p. 414] can contribute to a quick and happy apprehension of analogy; but its logical essence does not lie in this.

(1) On the formal side of the syllogism of analogy we have spoken above, see section XVIII. vol. II. p. 372 ff.

Analogy follows an indeterminate view. From the selfsame conditions the same phenomenon proceeds. For this no proof is needed. But must the same phenomena necessarily have *one* ground? Must similar phenomena have a kindred ground? The first is not necessary; the second still less. But since the similar approaches the equal, one sets the difference aside provisionally in order to arrive from an unknown domain at a known one. Every analogy, on account of this indeterminate foundation, remains a hypothesis until it proves itself. But as an attempt to form a concept it has great significance.

Analogy presents itself in the sciences partly as analogy of identity, partly as analogy of co-ordination. In the first case the circle of the same concept widens, and phenomena that were separate flow into a unity. In the other case the phenomena do indeed meet in a higher universal, but they shape themselves out of it anew and peculiarly. The pull of the similar has, in the one kind as in the other, initiated the greatest discoveries, but not completed them.

The phenomena lie there separated. The less known is compared with the known. The similarity is taken as the point of attachment, and the unity running through both is found. In such cases analogy runs out into identity. When Newton comprehended the motions of the heavenly bodies from terrestrial gravity, so that in his view *one* force of attraction reveals itself in both; when the properties of attraction and repulsion first observed in rubbed amber extend into the most various phenomena, as far as the electrical phenomena of meteors; when the perceived force of the [p. 415] lodestone, like an inconspicuous beginning, widens into terrestrial magnetism; or when the currents of the winds, dependent on the sun, are understood from the draught of heated rooms: then in these cognitions, on which the centuries labour, it is analogy that is first at work. It is the nearest point of view for connection and illuminates what is remote. Identity is its result.¹

It may happen, however, that the phenomena do not have an identical ground and do not run out into *one* substantial determination, but nevertheless agree in individual cooperating conditions of the ground or in the species-forming differences. Then analogy leads to a co-ordinate concept. What is common, uniting the phenomena, shapes itself in each in accordance with the other, differing conditions. An example of this kind lies before us in the theory of light, of sound and of heat, in which more and more analogies are being worked out, e.g. in propagation, reflection, etc.² The agreeing phenomena lead to an agreeing element of grounding. The analogies of history which instruct us accomplish the same; for events do not recur as the same; but equal conditions which emerge in the sum of the events of an age remind us in advance to expect equal phenomena, even if these are determined differently by the other influences, and equal phenomena remind us to seek similar conditions.

In the first case analogy hits upon the substance of the concept; in the second, with differing essence, an equal secondary determination. In both cases it attempts to form a [p. 416] concept or its essential constituents. But it does not complete the concept; it generates it only by half and skips the closer determination, since it is directed only to what is equal, whether this be the essence or the manner in which something otherwise different appears. This other half of concept-formation, which first gives analogy support and firmness, is a peculiar synthesis in the midst of the analysis of experience.

(1) This process of knowledge extending itself through analogy has been presented in detail by Gruppe in individual examples. Wendepunkt der Philosophie im neunzehnten Jahrhundert. 1834. p. 34 ff.

(2) Cf. e.g. Baumgärtner's Naturlehre. 5th ed. §. 254.

Examples readily illustrate this. If at first the analogy of free motion guided Newton's thought when he traced back the fall of bodies on earth and the motion of the heavenly bodies to one and the same attraction of masses, it was his penetration that, in the solar system, balanced this attraction toward the centre by the centrifugal force and diverted it into elliptical motion. This fusion was the synthesis in the analogy. The analogy led to the decomposition of elliptical motion into centripetal and tangential force. Without a construction comprehending both, the thought was not possible. When further Newton, following the analogy of a rotating soft mass, asserted the flattening of the earth at the poles before any investigation by measurements of degrees, the analogy gave only the universal. How great this flattening is, the specific difference of the concept, remained to be determined. When finally Newton, in whose scientific discoveries analogy plays so great a part, surmised from optical grounds, namely from the ratio of the refracting power of a ray of light, which he investigated in a series of transparent substances, to the density of their masses, a combustible constituent of water, which until then had been believed undecomposed and simple (for water had in that series a middle position between combustible and incombustible substances¹), the acute remark was only an indication; but later [p. 417] chemistry fulfilled it, when it separated water into hydrogen and oxygen, a combustible constituent and one that serves combustion. In the first examples analogy divined the essence of the thing, in the last only a single side or relation; there the task remains to establish the universal essence in the peculiar difference of the thing; here, on the contrary, to carry the difference in its determinateness over to the essence of the thing. When analogy, as we mentioned, led to tracing back the phenomena of colours and of tones alike to wave-vibrations, this gives only *one* common side; the domains throw light on one another in this *one* respect; but the determination of the concept is only half. In what different element do these vibrations take place in these phenomena? Does the wave-motion have the same direction in both, or is it longitudinal in the one, transverse in the other? Such and similar questions, in answering which science first strives to give its object full determinateness, complete the acquisition of analogy.

(1) Is. Newton optice 1706. p. 232 ff.

In recent times language has been conceived as an individual function of the whole organic life, and the investigated laws of the organism illuminate the phenomena of language in a great analogy. But if what is most significant was not to be lost in this resemblance, then the peculiar essence of language, as it proceeds from the spiritual life of man, had always to form the ground-plan, for which those analogies supply the points of view of the execution. This apprehension of the particular essence, and this working of the analogy into this essence, is a synthetic and as it were artistic deed. What is here indicated in actual events of the sciences could also be made evident in the example borrowed above from Aristotle. "The war of the Athenians with the Thebans is ruinous; for the war of the Thebans with the Phocians, their neighbours on the border, brought calamity." So runs the analogy, which, in the convincing power of the individual case, warns against [p. 418] war with neighbours in general and therefore also against the war of the Athenians with the Thebans. The analogy, however, gives the matter only by half; and the orator who chooses this example has to complete the universal thought into a picture, by presenting, in an insightful connection of the prevailing circumstances, the calamity that is to be expected in the case at hand.

In individual investigations it can still be shown historically how analogy formed the thread by whose guidance they advanced. Thus, for example, the conditions of the sense of sight have been investigated most finely and most completely of all the senses. One knows the after-images, the subjective phenomena of vision, and so on, and their laws, to a great extent and to a high degree of depth and precision. But since the senses, in their common vocation of appropriating the external world to the mind, must also present common phenomena, the known conditions of the sense of sight have been used in order to search for similar phenomena of the other senses, for example for subjective phenomena of hearing, of taste, and so on. The transference of the points of view from one domain to another, the forming of the analogy into the particular sphere, at once oversteps the analogy itself. In the sciences of language the richer languages already investigated form the standard that is applied to the phenomena of the new ones. The comparison leads to knowledge of what is peculiar.

If we trace in general the first beginnings of scientific discoveries and theories, they lie for the most part in the connection of analogies. Such a contingent view opens a deeper glance. Since, however, it always presupposes relations already known, from which the points of view are borrowed, it already follows that analogy cannot be the original method of investigation, and that other domains must open themselves to the mind independently of [p. 419] analogy, through the consideration of the matter itself. As, therefore, according to the above, analogy, where it is the guide, leaves the most essential part of the task to be solved by another procedure, so it itself moves on a foreign basis.

Usually analogy is relegated, as an individual and subordinate procedure, to natural science, or is treated contemptuously as an element of Epicurus's unscientific logic. But no procedure governs all the sciences more universally than analogy, and one forgets what insights one owes to it. Whence has Plato's system its grand unity and its surprising symmetry? The same analogy of the whole that is mirrored in the part and is therefore to be known from the part, the same analogy of archetype and copy, of the Same and the Other, the same harmony of measure, recurs everywhere and illuminates the most diverse domains with the same creative unity, whether Plato in the Timaeus compares the world-soul and the human soul, or in the Politie sketches the state from the individual or the characters from the constitution, or finds in the conditions of the sense of sight the higher relations of knowledge as a whole.¹ The survey of affinity which Plato demands of dialectic, the pleasing proportion which distinguishes the architectonic of the whole edifice, rests on the logical ground of analogy. But from Plato one also learns to distinguish a deep analogy, which penetrates into the essence of the matter, from a shallow comparison.

6. Analogy by itself alone is nothing but a hypothesis or the provisional basis of consideration. For it is not necessary that a similar phenomenon have an [p. 420] equal ground. The hovering thought seeks a hold and strikes root only through foreign help.

(1) Particularly in the last passage (Staat VI. p. 507ff. St.) the beautiful analogy is carried through quite evidently, and it is mirrored still in the symmetrical sections of the domains of knowledge.

The confirmation of every hypothesis lies in a peculiar combination of analysis and synthesis. The provisional concept is constructed synthetically in its consequences. With these consequences, which must result if the concept is true, the phenomena which the concept is to satisfy are compared analytically. Two processes are to coincide with each other: the logical, which would reproduce the world in the mind, and the real, which lies before knowledge as its task. The end-points of the real process come to light in the phenomena. The starting-point of the logical process is seized by thought. From this germ the mind develops what it contains, and thereby also gains end-points of the logical process; and now the judgment becomes possible whether the end-points of the two processes correspond. If this is the case, then with every compared consequence of the provisional concept the hope grows that the starting-points too, and thus the whole motions, coincide; but only the hope grows; for possibly false premisses have yielded what is true. From the phenomenon the ground is divined, and the divined ground is driven out into the consequences which it must have, as into its proper phenomena. Whether these coincide entirely and in every respect with those is the test of the assumption. A single incongruity already makes it doubtful, unless the phenomena of the real ground have not been correctly observed or the phenomena of the logical ground not correctly derived.

A hypothesis maintains itself by combining with those concepts that already stand secure. Where these contradict the assumption, it suffers an attack and runs into danger; where, on the other hand, they confirm the view in a concordant spirit, it fortifies itself through this support.

(1) See above II. p. 394.

[p. 421] Our whole world of concepts presents the spectacle of *one* great hypothesis. Our representations are always measured against the phenomena. The concepts that have been investigated stand firm; those that are forming still hover. The hovering ones seek to gain ground by wishing to support themselves on the firm ones or to hold on to them. Thereupon an attracting and repelling arises, according as they are compatible or incompatible. It may happen that in this struggle the concept believed to be firm is defeated by the hostile new one, in that the latter knows how to set the firm concept at variance with the other concepts and with the phenomena, and itself in harmony with them. Before the firm ones took root, they had to withstand the same struggle. In this interaction the realm of the knowing mind arises and grows and maintains itself. Whoever regards truth as a finished and secure possession of the mind will no doubt, when he perceives this pervasive struggle, fall into sceptical misgivings. But the mind knows no idle inheritance; it calls its own only what it has acquired and maintains. This labour is its pride and the common good of the race.

The form of hypothesis is the manner of every concept in the making. When the representations of the child are educated by the things themselves, it proceeds unconsciously according to the same law according to which mature science attempts to establish a provisional concept. The child has a representation of the shining object that is held out to it. It reaches for it. It misses at first, and now tries to sharpen the representation and reaches anew, until it attains the object and, as it were through the consequence of its representation, becomes certain of the truth of the latter. So man grows up, regulating his representations by success and by the phenomena. What is certain to him stands firm for him through this agreement. Science proceeds no differently when, instead of the mere representation turned toward the phenomenon, it seeks the concept of the ground. All that happens is that the [p. 422] intermediate links multiply, and the synthetic deed of the mind becomes more chained together and more intertwined.

In knowledge produced in this way there arises between concept and consequences an organic interaction. The provisional concept produces the consequences, and the consequences confirm the concept. Thus *one* life pervades the whole process.

If, according to the whole investigation we have just conducted, the analytic method advances only through the synthetic, the dissecting only through the inventive, then the creative power rises in all the sciences, and the humility of the empirical sciences is mere show when they claim to arise and grow only through observation, only through what they faithfully take in from without. Through perception alone they would forever remain only on the surface of things, just as, conversely, without observation they would never reach the depth from which the wide, shining surface rises.

7. In the above the genetic method has been presented as the last and consummating one. It rests on the matter's being known from its producing grounds. If these are only the efficient cause, the method follows this alone; if, on the other hand, the end determines the efficient cause, then the end becomes the guiding thought of the method in the same measure as it conditions the origination.
