In the former case, what precedes in the ground is also earlier in actuality; in the latter, the grounding end is indeed earlier as a co-operating thought, but later as attained actuality, and is precisely only the result. In the genetic procedure, therefore, the grounds of the matter are also the grounds of knowing, and because the former are earlier, be it really, as in the efficient cause, or ideally, as in the end, so too are the latter. What grounds cannot in this method be the result, as it is, say, in the regressively inferring, dissecting procedure of analysis.

[p. 423] Against this view an important declaration of Hegel's is raised. In the speculative, everywhere "what is at first posited as following is rather to be the absolute prius, the truth of that through which it appears as mediated." The appearance in the scientific sequence would accordingly not be the sequence in the development of the matter; rather, the order would be precisely reversed. The case for which this assertion is inculcated may serve as an example. From the dialectic of subjective spirit there develops in Hegel's system objective spirit: first formal abstract right, then the right of the subjective will, morality, and finally the substantial will, ethical life, and indeed as family, civil society and state. In the dialectic of world history, further, objective spirit sublates itself. In the objective knowing of living ethical life the externalities of the world-spirit and the oppositions of finitude are stripped away, and this knowing thereby raises itself to the knowing of absolute spirit and gives birth to itself first in art, then in religion, until at last it frees and completes itself in philosophy. That is the course of the highest method, dialectic; but the course of the matter is precisely the reverse. Art is begotten and nourished by religion above all; and the whole history of art bears witness to this. In the "appearance of the scientific sequence," however, the dialectical spirit of art conversely brings forth religion. The state rests in its actuality on the ethical disposition, and this on the religious, and "develops out of religion." In the dialectical method, which alone claims to be method in the true sense, the state is conversely developed without religion, without consciousness of the divine, and so strictly by itself that the church is wholly foreign to it. But since the state goes first and [p. 424] religion follows after, it is precisely "in the nature of this transition from the state to religion" that it is supposed to lie expressed that religion is "the basis of the state, being in and for itself, the source and power which has founded and brought forth it and its constitution," since, namely, religion, in which individuals have their deepest consciousness, pervades and shapes the state. Now can one understand the state scientifically without having understood this producing ground? The dialectical method demands it, and since it comprehends the state without religion (its basis), it sees precisely in this a guarantee that religion really is its basis. This paradoxical doctrine is extended to the appearance of the scientific sequence in general. For, as we have already stated, in the speculative "what is at first posited as following is rather the absolute prius." "The backward-going grounding of the beginning and the forward-going further determining coincide and are the same." In other words: the consequence of the concept is precisely the ground of the thing. The development of the highest scientific method stands in inverse relation to the development of the matter. Thus the genetic procedure, in which ground of knowing and ground of being go together, is turned outright on its head.

(1) Encyklopaedie §. 563. Remark.

(2) ibid. §. 563. p. 511. 2nd edition.

(3) It stands only like an allotrion in a remark, Hegel's Rechtsphilosophie §. 270.

The scientific order and the order of actual origination do, to be sure, stand in inverse relation when one infers back from the consequences to the ground, when from the indications of the phenomena, as mere grounds of knowing, the ground of being is gathered. This hardly needs explanation. When, for example, the shape of the terrestrial spheroid is worked out from the segments of the arc measurements, or the former whole shape of a building from its ruins, or the essence of the primal ground from the fragments of our view of the world, then what is inferred, which in [p. 425] the scientific appearance comes after, is indeed, according to the order of the matter, what is absolutely earlier. What grounds the matter and goes first in the matter is found in knowledge as what is grounded, and is therefore what is later in consideration. We have shown above how such a procedure must still supplement itself. Does dialectic perhaps wish to be nothing other than such a regressive inference? Then its laborious course, its artful unfolding, would be only a history of human consciousness, in which the grounds lying behind spring forth little by little. Whoever took it for this alone would earn no thanks from it. Often enough it has declared that it merely looks on at how the matter makes itself. Where, therefore, this inversion of earlier and later takes place, there dialectic does not wish to be; and where it wishes to be, there this common inversion does not take place.

(1) Logik III. p. 350.

Dialectic seeks to comprehend the shape which it lets arise in the mind in its origination. If the origination does not take place from the full grounds (the source and basis of the shape comes only afterwards), then the shape remains incomplete and distorted; and since the concept has its measure only in that origination which it follows, it becomes just as incomplete and distorted.

This shows itself precisely in the example of art and religion, whose position in the system is chiefly supposed to be protected by that doctrine of the reversed course.

The state does not produce religion as free fall produces accelerated motion, or a throw a curve, or motion in general a figure. Hence the state does not precede religion as the concept of the efficient cause from which the product is comprehended. Just as little is the state the means of religion, religion the end of the state, such that religion, as the end attained through the state, would have to follow the state. And were this the case, the very concept of the state would be governed by the thought of this end, and even then the state [p. 426] could not be comprehended in its directions without religion. Rather, it is acknowledged in a fine way in the same passage that religion, as the animating disposition, determines from within the directions of the state and pervades its institutions. The state "rests on religion" and "develops out of religion." Hence the state is evidently as little comprehended without religion as the body without the moving, directing soul. One would not even believe one had understood a machine if one knew only the gearing of the wheels and not also the moving force, or knew the latter but not the directing end. How then would one comprehend the state with such gaps? For in the state the religious disposition that animates it is at work, now moving quietly, like a driving wind, now directing in the midst of the passions, like the pole star upon the restless sea. One must therefore regard the clause that the scientific order is the reverse of actual origination only as a clause, since it is no more than that. If one brings to life the real content of what is conceded in that passage as the basis of the matter, and lets it react upon the conception of the state, then the dialectical development of the state reveals itself as incomplete and insufficient. Either the state rests on religion, and then the state is not comprehended. Or the state is comprehended, and then it does not rest on religion, and religion comes afterwards and appears at most like the ornament attached to the finished house. As little as the development of the Germanic state can be understood without Christianity, so little is religion a dialectical shape which first raises itself through the negation of the state. If comprehending constitutes the concept, then the sequence of the concept, which develops the state by itself and religion out of the state, is a hysteron proteron of dialectic. The inconsistency betrays itself. For in the philosophy of world history, which concludes the philosophy of right and [p. 427] precedes the philosophy of religion, the substance of the individual states is everywhere derived, profoundly and in accordance with the matter, from their religion. Thus in the midst of the system concrete religion appears with its power before one knows through the system what religion is, before the method has grasped religion. The same inconsistency repeats itself in the philosophy of art. In the dialectical system it precedes religion. For revealed religion is supposed, through the negative moment, to set itself over against art,¹ until both (through the negation of the negative) sublate themselves into their truth, philosophy. But in the matter it is otherwise. Art in its greatness and depth was conceived and born of the devotion of religion, and grew and ripened in the life of the cult. Art builds temple and church for the religious idea, presents its image, and lets its soul become tone and its spirit word. The different epochs, the different styles, are comprehended only from the different directions of religion. Aesthetics must therefore, as it in fact does in Hegel, reach ahead into the following shape of the system, into revealed religion. Thus the edifice is broken through in order to borrow light through an opening. If, with respect to the whole system, which strictly seeks to comprehend the one shape from the other, such an anticipation appears as inconsistency, it is on the other hand the consistency of the individual matter and its right. The eye for the matter has here grasped more correctly than the artificial dialectic.²

(1) Cf. Encyklopaedie §. 556 ff.

(2) It is by the same consistency that an exposition of the philosophy of right, whose author originally started from Hegel, drew the religious moment into the very midst of the state and thereby destroyed the whole dialectical articulation. People have not failed to designate this shaping as an apostasy. But such an apostasy is necessary as soon as one ceases to rest content with the formal distinction of that remark, which is thrown up like an entrenchment of the dialectical course, and as soon as one begins to introduce the living material it contains into the life of thought. That remark is caught in a conflict. Either it prevails with its end, that the state should scientifically precede religion, and then it kills the rest of its content. Or this content prevails, and one recognises that religion is the soul of the state, full of disposition, and then the remark annihilates its own intention, and one will no longer believe in the possibility of comprehending the state without religion, as the dialectical system had undertaken.

[p. 428] What takes place in the scientific sequence of state and religion is supposed to be, in the speculative in general, the legitimate order. What is at first posited as following is everywhere to be the absolute prius. This expression has been explained, with regard to the position of the state relative to religion, to mean that the state rests on religion and develops out of religion. What follows (religion) is a co-shaping ground of what is earlier (the state). This relation is supposed to repeat itself over the whole domain of dialectic. Alongside it stands the indeterminate expression that what is later is the truth of what is earlier. If this is understood according to the image that originally underlay this manner of speaking, then what is later is the truth of what is earlier as the fruit is said to be the truth of the blossom.¹ Then the state would be the blossom and religion its fruit. But what is later is rather supposed to be the "basis" on which what is earlier rests, the "source" from which it springs. This view cannot be carried through, in particular, in the dialectical development of nature. Or are, say, magnetism and electricity in the so-called physics of total individuality the truth of an earlier sphere, for example of fall, in such a way that fall rests on magnetism and develops out of magnetism? Or are, say, in the unfolding of subjective spirit, imagination and thinking the truth of the natural soul, of sensation, and so on, in such a way that those higher stages would be the "basis and source" of these lower ones? And yet all this and much more would have to be made to rhyme if that supposed reversed order of actual origination [p. 429] and scientific appearance really extended over the whole system. Rather, the dialectical development, from mechanics on into psychology, keeps at least on the whole to the course of development of nature. What has been pronounced as a universal law of the speculative we can therefore, on the testimony of the matter itself, regard only as a particular makeshift, to appease the suddenly appearing conflict between the sequence of the method and the sequence of the matter. The only question is how long science can rest content with such a cleverly devised distinction. In the Middle Ages the greatest struggles over scientific questions were talked to rest by distinctions, for as long as that would serve. Nor is more than a distinction given in that remark. But the matter breaks through such a separation, and once the contradiction is recognised at so clear a point, people will soon also cease to believe that the contrived form of dialectic is the strong natural pinion of the mind.

(1) Phänomenologie, Preface, p. 4.

Thus, then, what the whole investigation yielded is confirmed by the objection itself. A matter is fully understood only on the path by which it itself originates. Let the dialectical method go on disdaining the genetic, which in its opinion presents only the historical development of objects;¹ let it for a while yet sustain in the world the belief that one must go still higher than to know from the actual grounds of the matter, from the full conditions of origination, and thus from the origin itself. It furnishes the counter-proof itself.²

The goal remains the ultimate one which Spinoza already set for science when he demanded that the concatenation of concepts should present the concatenation of nature. Spinoza, to be sure, could [p. 430] demand this with twofold consistency, since he admitted only the efficient cause. He also restricted consideration to the series of "fixed and eternal things" and excluded the changeable ones.¹ But what Spinoza confined to this narrow circle has a more universal significance beyond it.

(1) Rosenkranz Wissenschaft der logischen Idee. 1858. 1859. II. p. XI.

(2) Seevol. I. p. 80 p. 92 f. Remark.

(1) Cf. Spinoza de intellectus emendatione opp. ed. Paul. II. p. 449 ff "concatenationem intellectus, quae naturae concatenationem referre debet" etc. Sed notandum est me hic per seriem causarum et realium entium non intelligere seriem rerum singularium mutabilium, sed tantummodo seriem rerum fixarum aeternarumque."

[p. 431]

## XX. DER INDIREKTE BEWEIS. — XX. THE INDIRECT PROOF.

1. The genetic proof does not depart from the course of what is, and finds its measure in it. The indirect proof, which has precisely what is not as its basis, forms the opposition to it. Whereas the former lets necessity come to be, the latter establishes it by delimitation. It is shown that the assumption of the (contradictory) opposite is impossible.

Everything that falls outside a posited concept is repelled and annihilated from other fixed points, so that the boundaries are thereby closed and only what lies within them remains over as the sole possible remainder. But what all falls outside a concept? If the concept itself is affirmative, an infinite circumference of the opposite is designated by the negation. In order to find out the affirmative cases that are contained in it, there is need of a universal insight, of a larger, encompassing concept, which lies beyond mere negation. The acuteness of the indirect proof shows itself further in this, that something which is merely thought (the contradictory opposite) is thrown into the connection of the actual as if it were actual, in order that it may maintain itself in this connection [p. 432] or give itself up. Since the basis is what is not actual, the help of intuition is lacking here. The whole procedure remains within thinking. While the direct proof keeps calmly and simply to the indicative, the indirect is as it were the struggle of the decided indicative against the supple conditional. The victory is the confirmation of the necessary.

In the indirect proof it is not the generating power of the origin of a concept that expresses itself, but the repulsion of the neighbouring propositions, or in general of what is already known.

If a negative judgment is to be proved, this happens genetically in the indirect proof; for negation is nothing other than the repelling force of the positive. The indirect proof leads to this source. For example, an equilateral triangle is not right-angled; for otherwise the sum of all the angles of the triangle would be equal to three right angles. The fixed proposition that in a triangle the sum of the angles is equal to two right angles refutes the consequence and thereby denies its ground. The first negative theorem in Euclid (elem. I. 7) is proved indirectly. Cf. elem. III. 4. III. 5. III. 6. In German the conjunction *sonst* ("otherwise") introduces the indirect proof.

Since the negative judgment is grounded indirectly, the indirect proof is the proof of refutation, which with the power of the actual defeats the false presupposition, and in particular the proof of negative criticism. Refutation rests everywhere on indirect proofs. For example, before Olaus Römer's discovery it was assumed in natural science that light appears instantaneously at the illuminated body. But were this the case, the eclipses of Jupiter's satellites would not be perceived a quarter of an hour later when the sun stands between Jupiter and the earth than at the time when both planets are on the same side of the sun. In this fact the velocity of light is observed. Therefore illumination does not take place [p. 433] instantaneously. — Newton assumed that light passing close by bodies is bent, as though attracted by them. Fresnel refutes him. His proof is indirect.¹ "If forces of attraction or repulsion proceed from the edges of the diffracting body, acting with less energy upon the more distant particles of light than upon those grazing past more closely, then one does indeed understand how condensations or rarefactions now arise in their previously uniformly dense mass. But the particles of light emerging from the not far-extending sphere of action of those edges would then, moving in a medium acting equally upon them on all sides, have to shoot onward in straight lines. Those alternately bright and dark bands arising at the edge of the shadows, however, prove, when they are caught at different distances from the shadow-casting body, to be hyperbolically curved; such a bright band cannot therefore be the visible path of the same particles of light." What is here to be refuted, and in the end turns out not to be actual, is at the beginning assumed as true. From this assumption there follows, according to the co-operating conditions, as soon as a certain distance is reached, rectilinear motion. The fact, however, shows hyperbolic curvature. This actuality defeats the mere assumption. There results therefore (modo tollente) the negative judgment that those so-called phenomena of diffraction do not arise through attracting or repelling forces. — What appears here in examples from natural science shows itself likewise throughout the domains of the science of language and of history. For example, the peace of Cimon was not concluded; for had it been, Thucydides could not have kept silent about it, Cimon could not [p. 434] immediately afterwards have undertaken his incursions into the Thracian Chersonese, and so on. Such facts overturn the assumption of the peace, and the negating assertion draws its force from these positive grounds.

(1) Dove die neuere Farbenlehre mit anderen chromatischen Theorien verglichen 1838. p. 3. Cf. another example in the same work p. 10, Brewster's proof that the colours of the prismatic image of the sun are not homogeneous. What is added as positive to this indirect proof is, logically considered, only hypothesis.

In all these cases the positive opposite of the purely negative judgment is the point which stirs up a whole series of thoughts, in order to rule or fall with it. If the assertion is correct, it can take into itself what is correct lying alongside it, or at least be compatible with it. If it is incorrect, it will either annihilate itself in its consequences or be annihilated from the side of other knowledge. The consistency of concepts is always the power of the indirect proof. One sees this in an instructive way in the refutation of theories. The reproducing motion animates the supposed principle on all sides. Thereby there arises a world of thought consistent in itself, which now offers points of comparison by which to be measured against facts. Without such a development error hides itself and is impregnable, like a single point that conceals itself within itself. But in that the false draws nourishment from the true (from the causal connections of consistency), it grows and now reveals itself as semblance. Isolated, error maintains itself; but it annihilates itself as soon as it enters into relation on all sides. For the true at first checks it, until it clasps it so tightly that it suffocates. One sees this in the history of hypotheses. Whoever first puts forward an explanatory thought gives it hold and root within itself, and usually perceives only the factual that supports it. Whoever refutes it abolishes this happy, self-assured narrowness. The art of criticism consists partly in driving the necessary consequences of the assumed thought out to the point of impossibility, partly in directing the points fixed in knowledge, and their consequences, against the presupposition. We admire in it the greatness of the cool, penetrating [p. 435] acuteness, in that the germ of the foreign thought is fertilised on all sides so that it may betray its misshapen essence. The basic type in this is always the indirect proof, which starts precisely from the opposite of what is recognised as true.

In the philosophical investigations of the masters many instructive examples are found. We recall, say, Plato in the Theaetetus. There he combats Protagoras, who asserts that man is the measure of all things. On the one hand he develops the grounds of the thought with full consistency to the point that, accordingly, not only man but equally every animal (the pig or the ape) would properly be the measure of things. On the other hand he directs the fixed facts of knowing that go beyond mere perception, such as the concepts of the universal and of the useful, the activities of remembering, understanding, and so on, against the assertion and lets it shatter powerlessly upon them. We recall further the manner in which Plato in the Philebus refutes the view that pleasure is the highest good. First he assumes it. But in sharpening the concept of the highest good, which is sufficient to itself, and of needy pleasure, they repel each other, and pleasure is not the highest good. We recall Aristotle's polemic against Plato's Ideas, and the criticism which Aristotle exercises on the earlier views about the essence of the soul.⁴ By letting them have their way in their consistency, but also granting them no consistency, he lets them ruin themselves. It does not belong here what Hegel has otherwise significantly brought out in Aristotle's critical art, that Aristotle knows how to prepare precisely in the negative the future positive, precisely in the contradictions against the untenable the future reconciliation of what is correct. Among the moderns we mention by way of example the procedure by which Leibniz [p. 436] refutes Locke's empirical view,¹ or how Kant combats the ethical principle of one's own happiness.² In the individual sciences the path of refutation is the same, the universal course of the indirect proof.

(1) p. 161ff. Steph.

(2) Cf. especially p. 20 B f. and p. 60 A.

(3) E.g. Metaphys. I. 6 f.

(4) Ueber die Seele I. 3 ff.

2. Accordingly the indirect proof is the proper proof of negation; yet in combination with a disjunctive judgment which sets the possible cases side by side it can ground an affirmation. The disjunctive members exclude one another; if the one is, the others are not; and if the others, all but one, do not belong to the subject of the universal sphere, then the *one* belongs to it as predicate. In this procedure the strict and complete division of the possible cases is necessary, but often extremely difficult. The indirect proof does not yield in and for itself the knowledge of the affirmation, but acts only as a member in a larger methodical whole.

Aristotle often made use of this procedure, and shows in it both the comprehensive view in the outline of the possible cases and the penetrating acuteness in the indirect proof, through which what is possible in the universal becomes impossible for the particular. He found, for example, the formal laws of the syllogism, down to the individual moods of the figures, by way of this method. First he outlines, according to the inner relation of the three terms, the three figures of the syllogism.⁴ In the individual figures he combines the possible cases of how, in the premisses of the syllogism, the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative and the particular negative judgment can be intertwined. These 16 cases, which result from such an external enumeration of the possibilities, he treats in the [p. 437] first figure all of them and with particular diligence.¹ The valid cases of the first figure he proves directly, and directly for the most part also the valid cases of the other figures, by reduction to the first. The invalid ones he removes by an indirect proof. Thus here the indirect proofs delimit, while the direct ones generate. As the two unite, the strictly closed ground-plan of syllogistic arises. Where development cannot yet proceed genetically, such an indirect procedure in the service of a universal division of the possibilities often leads to the goal. Here belongs in particular the so-called method of exhaustion of the ancient geometers. It is proved indirectly that a magnitude is neither smaller nor larger than another. Consequently, one concludes, it must be equal to it, since only this third possibility of a relation remains. The simple principle of division of the disjunctive judgment which is present in these cases here gives a perspicuous clarity. One contents oneself with such a necessity of delimitation where an inner development is not yet possible. So, when we deliberate about the [p. 438] possibilities and ends of the future, we are accustomed to take such a course.¹ And even in the judgments of ends by which nature seems to be guided in the organic, we might recognise a similar excluding procedure. Where we wish to guess a hidden inner ground, we seek such universal points of view of possibilities, in order to experiment with them and thereby to find indirectly what is sought. If now in this way the knowledge of the impossible forms the insuperable boundary of the actual, then for the matter a ground of knowing has indeed been found, but not yet the inner ground of origination.

(1) In the nouveaux essais sur l'entendement humain.

(2) In the Kritik der praktischen Vernunft. 1788. p. 61. Werke. VIII. p. 147ff.

(3) Cf. especially analyt. priora I. c. 4-6.

(4) On the necessity of this division in Aristotle's sense see above Section XVIII., the syllogism. Vol. II. p. 342ff.

(1) Analyt. pr. I. 4.

(2) The indirect proof proceeds thus. In the invalid cases, for example in 12 of the first figure, one would have to be able, were something true to result, to conclude, according to determinate examples, now affirmation, now negation (τὸ ὑπάρχειν and τὸ μὴ ὑπάρχειν). This ambiguity, which is shown in individual examples, is the indirect proof of inadmissibility.

(3) A similar course is shown by the determinations of concepts in eth. Nic. II. 4. phys. IV. 4. ff. In the first passage it is asked what virtue is psychologically, in the last, what space is. The result, however, does not convince in these passages, because the division of the concepts which may possibly come into consideration is not derived, but only taken up as if with a single grasp.

(4) Cf. Montucla histoire des mathématiques. Paris an. 7. tom. I. p. 282. Archimedes proved two propositions in this way: 1) The circle is equal to the rectangle formed from the radius and half the circumference; 2) in the book de conoidibus et sphaeroidibus: The parabolic conoid is equal to half the cylinder of equal base and height.

3. In the procedure just described, knowledge is directed to a determinate place and fixed in it through the union of the complete disjunction and the indirect proof. In this no disjunctive judgment suffices that is divided only contradictorily into an affirmation and its pure negation (A and not-A). For pure negation (not-A) as such cannot be the basis of a development. It is wholly indeterminate and contains a wide possibility which must first be translated into the positive cases.

If the disjunctive judgment arisen from universal insight, which subordinates the indirect proofs to itself as members, is lacking, then the procedure stands halfway. Then the indirect proof yields only negative results. With every negation we gain, we are indeed brought nearer to the affirmation. But whether we have exhausted all possibilities, whether we have now grasped the actual, is not guaranteed to us.

The empirical theories necessarily stand at such a standpoint. They get as far as the negation of a [p. 439] view by means of the indirect proof flowing from the consequences; but in letting go of this old possibility they merely seize a new one. Whether there are not yet others is not established; for the closed circle of the disjunctive judgment proceeding from the higher universal is lacking. Since, by the nature of experience, the genetic proof of what is correct is also lacking, it is again only the consistent elaboration of the theory and its agreement with the fixed points of knowledge that stand in for the positive proof. But what is agreement with the fixed points? These points are relatively few, and agreement means only that these few do not refute the theory and that no indirect proof speaks against it. Thus the hypothesis is confirmed in its consequences; but the confirmation is always only conditional. For those hypotheses are only chance grasps, since the ordering universal is lacking. The struggle of theories is nothing but an indirect proof, but still without that comprehensive whole which excludes the contingency of the possibilities. The less, therefore, an empirical science has yet been worked through, the less it has yet succeeded in leaning upon a higher universal, the more are the hypotheses of explanation still determined by mere hitting the mark and groping about. Nevertheless, in contradiction with what is fixed and certain, what is false and uncertain annihilates itself. Contradiction appears here as the goad that drives the knowing mind out of what is nearest and superficial into the depth of truth. Therein lies its great significance.

(1) Cf. e.g. Aristot. eth. Nicom. III. 5.

(2) See above the examples vol. II. p. 3.

If we look at the form of this process, it goes no otherwise with the mature mind of science on the paths of its research than with every child whose senses and representations are educated by the surrounding objects. When, for example, the child, prompted by the image of sight, reaches out with its hand but misses the object, when it forms a speech-sound after hearing but is not understood, [p. 440] or when in some other way things do not answer to its representations, it finds itself refuted by this indirect proof; it gives up, as it were, its hypothesis and tries a new one, until it knows itself in harmony with life.

Thus the small repeats itself in the great and the great in the small, and as the highest calculations are only an enhanced counting, so the deliberate method is only an enhancement of unconscious and earliest thinking. Everywhere unity shows itself to whoever penetrates more deeply.

4. The indirect proof, as Aristotle already shows, has less scientific value than the direct. If it is to demonstrate something positive, it passes through a double negation and comes about through the negation of the negation. For since the contradictory opposite is determined by negation, this negation is cancelled by the consequences. The provisionally assumed not-A, even if it should divide into the cases α, β, γ, is cancelled in the consequence, which shows itself to be impossible, and thereby the positive A is restored. The impossible results from the collision with propositions already known. The indirect proof therefore opens no insight into the inner grounds of the matter and is properly possible only where propositions already stand as proved. Its force lies in the repelling power (in the repulsion) of these propositions, thus outside the matter to be proved, outside its creative process.

Such fixed points, which are the condition of the indirect proof, form only within the system. How does it happen, nevertheless, that precisely the principles of systems, on which all stability depends, mostly fall to an indirect proof?

That this really happens can easily be observed. Aristotle already remarks that the logical principle of identity and of contradiction can be proved only indirectly.¹ [p. 441] The many proofs which, in the principles in particular, from Aristotle¹ to Hegel, turn on the impossibility of a regress into infinity are indirect. In Spinoza the proofs of the first propositions governing the system are indirect, if they are not tacitly presupposed in the definitions. The foundation of the Leibnizian monadology is grounded indirectly. When Kant sets matter, according to its fundamental concept of the filling of space, into an equilibrium of attraction and repulsion, the proof is indirect; for the repulsive force alone would disperse matter into infinity, the attractive alone would contract it into a mathematical point. In both cases matter would be annihilated and no space filled. Whoever examines the establishment of principles will easily multiply these examples for himself.⁶

(1) At least the ἐλεγκτικῶς ἀποδεικνύναι amounts to an indirect proof, even if one conducted only subjectively. Metaphys. IV. (Г.) 4.

The matter is grounded in itself. Principles as such cannot be developed genetically; for otherwise they would not be principles and would rather have a foreign beginning. They can therefore be demonstrated only through a ground of knowing, in opposition to the ground of the matter. All mere grounds of knowing amount to an indirect proof. Here the question now is which point appears as the fixed one, through whose collision the contradictory opposite is cancelled. The impossibility of the opposite is the necessity of the principles. But it has been shown above⁷ that [p. 442] in this negative expression a positive point is contained, from whose force the negation proceeds. According as this fixed point is only an isolated perception or a universal phenomenon, according as it is apprehended more deeply or as less significant, it possesses more or less of the compelling power required to strike down every objection to the principle put forward. For the unconditioned principle — for God — not an individual thing but the universe is this indirect proof.

(1) Cf. metaphys. a. 2.

(2) See above vol. I. p. 66 ff.

(3) Cf. e.g. eth. I. 5. Omnis substantia est necessario infinita.

(4) After Leibniz has conceived the monad in its rigid, inalienable unity as, in a certain measure, the last point of nature (monas non est nisi substantia simplex), he takes the multiplicity of properties into the monads without further ado, merely through an indirect consideration. Opus tamen est, ut monades habeant aliquas qualitates; alias nec entia forent. Princip. philos. §. 8.

(5) See above vol. I. p. 255 ff.

(6) See e.g. above vol. I. p. 141 ff. Vol. II. p. 70 f.

(7) See above Section XIII., modal categories, vol. II. p. 186 ff.

In this way the application of the indirect proof is graded. First and properly it grounds negative judgments; next it serves in the disjunctive method to find the positive through exclusion of the inadmissible; finally it recurs as an emergency aid in the knowledge of principles.

[p. 443]

## XXI. DAS SYSTEM. — XXI. THE SYSTEM.

1. The various modes of grounding have been set out. We have drawn attention to how they demand one another and work together in the living act of knowing. An example may illustrate this unity, which at the same time leads over to a larger logical form.

All understanding is interpretation, whether of the spoken word or of meaningful phenomena themselves. The inner process has in both cases a great affinity. We therefore call to mind the course of the mind in philological explanation, in order to rediscover in this more easily observed activity the more intricate one; and we shall recognise the unity of the methods if, for example, we observe in [p. 444] detail what turns our thinking tacitly makes in order to understand a difficult and obscure passage of an ancient classic.

(1) In the "Erläuterungen zu den Elementen der aristotelischen Logik," 2nd ed. 1861, the author has given examples from the most diverse disciplines, and in the "Naturrecht auf dem Grunde der Ethik" he has devoted a whole section (§§. 71-82) to presenting the logic of law, in its origin and application, according to the various methods that intertwine in it. It is important not to keep abstract logic in the abstract or to enfeeble it in contrived examples, but to follow it into the actual sciences and to behold it there in its full significance. To this the writings named may serve as a guide, in agreement with the "Logische Untersuchungen."

The procedure here is, in its whole direction, analytic. From the written word as the visible phenomenon, the producing ground, the thought, is to be found. But in solving this task we at once proceed synthetically. For we understand the individual passage, as we read on, through the living reconstruction of the whole. Hence, when a passage strikes us as difficult, we already stand in the midst of the propelling ground of the thought. We stumble precisely because the analytic procedure, which as it were gathers the sense from the signs, comes into contradiction with the synthetic, which from the whole illuminates every part that arises through analysis. The new part will not fit into the image of the whole already gained, and the power of the unity in which all understanding takes place rejects it as foreign. At once the previous synthesis becomes problematic, and the question arises: is the new part or the old whole, or are both, wrongly taken, and how can they be reconciled? The means we apply to such a question are in the first instance analytic. We construe the passage, say, according to the word-forms, which, like grounds of knowledge, permit an inference back. Now a sense is brought out. Is it the right one? The connection of the whole passage, that is, the synthesis, is the test of this analytic result. The attempted explanation is perhaps false. The refutation then appears in an indirect proof. For if that view gave the correct sense, we infer, then this and that in the whole or in the particulars would be absurd. The context offers that resistance from which an indirect proof in general starts. The explanation is given up; a new one is tried, until the analytic procedure, which rests on the grammatical relations, and the synthetic, which from out of the whole recreates the inner [p. 445] thought, mutually confirm each other. The inner genesis of the thought, which clothes itself with necessity in the given form, is the direct proof. In the whole process the gaze is directed to the individual, and hence the syllogism, which derives the individual from the factual universal, easily vanishes from observation. But it is tacitly present. If, for example, a universal grammatical rule is applied in the course of it, or if in the indirect proof one argues from a universal, this happens through the rapid linking of a syllogism of the first figure. The exclusive refutation usually ends in a syllogism of the second figure. Induction is active as an auxiliary power, for instance in establishing a lexical meaning which is tried out for the understanding.

In the rapid interchange of thoughts we do not distinguish these different directions of method. But if we attend to it, we admire our own weaver's masterpiece:

"Where *one* tread stirs a thousand threads,

The shuttles shoot across and back,

The threads flow on unseen,

*One* stroke strikes a thousand connections."

We think in a manner similar to the way we move. In an instant we set the hand in free play. How many muscles work together in *one* unity to do so! When the physiologist shows us their intertwined activity, we admire the organism. The forms of thinking work mentally as the muscles do bodily. We exercise both without seeing or knowing them.

The understanding of a difficult passage, as we have just analysed it, is as it were a model of all knowing. If in general the reconstruction of the thing from the whole (the synthesis) grows into the forms of the phenomena (the grounds of knowledge of analysis) in such a way that the two affirm and attest each other, then what [p. 446] can be attained is attained. It is only the task of the human mind to understand the world as a whole in the same way.

2. In the preceding example, which presents the knot in which the methods are tied together, it emerges anew that the mind is directed towards a unity of the whole of knowledge. This unity of the whole is everywhere the silent presupposition. All cognitions seek to gravitate about *one* centre. What is remote is not to fall apart, and what is near is not to shrink together. Unity is not merely absence of contradiction, which is demanded in the first instance in the indirect proof, but community of thinking and being, out of which alone mental necessity weaves its eternal bond.

The system presents this great unity and is, as it were, only *one* expanded judgment.

Thinking and being correspond here too. The concept became living in the judgment, as substance in activity. The ground poured itself out into its consequences, as the cause into its effect. The connection of concepts and judgments forms the system, as the connection of substances and activities forms the world.

The logical unity that corresponds to the metaphysical has been treated above. The reproduction shows itself here only on a larger scale.

We distinguish a system of arrangement and a system of development. Both master a multiplicity of cognitions through unity. In the one the survey of division prevails, in the other the living generation from a principle. In the former, finished substances are put together according to their affinity; in the latter, they arise from their grounds.

The rule of a principle of division determines the system of arrangement; the genetic method, when it completes itself, produces the system of development. [p. 447] The former is meant to be a preliminary stage of the latter, and only the latter is system in the eminent sense.

When first, through a view from the standpoint of the onlooker, a flash of light falls upon a mass of representations, and these now link themselves in a fundamental thought, even if still a subjective one, and when the theory then presses further into the explanation of the thing, these attempts complete themselves in the system.

The system seeks in its development to cover a developing domain of phenomena, and seeks the independent whole.

The individual systems of the sciences are themselves only members of *one* great system. They grow into one another by drawing nourishment from one another. When these dependent members close together into *one* organism that realises itself, there arises the image of the great system, which seeks to be the mental counter-image of the world.

3. It lies in the nature of that fundamental science which we designated at the outset and have pursued in our investigations that, in seeking out the logical and metaphysical principles, it should obtain the basic outlines for the articulation of the system of the sciences. We therefore attempt, in a glance at the results, to mark the lines that form the ground plan.

We laid weight on the concept of stages, on such a progression that not only does the earlier prepare the later methodically and really, as the simple prepares the compound, but also the earlier, measured by the end of the whole, appears as the lower, without which, however, we do not reach the higher. Such a relation we saw in particular in those two groups of principles which were distinguished as efficient cause and end. The stages rise, and in [p. 448] development we see the lower striving toward the higher, and the higher, even at a time when it is not yet outwardly there, drawing the lower to itself or preparing it as its organ. In the same sense the sciences form stages of knowledge. In order to present them, we attach ourselves to the questions in which at the beginning we saw the motives for logic and metaphysics; and it will thereby become clear whether, and how far, we have kept them in view. These questions could be put in two expressions which at bottom intend the same thing. Taken universally, they ran thus: how is science possible at all, and how does the mind produce necessity? These universal questions articulated themselves of their own accord, through the principles that set themselves off from and graduate one another, into the particular questions comprised under them.

(1) Vol. I. p. 3 ff.

Through the elementary mediation of thinking and being that was demanded, which turned out to be constructive motion, the foundation was gained. With this an unconscious causal activity, motion in space, was connected with a conscious one, the constructive, the two were regarded as corresponding to each other, and the unconscious one, by entering under identity in consciousness, was made knowable. Since with the figures of designing motion there arose the possibility of intuiting a priori, i.e. before experience and as conditioning experience, the question was answered: how is mathematical knowledge possible? The logical deed, growing consistently in this domain within the human race, was explained by the possession of a real principle; for constructive motion, generating figures and numbers, must be designated as such a principle. Without a real principle at its origin, pure knowledge would remain empty. In the same act we see mathematical necessity arise. If in all necessity, as emerged in the investigation of the modal categories, ¹ subjective and objective [p. 449] agree, then in pure mathematics this relation takes the form that the law of the thing flows from our own activity and its inner determination. Mathematical knowledge is the seen-through consequence of a generating deed of our own. From construction and determination there springs the manifold in unity; and because this origin is known, it is possible to lead the given manifold back to the law of its origin and to follow out the consequence in the interaction of the figures that have arisen. The point is only to find out what is posited along with the generating deed; and to this the mathematical acumen is directed in the knowledge of laws. In Kant's example, 7 + 5 = 12, we count together, we set off, we have instituted the decimal order. The example of mathematical necessity, 2 × 2 = 4 (we say that something is as certain as that twice 2 is 4), is evident to everyone because it is our own deed. Once posited, it yields, through relations which it takes up, other necessary things, e.g. 4 : 2 = 2, 3 + 1 = 4, and so on. It is the same with the triangle that we construct, with the parallels that we draw. The trigonometric laws, which no one suspects in the triangle at first glance, are nevertheless in it; when the circle and its relations are combined with the triangle, they come forth. For the progress of mathematical necessity everything depends only on finding the means to follow out the consequence of the essence in its interaction with something else. Mathematical necessity proverbially counts as the strict one. It is alloyed with nothing foreign that might come from outside, and therefore with nothing contingent.

(1) See above vol. II. p. 156 ff.

In the domain of experience, which appeared as the second stage, the given rules. The knower stands within it in real interaction with the real, and perception, which in the end becomes sensible to him in pleasure and pain, vouches to him for this actuality. From this arises, in this domain, the concept of fact. However [p. 450] far the inference back may move away from the first impression, the effect of the real underlies it. In opposition to plays of imagination, to detached representations which carry on their doings within us, experience bound by fact instructs through the things themselves and creates power over things. In the new that this stage presents, the old is at work. Appropriation through the senses takes place with the help of constructive motion; investigation goes back into mathematical laws; matter is in the end intelligible only through motion. Thus the question was answered how experience of material forces (physics in the narrower sense) is possible. In it the understanding once more produces necessity — let us call it material (physical) necessity — whose peculiarity within the efficient cause is the interweaving of fact and ground. The compelling fact, the basis of this necessity, exercises indeed only an external constraint, but the mathematical consideration of the ground transforms it into mental necessity. Let one but think away from physics and technology the mathematical element, all constructions and calculations, and one sees that no necessity remains in them. The proposition is therefore correct that there is only as much necessity in physics as there is mathematics in it. The material fact is permeated by mathematical necessity.

A third stage appears where organic nature reveals a new fundamental concept, to which the earlier principles serve as the condition of its existence. In the end, which the inventing mind designs and the contemplating mind recognises again where it is realised, in the end, which is intelligible only from the prefiguring thought that anticipates the effect to the cause, the question is answered how a knowledge of organic nature is possible. It yields organic necessity. Resting on the two preceding stages, for these become its organ, [p. 451] it becomes peculiar through the thought as the designing unity that subordinates the many to itself; it is necessity from the determining thought of the whole. As in a geometrical problem the known laws become the means of solution, so for the end from which organic necessity springs, mathematical and physical necessity become means. The thought of a whole becomes the soul of a physical necessity. Constructive motion makes possible the saying attributed to Plato, that God is in the world a geometer; and if he is so, in the physical as in the organic, then the principle of this divine geometry had to form the beginning. Since necessity, as it were acknowledged being, arises only from a community of thinking with what is, from a contact of the subjective and the objective, the subjective element has now risen. Where in the physical the thought still empties itself out into material multiplicity, in the organic it finds its ownmost concept again as a formative one.

Out of the organic stage, finally, the ethical stage rises. It masters the earlier ones and at the same time liberates them. If one asks how a knowledge of the ethical is possible, the answer lies in this, that the ultimate end of the human essence, and human nature as means or organ for this end, can be known. Now, as the law enters into the will, ethical necessity appears, and as the will satisfies the law of its essence, the same necessity appears as freedom. In ethical necessity organic necessity, which determines multiplicity from unity, is presupposed, and with the organic, physical and mathematical necessity. The forces which in the organic are means rise in the ethical to persons, who are means and at the same time ends in themselves.

From stage to stage the principles become more concrete, more intergrown, more bound, but also, through the known conditions [p. 452] of the preceding ones, clearer and freer. In that element in which at each stage the thinking mind has community with them, the possibility is given it of so fitting itself to the objects determined by these principles that it grasps them. Its logical forms therefore belong to all the sciences, but are determined in them specifically according to the object, so that through them the knowledge of necessity may ripen.

It cannot be denied that these stages, which must form the division of the system advancing according to inner principles, rise towards us, and it is as if on the last we crowned ourselves. Do we really do so? We confess that what we men call system stems only from a little piece of the world and is thought only on the earth, that is, perhaps only on a splinter of the glowing and shining ore of the sun flung out into great space; but we feel that already in all necessity a trait announces itself which is mightier than man and points beyond man, who is everywhere conditioned.

4. Already in the thought of the world we overfly the circle of experience. For wherever we look, there is fragmentary work. But driven by the impulse of the mind, we seize the whole.

The idea of science here goes further than its realisation. Not even the whole of the phenomena, infinite in great and in small space, is accessible; much less the depth of the whole ground. Only the Promethean defiance of human knowing points to the earth as the sole dwelling-place of mind and says presumptuously: hic Rhodus, hic salta; as if there were nothing else. Does not experience itself already show us the worlds that we do not know? But to be sure, enough is given us, and it is our task to understand from the fragments the spirit of the whole; for the phenomena are its revelations.

[p. 453] Herein a new concept announces itself, a concept of the mind boldly surpassing conditioned experience, the unconditioned, the absolute, which is regarded as the proper object of metaphysics. We are led to the same concept when we follow the grounds of things backwards into their conditions, proceeding from conditions to the conditions of the condition. The first ground, which would condition all, will itself be the unconditioned. There remains for the next chapter the question whether, and how far, a knowledge of the unconditioned is possible. The answer must stand in close connection with what is necessary, as the preceding investigations have yielded it.

Before we pass on to this last question, only one more point may be discussed, so that no gap may remain in the articulation of the sciences just indicated.

If we saw the sciences graduate themselves with the principles and rise as mathematical, physical, organic and ethical, the question arises: where, then, do logic and metaphysics belong, whose unity we have held fast? We designated them above as the fundamental discipline, and we remark the following in justification.

In the division and sequence of the sciences two guiding points of view easily cross: the order that follows the origin of the thing, and the order that the course of teaching and learning makes necessary. The methodical consideration cuts across the genetic rigour. For the genetic consideration draws from the ground of the thing, whereas the methodical arrangement adapts itself to the needs of the developing, learning mind. The position of logic in the systems therefore not seldom appears like a hysteron proteron. As theory of science it must enter into principles which belong to the other sciences and which it first receives from them; and yet in the philosophical system of the disciplines it can hardly come after them; for it is meant to secure their ground [p. 454] and to sketch out their structure. As the investigation of subjective thinking, logic becomes in the genetic system a part of psychology; but as theory of knowledge, as theory of science, it must serve as guide not only to psychology but also to the sciences that precede it. This double relation brings a wavering into the position of logic.

If one places oneself at the point at which philosophy first arises at all in its difference from the individual sciences, the circle will be resolved in which such a science seems to ground the following philosophical disciplines and yet to stand on their ground.

Although philosophy, if we ask history, arose in a unity with the other sciences, this bond has nevertheless long since been dissolved through the division of labour, and philosophy now finds the individual sciences before it in their dispersion and in the form they have given themselves on their own account. Logic and metaphysics have in them their material for consideration; they find in them methods and presupposed principles, and have the task of seeking out their origin and their unity. Through this apprehension of the common source, through this mutual regulation and animation, philosophical content is generated, and those germs arise which, in the development of the system, become the principles of the philosophical real disciplines. In this way, the isolated sciences in their historical forms are indeed presupposed by the fundamental science of logic and metaphysics, but the philosophical disciplines proceed in their articulation from the latter. Logic and metaphysics thus do not reach forward into the philosophical disciplines, but back into the empirical ones.

In this sense philosophy is neither an idle repetition of the particular sciences nor an ency[p. 455]clopaedic digest of them; rather, on the ground of logic and metaphysics, of fundamental philosophy, it completes the knowledge of the human race at any given time, in that, intent on the idea of the whole, it brings the philosophical principles to bear in the articulation of the particular, and generates or conditions the principles for the subordinate particular. How far it advances thereby into the individual sciences is left to the art with which it handles the principle formatively. Thus, on the soil of the fundamental science, logic and metaphysics, it designs those four graduated real disciplines and attaches them to the knowledge of the absolute as to the ultimate point of fastening.

5. The proposed division of philosophy is taken from the principles of the matter, from the inner relation of the objects, and only such a division will turn out sharp and determinate. According to a remark of Sextus Empiricus¹ the division of philosophy into dialectic, physics and ethics, which with the Stoics became the norm of the system, already lies in germ in Plato. In Plato dialectic is that fundamental science, demonstrating the idea, which unites logic and metaphysics, and physics and ethics are borne by it. According to the result of our investigations, physics must be differentiated into the knowledge of the mathematical, the physical and the organic stage. What is found in Cartesius as the indication of a division, and in Spinoza as a plan in the sequence of the books of his Ethics, corresponds on the whole to the original simple design of the Platonic division.

In Aristotle a subjective division early confronts it, which articulated philosophy according to the three modes of human activity, contemplating, acting and making, as theore[p. 456]tical, practical and poietic, as knowledge of contemplation, of active life and of formative art.¹ It was a falling away from the first point of view when, on a new, material principle of division, theoretical philosophy was divided into first philosophy, physics and mathematics, practical philosophy into ethics, economics and politics, and logic was then placed before all as the instrument of the disciplines; and this turn towards the objective may be left aside. The question is how far that first and most universal principle of division suffices. It is not to be overlooked that the three activities, contemplating, acting and making, are distinguished according to the directions of their end. Contemplating seeks to know for the sake of knowing; making seeks to produce in order to intuit a thought or to fix a feeling; acting, on the other hand, seeks an effect as such. But these different ends carry the others within themselves reciprocally as means, and are therefore unsuited to serve as specific difference. Contemplating is contained as a requirement in acting as in making. For acting must be permeated by reason, and making is meant to present an idea and bring it to intuition. Likewise making is contained in acting as in contemplating; for acting completes itself only in ethical beauty, in a presentation which, like the work of art, corresponds to its idea. Contemplating requires productions in order to reach its goal. In the disciplines one can set theorems and problems, propositions and tasks, against each other as science and art. Now whoever perceives how the solution of the tasks is conditioned by knowledge, and the propositions and the proof of the propositions by the carrying out of tasks, and how further in the natural sciences observation and experiment accompany each other, sees easily how science and art, contemplating and making, [p. 457] advance together, and that these concepts are therefore not suited to draw a boundary line between two domains of philosophy. Finally, acting fulfils itself in a peculiar way in the scientific calling through contemplating and in the artistic through making. If, therefore, a division of philosophy on the ground of these concepts is strictly carried out, repetitions are unavoidable. Already in Aristotle, the originator of this tripartition, into whose peculiar determinations we have refrained from entering, it becomes doubtful where individual disciplines, e.g. rhetoric, are to be reckoned.

(1) Adv. mathematicos VII. §. 16.

(2) Epist. ad principiorum philosophiae interpretem Gallicum p. 10 f. according to the Amsterdam edition. 1685.

(1) Metaphysik VI. 1, cf. nikomachische Ethik VI. 2-5.

It is similar with the ideas of the true, the good and the beautiful, much spoken of in recent times and set side by side. They express as object what in the concepts of contemplating, acting and making is intuited as activity. Only the superficial view is able to separate them. Whoever penetrates more deeply into them soon becomes aware that one cannot raise the content of the one without raising the content of the others along with it.¹

The Aristotelian division reaches into recent times. Christian Wolf divided philosophy into theoretical and practical. Baumgarten added aesthetics and to that extent restored poietic philosophy as a third part. Kant, as regards the division of philosophy, is dependent on Chr. Wolf. One sees this clearly when one compares Kant's architectonic of pure reason with the introduction to Wolf's logic. When Kant, like Wolf, divides philosophy first into theoretical and practical, the separation of mental activity into the faculty of knowledge, the faculty of desire and the [p. 458] faculty of feeling has an essential influence on this in Kant as in Wolf.¹ But the results in Kant testify against the correctness of the division. Practical reason in his case reaches back into the domain of theoretical reason, in that it produces postulates, that is, theoretical presuppositions which were doubtful to the *Kritik der reinen Vernunft*.

(1) See above vol. II. p. 162 f.

(2) Kant Kritik der reinen Vernunft. Methodenlehre. 3. Hauptstück. 2nd ed. p. 874 ff. Werke. II. p. 651 ff. and Wolf philosophia rationalis s. logica. 1725, discursus praeliminaris §. 60 ff.

Herbart belongs here insofar as he too does not divide philosophy according to objects. When he defines philosophy as the elaboration of concepts, his principle of division is the logical activity that they require. From the chief ways in which concepts are elaborated the chief parts of philosophy result. Insofar as the end is to make concepts clear and distinct, logic arises for him. Insofar as given concepts of experience carry contradictions within themselves and must therefore be altered and supplemented according to their particular constitution in order that they may become thinkable, there results for him the science of metaphysics, which, in a similar way as with Wolf and Kant, finds its application in psychology, philosophy of nature and natural theology. Finally, concepts are distinguished which in our representing necessarily bring about a judgment of approval or disapproval, and the science of such concepts is for him aesthetics. Applied to the given, it passes over into a series of technical doctrines, all of which may be called practical sciences; practical philosophy in the narrower sense is for him that one among the technical doctrines whose precepts bear the character of necessary compliance because we involuntarily and unceasingly present its object. This division is rooted wholly in Herbart's peculiar philosophical intuition and can be judged only together with it. Meanwhile the rigour of the division is doubtful already for the following [p. 459] reasons. First, according to the principle of division indicated, logic and aesthetics do not stand sharply apart. For the clearness and distinctness of concepts also pleases, and a technical doctrine can be directed to this too. In Herbart's school this consequence has in fact been drawn. Bobrik's logic¹ transfers the analogy of practical philosophy to the theory of knowledge and designs five original and five derived logical ideas, as Herbart presents five original and five derived practical ideas. The specific difference between logic and aesthetics thus does not hold through. Further, it was called into doubt above whether, with regard to the concepts of experience, there exists such a task as the metaphysical correction and supplementation demanded by Herbart. Partly the contradiction in the concepts of experience appears only by the falsely applied standard of the law of identity; partly, if it is assumed, it is resolved by Herbart only in appearance. Hence this kind of elaboration of concepts is unable to ground a metaphysics; and were it able to, the specific difference would again not hold through. For if one determines contradiction in Herbart's sense, the aesthetic concepts, namely the practical ideas, contain the same contradiction within themselves, as, for example, the idea of equity, according to Herbart's conception, is not thought without the change brought about by an action, a concept which according to Herbart's metaphysics contradicts itself. For these reasons Herbart's foundation of the division will not be able to hold even under his own presuppositions, and much less as a universal one outside his system. In particular, the unity of the system and of the world-view is torn apart by the fact that practical philosophy is deliberately detached from the foundation of metaphysics and [p. 460] the ethical concepts are made self-standing through the character of necessary approval. Thereby the community is abolished in which the sciences, without prejudice to their difference, flourish.

(1) Kant Kritik der Urtheilskraft. 1790. Einleitung III. p. XX. Werke. IV. p. 14 ff.

(2) Joh. Friedr. Herbart Lehrbuch zur Einleitung in die Philosophie. 3rd ed. 1834. §. 5 ff.

(1) Dr. Ed. Bobrik neues praktisches System der Logik. I. 1. ursprüngliche Ideenlehre. Zürich 1838. §. 12 ff.

(2) See above vol. I. p. 181 ff. vol. II. p. 174 ff.

In this way, in all the attempts that order the philosophical disciplines according to subjective points of view, irreconcilable difficulties come forth; and they point us towards seeking the articulation, as was done above, in the objective principles.

[p. 461]

## XXII. DAS UNBEDINGTE UND DIE IDEE. — XXII. THE UNCONDITIONED AND THE IDEA.

1. Only in the concept of the whole does the restless motion of the mind come to rest. Unconditioned unity is the tacit presupposition in the process of knowing, if that process does not arbitrarily check itself on its way. We carry this result over from the last consideration. This unconditioned, which bears the unity of the whole, philosophical abstraction calls the absolute; livelier faith calls it God. In the absolute alone is the relative made fast; in the unconditioned the conditioned gains support and significance; in God creation gains unity and end.

In this proposition we combine two things which, psychologically taken, are not of the same origin: the unconditioned and the concept of God. The representation of God is there, in some shape or other, before science; the concept of the unconditioned, by contrast, is produced by science.

The representation of God has its own phases in the history of human consciousness, from that lowest shape in which it is connected with the same affects that produce superstition, up to that in which the rational concept of [p. 462] unity has already cast multiplicity to the ground, ethical concepts have purified and exalted the God of fear, and reflections akin to science have formed a God of thought. This tendency of human consciousness sets out from another side than science; it sets out from what is first for man; the concept of causality appears in the mirroring of human affects or in the certainty of ethical need. Science, by contrast, pursues what, as the essence of the matter, is first by nature. Where it thinks the ultimate ground, it meets with that tendency which immediately seizes upon the ruling power and shapes it into that in which man shelters and makes fast the destiny of his transient existence.

When Parmenides set over against the existent, which is here or there, is today and tomorrow is not, and which announces its limitation, and so its not-being, on every side, what is, simply and absolutely, the unbecome One; and when Plato's dialectic, perceiving the conditioned basis of all the particular sciences (the ὑποθέσεις) in the presuppositions of the object and of the principles, pointed to the concept of the unconditioned (the ἀνυπόθετον): then the absolute appeared as the necessary consequence of scientific thought.

Plato already carried the unconditioned over, in the Idea of the Good, to God and the divine; and Platonism, taking the word in the widest sense, has always posited the concept of the unconditioned, which is produced by the logical path, and the concept of God, which originally belongs to religion, as one and the same. Only Democritism, with Epicurus at its head, has separated the two domains. Even Spinoza, whose concept of God is the necessary, the aeternum, always calls the unconditioned God.

It would perhaps be more correct to keep the two concepts apart here. Now and then we have already anticipated above in the sense [p. 463] of this unification, and, for example, in the end of our existence have called the inner destination, as the unconditioned within this sphere, the divine. But at bottom, in all those considerations which do not make matter alone the unconditioned, the two coincide in one.

Philosophical theology inherited the concept of God as a given one, and in the face of doubt it had the task of grounding the reality of this concept. Hence comes the peculiar form in which metaphysics treats the unconditioned. As the jurist demands proofs of a fact that has been called into doubt, so metaphysics demands proofs of the existence of God and examines the proofs, as Kant does. We shall follow them up after we have sent ahead some general remarks on the concept of the unconditioned and the knowledge of it.

The unconditioned is no negative concept. The negating expression refers to the path by which we arrive at the concept; it negates the negation which is proper to the conditioned as something limited. The concept itself is positive and, if it has truth, the most affirmative of all; for the unconditioned, borne by no other but bearing all else, sufficient to itself and grounded in itself, affirms itself and everything conditioned. Given nowhere, for what is given is what is limited, the concept, which in metaphysical consideration first appeared in the "what is" of Parmenides, is the highest divination of the mind.

Is this unconditioned, then, in truth? or is it only the necessary but deceptive ideal of the mind? And if the unconditioned is in truth, what is its life, and how is it to be known?

Kant dissolved the unconditioned into a manufactured ideal, into the illusion of an inner phantasm. When we have the coloured rainbow before us, we have the sunlight, [p. 464] the changeless One, behind us, and we need only turn round to it. So too in that archetype of the human mind the eternal light will be mirrored. Nowhere in nature is there an appearance that would not have a mightier being behind it and stream forth from it. Should there, then, for the first time in the human mind, be such an appearance without a being that produces it? Let us only turn towards that being.

It might be said that the unconditioned which we posit arises for us only through the determinateness which is, once and for all, the character of our knowledge; that it is only an analogy which we transfer from the individual things we survey to the whole. This sceptical possibility has at least in part already been refuted in the history of the sciences, and it refutes itself by an indirect path, unless knowledge is to fall to pieces.

It has already been shown above that principles as principles admit of no direct proof but only of an indirect grounding. This case occurs here with doubled force. For the unconditioned is what is original; it has nothing before it from which it could be known, as, for instance, the circle has motion and the radius before it, from which, as from its grounds, it is known. But the fixed point which, in indirect grounding, has the power to annihilate the thought of the opposite, is in this case not an individual thing but the whole of knowledge and whatever has any hold for man.

But if we now wish to think the absolute, with what determinations are we to think it? The categories were derived from motion, the first act of finite thought and finite being, and the end, which gave the categories a new design, was understood from the community of the two. They can therefore hold for us only of the [p. 465] finite. We have no right to extend space and time, quantity and quality, substance and accident, effect and reciprocal action, as they flowed for us from generating motion, beyond this finite domain. We have no right to grasp the infinite in these categories, won and tested only in the finite, and thereby to determine its innermost essence. The critical consciousness of the conditioned origin of the categories would be lost to us if we wished to grant them, in and for themselves, the right to present the innermost essence of the unconditioned. At this boundary we lay down the arms of our finite knowing.

(1) See above, section XX.

In this respect there is no proof of the existence of God, if by proof one means the genetic one; in this respect also no constructive knowledge of his essence, provided that all construction is possible only through the intuitive categories which we derived.

2. The so-called proofs of the existence of God therefore have value only as points of view which cannot be understood without the absolute. They are indirect groundings which work out, each in its own way, the fundamental theme of the unconditioned. How little they prove outright with strict necessity, Kant has demonstrated. Nevertheless they indicate what discord would arise if God were not posited. In this thought lies their compelling power. What is true in the finite by its necessity cannot be untrue in the infinite. Rather, what is necessary in conditioned knowledge becomes the reliable point to which the presupposition of the unconditioned is made fast. But let no one believe that the proofs alone could give the concept of God the life which it has through tradition from generation to generation.

It is customary to enumerate the ontological, cosmological, teleological and moral proofs without inner order [p. 466] or without the guarantee of completeness. They appear like torn-off parts of a view of the world.

One could order them logically according to the thought that underlies the task of knowing. First, God appears as a presupposition of thinking, and we could compare this grounding, even if in a different sense, with the ontological proof. If, further, God is known as the presupposition of all being, the cosmological proof arises. If, finally, God is regarded as the presupposition of that mediation of knowing and being which we grasp as realised in the world permeated by thought, then the teleological proof results, and, in the particular sphere of human action, the moral proof.

The teleological and the moral proofs are mostly separated from one another, and in this separation one still recognises the preponderance which Kant gave to the practical proof. From a higher point of view the two come together into a unity. Both have their force in the harmony of the end, which God posits and upholds; in the one this appears in the instrument of nature, which is strange to itself, in the other, by contrast, in the self-determining and self-surrendering organ of free man. This difference shapes the different course, but it does not blur, rather it realises, the one fundamental thought of the divine end.

3. The ontological proof, as it has occupied metaphysics and the philosophy of religion since Anselm, seeks to demonstrate the existence of God from the concept of God. Sometimes this concept is taken, as by Anselm, as the concept of the highest being, which, just as the highest, could not be imagined merely, since the actual is higher than what is merely thought; sometimes as the concept of the being that includes in itself all perfection and therefore also the perfection of existence, as Cartesius took it; sometimes as the concept of the being that contains only [p. 467] affirmations and therefore no obstructing contradiction, as Leibniz determined it.
