However these concepts are taken in detail, and whatever particular defects each may suffer from by itself, all have one and the same infirmity. We have only thought these concepts, and therefore have also only thought the existence that may lie in them. Everything remains enclosed in thought. What compels us to posit this thing thought and to determine it as an actual one? This compulsion does not stem from the proof itself and can be brought in only by considerations from elsewhere. The proof, then, is no proof. If, within formal thinking, one wishes to reach God from thinking, one arrives at no being, because one looks away from being. Kant is therefore right with his well-known critique against these shapes of the ontological proof.¹

When we showed above that it is the highest stage of knowledge that what is dependent is developed from the concept of the thing, the ontological grounding is not to be confused with this. There either the intuition of existence or the construction of the coming-to-be was to be presupposed; here this basis is lacking.

The ontological proof is the boldest attempt a priori. Hegel brought it into honour anew. With him, however, it means something quite different. With him it is not, as with his predecessors, compressed into the force of a single syllogism. Rather, for him the whole of logic is the one ontological proof. "The pure concept is the absolutely divine concept itself, and the logical course is the immediate presentation of God's self-determination to being."² Accordingly the ontological proof is the dialectical development in which the absolute concept gives itself objectivity. But the dialectical development has been refuted above, and with it this shape of the ontological proof as well.

(1) Kritik der reinen Vernunft. p. 620ff. Werke. II. p. 462ff.

(2) Logik II. p. 175.

(3) Section III.

[p. 468] Accordingly there is no ontological proof in the previous sense. In its place one could set a logical proof, parallel to the physical proofs (the cosmological and the teleological) and to the moral proof, by starting from the nature of human thought. Its moments would be roughly the following.

Human thought knows itself as finite thought, and yet it strives beyond every barrier. It knows itself as dependent on the nature of things and the nature of things as independent of itself, and yet from the very outset it proceeds as if they were determinable by it, and it rests only when it has subdued them. This confidence would be a contradiction if something thinkable were not presupposed in things, truth in the actual. All thinking would be a game of chance or a boldness of despair, if God, the truth, did not underlie thought and things as their common origin and as their common bond. Without this the right of thought would be presumption.

This proof, if one wishes to give it this mathematical and juristic name, is indirect. Such a proof is the more compelling, the more firmly the proposition stands against which the assumption of the opposite is to break and be annihilated. Here thought itself, and so what is in itself most certain, is this secure point. Were there no truth in things, thought would contradict itself. The intelligible is its postulate.

No more is to be drawn from the consideration than lies in it: truth in thought and truth in things through a higher mediation, the intelligent in thought and the intelligible in things. Fichte once showed how from ethical action, if it was not to contradict itself, there follows faith in an ethical world-order, in the world as the material of duty. In the same way there follows from knowing thought, if it is not to contradict itself, faith in an intelligible world-order, in the world as the material of thought.

[p. 469] 4. The cosmological proof infers from the contingency of the world to an absolutely necessary existence as the ground of itself and of all things. So Aristotle already inferred from motion to an unmoved that moves. Finite things are rooted in others, and these again in others. This series of effects and of the causes to be found for them runs on into infinity. This indeterminateness is cancelled only by breaking off the series and placing at its head a self-creating cause (causa sui). This all-generating unity can be further confirmed by the fact that the explanations which penetrate into the grounds from the most diverse phenomena form a converging series which seems to point to one ultimate common point. This essential consideration, which is forgotten in the abstract proof, must support the cosmological inferences, which might otherwise lead to a plurality or multiplicity of the unconditioned.

The contingency of the individual, which drives towards the necessary and, like the transient, awakens a longing for the eternal, can easily be worked out further. It meets us everywhere; but the kernel of the proof lies in that simple view.

The grounding is only indirect, inasmuch as the assumption of the opposite is refuted on that impossible course into infinity. It has as much power in itself as that indeterminate progress is unbearable to thought. Examined more deeply, it is necessity itself, which is one with thought, that thrusts from itself the indeterminateness of the infinite course.

The difficulties do not hide themselves here. Since the individual is always only contingent, the sum of all these contingencies is supposed to make up the necessary. To escape this contradiction, thought bends the series of causes and effects back into itself and posits the unconditioned as cause of itself. The concept is consistent; but the [p. 470] intuition is lacking. One may illustrate it by the analogy of the living being which moves itself, or of the I which has self-consciousness only from itself. In these examples, nevertheless, the cause of itself (causa sui) rests on foreign conditions and a foreign foundation. The analogy of everything conditioned does not help in the unconditioned. Rather, at this point too the absolute withdraws from the finite categories that have been developed. Where the cause presents itself in the finite, it is in itself something manifold, a sum of several conditions; otherwise it would remain unchangeably shut up in itself. In the unconditioned it is supposed to point to an ultimate unity.

Here too no more may be taken from the premises than really lies in them. The unconditioned appears here as the cause sufficient for the world, and consequently as the absolute power. Further, nothing in the cosmological proof drives out of the world to an unconditioned being beyond it. The series of causes and effects runs on within being. In being closed together into a necessary whole, they nevertheless remain within themselves. Hence the most consistent expression of the cosmological view of the world is the system of Spinoza, in which substance is the cause of itself and of the accidents. The finite, selfless in itself, is surrendered to the infinite because it is contingent. In the cosmological proof, in its old shape, only the efficient cause is grasped, which is the character of being when it has not yet been determined by thought. The yield is therefore the unity of efficient substance.

5. The teleological proof does not stop at the general dependence of conditioned being on the unconditioned, but shows the harmony of the conditioned through the end that rules the world. The end can only be understood through the anticipating [p. 471] thought which determines the present out of the future. So far, therefore, as the end rules, so far thought rules. The blind power of substance, the yield of the cosmological proof, rises to creative wisdom.

(1) See above, vol. I. p. 343. Vol. II. p. 183ff.

In this consideration the intelligible world-order tacitly presupposed by subjective thought, and the view of real substance that arises in following up the efficient cause, are gathered together into an unconditioned realisation of reason. The world is rational, and reason is actual.

What has been objected against the teleological proof, both by Spinoza, who denied the end, and by Kant, who blunted it into a principle of reason that is regulative indeed but not constitutive, and flattened it into a subjective maxim of the knowing mind, has been refuted above in the consideration of the end.¹ In that the objective significance of the end has been demonstrated, the foundation of the teleological consideration is established.

If in recent times the intelligence that determines ends is circumvented by putting an unconscious formative drive or a plastic principle of life, as the ground of harmonious purposiveness, in the place of waking reason, then the universe is conceived after the analogy of the sleeping plant or of dreaming animal life. What is possible in such individual phenomena precisely only through the unconditioned cannot be the form of the unconditioned itself. The analogy is therefore absurd. It has also been shown above that the concept of the formative drive, when it is analysed, becomes intelligible only through the free thought that gives it its direction.

The realised end can be comprehended only through the prius of thought, into whose hand power over being has been given. Hence the end-governed [p. 472] world guarantees the unconditioned, almighty thought. Deus cogitat; ergo est.

(1) See above, vol. II. p. 39ff.

But we must not conceal the difficulty from ourselves. Only the completed view of the world, which has carried the end victoriously through all shapes, will give this full certainty. Has the world, then, already been so transfigured in science? At bottom matters stand no differently than they stood in the time of Plato, who complains that Anaxagoras calls in understanding only when the physical causes do not suffice for explanation. The sciences almost without exception take the direction of comprehending the nature of things from the necessity of the efficient cause, and only under compulsion do they accommodate themselves to ends. They do well in this, so far as they can get through with it; for the proper right of the matter must not be curtailed, nor anything foreign forced upon it. But until this discord of directions is settled, until knowledge of the end governs the whole world with thought, so that nothing withdraws from it and all efficient cause has become means, the foundation of the teleological proof still wavers. We are still far from this goal, not to mention that every malformation seems to betray an impotence of the inner end.

The settlement of the dispute must take place still more methodically than hitherto. It must be investigated exactly how the explanation from the efficient cause stands in relation to each phenomenon, and whether such an explanation does not, in the great connection, after all have before it an end from which it proceeds. All means which are not recognised as such appear as efficient causes and contend for the mechanical view until, seen through as bearers of an end, they rather confirm the organic view.¹

(1) Cf. as an example Ulrici's consideration in the work: Gott und die Natur. 1862. p. 318, a work of full and stimulating content.

[p. 473] The organic world may, in view of the consideration of the end, be called the body of God. But the image remains an image. Nowhere in the world does the bond show itself which, like the nerves and muscles in the body, would mediate between the will of the centre and the life of the circumference. The relation is all the more wonderful.

The end has yet *one* difficulty in the unconditioned. Only in division, in opposition, and so in the relative, does it come into activity. Whence this opposition in the original unity? We have reason to answer this question with an ethical motive in God, with the motive of love.

6. The moral proof has been worked out especially by Kant and Fichte. If one looks away from the peculiar form which it has received from both, it rests on a teleological view of the world. Its basis is the end; but not as the end rules in nature, in a foreign element that obeys selflessly, so that organic life appears only as a wonderful play of a foreign intelligent power. In the ethical sphere too, it is true, the universal end is given, not arbitrarily made; but the given end is freely received, shaped in an individual way, and consciously carried out. The end is surrendered into free action; and freedom, determining itself to be the organ of the end, becomes wisdom and love, the one knowing, the other forming and creating. The disposition that surrenders itself to the end is the centre of the so-called moral proof. Its obedience to the unconditioned moral law, its following of the law for the law's sake, its self-sacrificing deed, would be senseless and would fall into irreconcilable contradiction with other legitimate tendencies in man, namely with happiness, if there were not a settlement which has its guarantee in faith in immortality and in God. Thus, roughly, did Kant conceive this [p. 474] postulate of practical reason. Fichte did not reach so far. Our duty is what is most certain. Our world is the material of our duty made sensible; this is the true stuff underlying all appearance. To accomplish joyfully and without constraint what duty bids on each occasion, without doubting and subtle reasoning about the consequences, is the real confession of faith. Every one of our actions is carried out in the presupposition of the divine, and all its consequences are preserved only in the divine. The living and actual moral order is itself God. Thus Fichte shows that the individual (conditioned) action, if it is not to contradict itself, presupposes the unconditioned.

(1) See above, vol. II. p. 17

This grounding is indirect and runs parallel to that consideration which inferred from the task of thought to the presupposed truth of things. We can neither think nor act unless with our thinking or acting we rest in the unconditioned, unless we were willing to think or act blindly and give ourselves over to contradiction.

If the inner end in the essence of man, becoming free in consciousness and will, is recognised as the ethical destination, then the relation to the divine lies still nearer to the man who thinks it. For in that end, in which he thinks the unconditioned ground of his existence, he thinks the divine will.

This consideration forms the summit. Since it proceeds from comprehending thought and from free action, it posits the unconditioned as spiritual and free, as the source of truth and of salvation.

7. In the proofs of God a graded sequence presents itself throughout. The cosmological proof grasps bare existence, and that solely in the determination of its dependence, and finds the unconditioned power. The teleological proof brings out the relation of end which expresses itself in individual existence, and finds the unconditioned thought that pervades the world. The [p. 475] moral proof seizes the end-determined law of freedom and finds as its ground the unconditioned free love. The logical proof, finally, examines thought in its own certainty and finds the unconditioned power, the end that rules the world, and free love grounded in the thinking primal spirit.

Each of these considerations, which are directed from the conditioned to the unconditioned, is by itself a torn-off part; each presents *one* side. Other groundings could easily be formed as well, such as an aesthetic or a psychological proof, if it were a matter of multiplying the number. For every point of the world must lead to God, as every point of the periphery leads to the centre. Grasped in living relation, the conditioned points beyond itself and rests only in the unconditioned. But all such considerations will fall into place under those given above.

As regards the aesthetic, we recall that philosophers such as Fries, who see in space and time and the categories only something subjective, who then treat the organic only mathematically, without real purposiveness, and who in general allow the laws of nature to hold only for man, as laws of the sensuous apprehension and combination of the appearances of things, nevertheless divine the eternal truth, even for natural appearance, in the feeling of the beautiful and the sublime, and claim for this divination the same degree of certainty as for knowledge. If knowledge is declared to be merely human and is sacrificed to the subjective, if in the realm of the living, with the organic apprehended only mathematically, the beautiful is robbed of the kernel of its essence, then it is not conceivable, and it is a vain undertaking, that in the weaving and hovering of feeling, which is after all really only a reflex of appearance upon one's own life, the eternal truth should be regained and rescued. Divination is no adequate form for grasping truth, and, in conscious contradiction with knowledge, it is scarcely even a dim, wavering guarantee. The consideration takes another shape if [p. 476] our investigations should have succeeded in demonstrating the inner end as objective, and with it an objective side in the beautiful. Then there is no conflict; rather the one is grounded in the other; and the feeling of the beautiful can now be an immediate expression, an expression of sensation for the knowable harmony of the thing. From remote sides the elements fused into harmony in the beautiful point to an underlying unity of the whole. If, for example, the colours and forms of vegetation, produced from the plants' own ends and sufficient to their own essence, at the same time do good to the human eye, which scarcely stands in any causal connection with vegetation, and accord with the organ of intuition, then harmony is knit to harmony therein from the remotest ends of life; and the inner destination of the whole, which makes itself known in such testimonies of feeling, may find a place in the teleological proof.

The questions of the philosophy of religion have metaphysical support only in the considerations indicated in the proofs of the existence of God: for example, the question of the transcendence or immanence of God, whether God is to be thought as transcendent, an extramundane being whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, or whether God is to be thought as exclusively immanent, comprising himself in the world, or whether and how both, for in him we live and move and have our being. Aristotle could still keep his first mover, the unmoved that moves, beyond the sphere of the fixed stars that closes the world, and so extramundane; but since Copernicus opened the heavens and disclosed the view into infinite cosmic space, this is no longer possible in that sense. If the question of transcendence and immanence is not to turn into a sensuous dialectic of the prepositions trans and in, beyond and within; if the self-contradictory attempt is not to be made to grasp the transcendent spatially, and so to think a beyond beyond infinite space; if the question [p. 477] is to have a meaning for the concept: then it goes back to the world-determining end; for therein thought is the prius, and in this respect the transcendent.

Every proof of the existence of God contains a pointing of the conditioned to the unconditioned by which it is conditioned; but each mirrors only *one* side of the unconditioned; whoever draws them together and permeates them grasps the *one* God as he reveals himself in this world.

8. Does he really grasp him? If God is known only through the conditioned and yet is not the conditioned, if all our determinations of thought move in the first instance only in the finite and only confess the insufficiency of the finite in order to point to the infinite, then a contradiction must arise as often as we think God. We give up finite thoughts in order to reach the infinite, and what we reach is, if we wish to be honest, after all only something finite. We annihilate the categories, and what rises upon their ruins is once again only through the categories. In this contradiction between the eternal Idea and its finite organ there lies a sublimity which already stamps itself upon the words of Augustine, when he rejects all the Aristotelian categories in order to think God, and yet, with clear consciousness, expresses what he thinks within these categories. Augustine writes:¹ Deus sine qualitate bonus, sine quantitate magnus, sine indigentia creator, sine situ praesens, sine habitu omnia continens, sine loco ubique totus, sine tempore sempiternus, sine ulla sui mutatione mutabilia faciens nihilque patiens. Never, perhaps, has the pale colour of logical abstractions presented a more sublime picture.

9. It is, to be sure, conceivable that the categories, which, as we saw, rise in stages along with the principles and deepen their content especially through the end, should now take the unconditioned into themselves and thereby undergo their final [p. 478] intensification. In this sense one speaks of absolute causality, absolute end, absolute personality (absolute subjectivity), or, since the Neoplatonists, designates this elevation by a "super-" prefixed to the categories, as for example in super-essence, super-being, super-substantiality. The sign of such a raising to a higher power is easily invented; but the question is how matters stand with the concept behind the sign.

(1) De trinitate V. 1 and 2.

If causality and substance (activity and thing) are those fundamental concepts on which the others (quantum, quale, measure) in turn depend, then it is with them that we are first concerned.

The causa sui, as was shown, no longer has what distinguished causality in the finite. In the finite, one thing is the cause of another, and the causa sui, measured against this form of causality, the only one evident to us, appears as a contradiction in the adjunct. Properly speaking, it even states that the concept of causality is not to be applied any further. We posit something as the first and last, beyond which, asking after the cause, we cannot go. For one, matter is this eternal that is from itself, this causa sui; for another, it is mighty thought as what is original; for a third, the indifference of both. But no one truly sees how something absolutely generates itself, is causa sui.

If the end is now joined with the causa sui, we obtain the unconditioned as an end to itself. But the end, now, has sense only in the relative. The division in the original unity, the opposition without which there is no end, follows in and for itself neither from the causa sui nor from the absolute that is combined with the concept of the end.

The category of substance seems at first sight to come into its own through elevation into the infinite, since in the finite no substance is absolutely grounded in [p. 479] itself and each is substance only relatively. But the difficulty returns in the content. Substance has risen in the ethical sphere to the person, and the unconditioned will accordingly have to be conceived as absolute personality. In opposition to the impersonal world-reason, which would properly be reason without consciousness and will, reason blind and lame, that view of the world which seeks the end as the inner power of things will conceive the unconditioned only as thinking and willing, and indeed both in unity. What the inner end, as the essence of things, expresses as the ought in the conditioned is, in its content, the will in the unconditioned.

With this the kernel in the concept of the personal God is reached. But philosophical knowledge, which wishes neither to overrate itself nor to overreach itself, must not forget its limits.

If the finite categories are raised into the infinite, for example the person into absolute personality, one follows a method similar to that which is used in mathematics when finite relations are carried over into the infinite, as for instance when in the ellipse the foci are moved further and further apart until their distance becomes infinite, and one thereby arrives at the parabola. So in the concept of the person one sets the finite intelligence, which is bound to a narrow circle of few objects and limited in its fathoming, as infinite in breadth and depth, in order to ascribe it to absolute personality. But this path nevertheless has its limit. Already in the will this infinite extension is impossible; for the will has its force in determinateness, which is limitation; and it is bound by the necessity of consequence, beyond which the will cannot go. In the finite the person appears to us only in opposition to other persons, through which it becomes conscious of itself, the I over against the Thou and He. It has its essence in self-limitation; it gathers itself together and shuts itself off from [p. 480] others. Absolute personality, thought as absolute, unlimited and all-embracing, does not bear this limitation. Thought as a person before all persons, it has a sublime solitude which, so it seems, became one of the impulses to think persons in God. In that the specific character falls away which the concept of the person has in the finite, the difficulty makes itself known of so transforming the finite concept of the person that it becomes adequate to the absolute.

When we saw above how the end drew the categories of the efficient cause up to itself, their content remained untouched and unimpaired. But in this elevation of the fundamental concepts to the unconditioned the previous content breaks off. When, therefore, philosophy, in correct self-knowledge, reflects on the means of knowing, it no longer dreams the gigantic dream of an adequate knowledge of God, in which spun-out metaphors are passed off as proven science. It is said of God in an old phrase: nesciendo scitur.

If, accordingly, knowledge renounces the attempt to construct the essence of the unconditioned from the concept, it is directed to sketch its representation in the direction in which what is given and conditioned offers guidance. This is the real sense of the so-called proofs of the existence of God which we have run through. The pointings of the finite to the infinite have doubled significance in a view of the world in which, unlike the Kantian, purely subjective forms, time and space and the categories, do not veil the thing in itself and frustrate every penetrating and certain look. Where it is denied to us, beings conditioned on every side, to know the essence and, as it were, the life of the unconditioned as it is in itself, they teach us its relations to us.

10. In these pointings to the unconditioned, the [p. 481] necessary that has been known forms the secure foundation; for it is impossible for us to think that the necessary, which cannot be otherwise, should nevertheless become otherwise through the unconditioned, and the unchangeable change. The necessary springs up for the human mind within what is limited; and it can therefore, seen from the unconditioned, enter into a greater connection so as itself to become greater; but in and for itself it remains what it is, necessary.

(1) See vol. II. p. 142 ff.

Since, now, the end in the conditioned, as was remarked above, points to knowledge and will in the unconditioned, it is an old question how the necessary, called veritates aeternae, is related to God's knowledge and will. By the eternal truths have been understood in particular the mathematical laws, in which necessity appears most purely: for example, that twice two is four, or that the radii in a circle are equal, or that the angles in a plane triangle are together equal to two right angles. Independent of God's will, for it appears absurd to make a consequence that is of a logical nature dependent on the decree of a will, as Cartesius did, they appear to some even as independent of God's knowledge; they are true, said some Scotists, even if there were no understanding, not even the understanding of God. Mathematical necessity is only the simplest example of such eternal truths; for the suggestion that they could be otherwise at once proclaims its own folly. With mathematics, which spreads through physics into the spiritual world, the realm of these eternal truths spreads; and Bayle already made the eternal truths in the ethical sphere clear by the contrast of the unchangeable Decalogue with the Jewish ceremonial law, once given but changeable. With the necessary advancing in all science, the boundaries of the eternal truths will advance. Where they carry the end [p. 482] in themselves, or are means in connection with the ultimate end of the whole, they appear, traced back to the absolute, as an outflow of the will; but considered prior to the end and in and for themselves, like the mathematical truths, as the consequence of something original, as for example of the constructive elements in mathematics. Whoever wills and posits what is original, for example the decimal number system or the design of parallels, posits and wills its consequences. The will that posits and wills the nature of the human being posits and wills at the same stroke the essence of justice, and thus, for example, the necessity of the Decalogue. Only when we wish to make God's knowing will free of its own consequences and detach it from them does that conflict arise in the thought of the unconditioned. Whoever, once and for all, wishes to descend with the lamp of human analogy into God's understanding and will as into the deepest depths must think what is original and what is foreseen in the original for all eternity. Few can bear this thought. But as before God a thousand years are as *one* day, so before him thousands upon thousands of syllogisms are as *one* concept, and the intricate world as *one* simple fact.

(1) See vol. II. p. 470 f. 479., cf. II. p. 68ff.

(2) Leibniz Theodicee. p. 560ff. after Erdmann's edition

11. In the history of philosophy *one* expression in particular maintains itself for determining the absolute in itself. It will be worth while to examine it in this connection. If the opposite ends of the world point back to the unconditioned, and if the whole presents itself intuitively in oppositions, then it is natural to bend what is opposed together and make it the expression of the absolute. And indeed dialectical thoughts and grand images have vied with one another in designating, deeply and comprehensively, the might and glory of the unconditioned in the unity of opposites.

We pass over the Neoplatonists, Cusanus and Giordano Bruno, and mention only those conceptions of this kind which have won great applause in the most recent philosophy.

[p. 483] No one has given a mightier impulse than Spinoza to the doctrine that the absolute is the identity of opposites, the indifference of the ideal and the real, of the subjective and the objective.

If until then either blind being (matter) had been placed as what is original before and above thought, and thought regarded only as the fortunate effect of blind force, as in Democritism, or thought had been placed before and above matter and matter regarded as determined by it, as in Platonism, then Spinoza grasped the fundamental problem of metaphysics, the real relation of thought to being, anew and in his own way; Spinozism, born of itself, joined those two as the representative of the third possibility, the only one that could still exist besides them.¹

Spinoza expresses God, the *one* substance, through two attributes, infinite thought and infinite extension, through which the understanding apprehends its identical essence in different ways. Since the two attributes, for the understanding the different expressions of the same substance, stand in no causal connection with each other, neither has precedence over the other, neither preponderates over the other, and neither explains what goes on in the other; what happens in extension happens also in thought; the two run parallel and are the same thing, only regarded under the other attribute. So the fundamental thought is conceived. It demands that there be no end, or that the end be at most a human invention; it properly demands also that there be no sensuous knowledge, for in that the body (extension) would otherwise encroach upon the mind (thought). It has been shown above that the denial of the end speaks against Spinoza. How Spinoza helps himself and yet falls away from himself, how it becomes impossible for him to carry through the [p. 484] fundamental thought, and how, in contradiction with it, he in the end nevertheless gives thought power over extension, has been shown in another place and must not be repeated here. Since Spinoza, keen and strict as he is, misses the goal, he leaves no hope that metaphysical truth lies along his path.

(1) Cf. on the ultimate difference of philosophical systems the author's "historische Beiträge zur Philosophie." vol. 2. p. 1 ff., especially p. 10 ff.

(2) See above, vol. II. p. 41 ff.

More recent philosophy, perhaps misled by Jacobi's indefinite exposition, dropped Spinoza's proviso that thought and extension, though distinguished in the understanding, are the expression of *one* and the same thing and therefore stand in no causal connection with each other. Without this caution it determined the absolute as the identity of the subjective and the objective, of the ideal and the real. Schelling, in his first epoch, brought these formulas into vogue. People then trusted the bold intuition and overlooked the weak grounding.

Let us compare, for example, an exposition such as the following.³ Being and knowing, says Schelling, are immediately, without a higher bond, and in themselves *one*. The being which we know as the absolute is, as surely as it is true being, so surely its own affirmation; were it not essentially self-affirmation, it would not be absolute, not wholly and entirely of and from itself. Conversely, this affirmation of being is nothing other than just being itself. Were it not this, it would be outside being and could not itself be. As surely, therefore, as it is really affirmation of being, i.e. [p. 485] is itself positive, so surely is it not distinct from being and is itself being. Affirmation of being is knowledge of being, and conversely. The eternal, therefore, since it is essentially a self-affirming, is in being also a self-knowing, and conversely. The unity between being and knowing in general is accordingly a direct unity, that is, one with which no opposition is mixed. Existence is self-affirmation and self-affirmation is existence. The one is entirely synonymous with the other; the relation of the two is a mere relation of indifference. It follows that no part of nature can be mere being or something merely affirmed, but rather each is in itself just as much self-affirmation as consciousness or the I is; it follows that every thing, grasped in its true essence, can be regarded with entirely equal validity as a mode of being and as a mode of self-knowing and self-revealing. Accordingly, neither is knowledge dependent on being nor being on knowledge; rather, knowledge is just being itself, and being is knowledge (in that higher meaning of self-affirmation).

(1) Cf. on Spinoza's fundamental thought and its outcome the author's "historische Beiträge zur Philosophie." Vol. II. p. 31 ff.

(2) Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi's Werke. 1819. IV. über die Lehre des Spinoza p. 183 ff.

(3) Schelling Darlegung des wahren Verhältnisses der Naturphilosophie zu der verbesserten Fichte'schen Lehre 1806. p. 49ff. p. 75; cf. on the identity of opposites in the absolute: Darstellung meines Systems der Philosophie in the "Zeitschrift für speculative Physik" 1801. II 2. p. 17. Vorlesungen über die Methode des akademischen Studium. 1802. after the 3rd ed. p. 56 ff.

If one looks in the above at the derivation, which alone makes philosophy philosophy, then the whole great identity of knowing and being hangs solely on the metaphor of self-affirmation. Being from itself is self-confirmation, therefore self-affirmation, therefore self-knowledge. Yet even someone who represents being from itself only as efficient cause, as blind being, can call this a self-confirmation and, in a transferred meaning, a self-affirmation. But who would permit him to turn this self-affirmation (causa sui) into a self-knowledge, that objective into this subjective? Real being from itself is unconcernedly slid over into logical self-affirmation, and self-affirmation into psychological and metaphysical self-knowledge.

Just as loosely held, in another passage, is the conversion [p. 486] of the bond between the finite and the infinite into the affirming, and of the affirming into the subjective.¹

In the word identity, or indifference, of the ideal and the real, unclarity and indeterminateness take refuge. As logical identity it cannot be thought, and as actual equilibrium it cannot be clearly grasped. Schelling, striving from the ready-made formula towards the living God, himself abandoned this standpoint and sought to show how God makes a part (a potency) of himself into ground, so that the creature may be possible, and subordinates this part of his essence (the non-intelligent part) to the higher. With this the identity is given up and the indifference converted into a superordination of the ideal over the real.

Schleiermacher arrives at the same formula of the absolute, at the identity of thought and being, of the ideal and the real. To be sure, by a path peculiar to him. He does not seize the absolute as this indifference of opposites in intellectual intuition, but only presupposes it to all knowledge as to all willing. The absolute, Schleiermacher teaches, can be neither known nor willed. A willing directed at the absolute would be pure nullity; for it would let man come to no determinate deed. A knowledge of God in and for himself would have to be nothing other than a concept which nevertheless still persists in opposition. Every particular knowledge exists as particular only in oppositions and through them; for it is only a particular one inasmuch as something in it is not posited or is negated, which, however, must be posited elsewhere. The highest knowledge, on the other hand, is not determined by oppositions, but is the absolutely simple expression [p. 487] of the highest being equal to it, and contains the oppositions bound within itself. Absolute knowledge is the expression of no opposition at all, but of absolute being identical with itself. Hence the absolute is subject-object, because neither as knowledge does it have being outside itself, nor as being knowledge. Absolute knowledge is, in actual consciousness, no determinate knowledge, that is, none that could be expressed in an adequate way in a plurality of concepts and propositions, but only the ground and source of all particular knowledge. The highest opposition, under which all others hover before us, is that of material and spiritual being. Being is material (real) as what is known, spiritual (ideal) as what knows. Each member of this opposition, taken separately by itself, is nothing in being and knowing, but remains only a dead sign. Hence the highest Idea is the Idea of the absolute unity of being, in so far as the opposition of thought and object is cancelled; and the ground of all and everything that is to be presupposed is the unconditioned interpenetration of knowledge and being, and that absolutely, so that they are not, say, still a twofold, as in human knowledge, merely held in correspondence, but pure and absolute identity of knowledge and being.

(1) Ueber das Verhältniss des Realen und Idealen in der Natur p. XXXIII as a supplement to the work von der Weltseele. After the third edition. 1809.

(2) Dialektik 1839. §. 133. p. 76. §. 166. p. 93. On §. 215 p. 152. §. 217. p. 159. p. 461. No. 29. Entwurf des Systems der Sittenlehre. 1835. §. 27 ff. p. 15 ff.

We cannot know the absolute, Schleiermacher teaches, since he raises the absolute above the oppositions within which knowledge moves. But even if the absolute is no object of knowledge, we must nevertheless be able to think the formula that has been found, identity of the ideal and the real, or to represent to ourselves the schema, as Schleiermacher calls it. The more insistence is laid on pure and absolute identity, the less do we consider this possible.

The formula to which Spinoza led the way is not, however, to be understood as with Spinoza, who regards thought and extension, distinguished in the intellect, as expressions of the same *one* substance. Rather, with Schleiermacher, knowledge and being, ideal and real, are taken as actual oppositions [p. 488] in the thing itself, and the unconditioned interpenetration of the two states something more real than a reunion of what, as attribute, was separated only in the intellect.

The absolute identity of knowledge and being negates both the dualism of the two elements and the subordination of the one and superordination of the other; but what it is and how it is to be thought, it does not state. No image reaches it. We may neither think it mechanically, like a mixture, nor chemically, like penetration and saturation; for otherwise the two elements, as separate, would be the more original. Is every point that is, also to think? and every combination of the possible also to be? It is proper to thought, so far as we know it, to sketch and compare what is possible; but the possible, wide and manifold, always shoots out beyond the actual. Thus in fact the formula cannot be thought, for indeterminateness.

The absolute identity of knowledge and being is neither a point from which one can set out in derivation, nor a goal towards which one can strive in action. One cannot set out from it; for absolute equilibrium persists in itself, and nothing therefore follows from it; and one cannot strive towards it; for a norm for action can lie only in the shaping of difference.

Has Schleiermacher, then, demonstrated the identity of the ideal and the real as a necessary expression of the presupposed absolute? For the answer to this question we go back to his exposition.

The highest knowledge, he says, is not determined by oppositions, but is the absolutely simple expression of the highest being equal to it. For if in ascending the oppositions diminish, one can only have ascended to the highest when they have entirely vanished. This ascent is only an abstraction. The pregnant unity of knowledge and being, which, binding the oppositions, is to express the absolute, cannot be an abstractum; otherwise it would [p. 489] after all be only the ens universalissimum, which Schleiermacher decidedly rejects.¹

The opposition of the ideal and the real is, as opposition, in the first instance only in our concept. It is correct that each member by itself is in the first instance only a dead sign. But does an absolute interpenetration of the two follow from this? The union can come about otherwise than through identity and indifference. The sign ceases to be dead when, for example, the subordination of the real to the ideal is intuited. The proof, then, falls short of the assertion.

The conditioned, in the high points of its appearance and in the question about its inner possibility, points to another presupposition in the unconditioned: to the determining power of the ideal in the real.

Schleiermacher cannot do without this same presupposition, and a teleological principle lies hidden in him. We shall try to draw it into the light at a few points.

Knowledge and being, says Schleiermacher, exist for us only in relation to each other, and each is the measure of the other. When we call a thing imperfect in its kind, this happens because it does not correspond to the concept, and likewise conversely.

This proposition carries a teleological relation within it. For the concept has a right to be the measure of perfection or of defect only if it carries the determining end within itself. Where being is blind force, the concept must conform to being, but not the reverse.

It is peculiar to Schleiermacher's ethics that it presents the action of reason upon nature, and indeed as organising and as symbolising action; the former makes nature into an instrument, the latter brings it to man's conscious knowledge. Both ethical processes are for him only the extension and heightening of an original union of [p. 490] reason and nature, partly of one that is given to us in our organs, partly of one that is given to us in our consciousness. Thus the rationality of the organs and of consciousness is presupposed, because otherwise, says Schleiermacher, the delimitation of science as well as the certainty of immediate consciousness would cease. This proof demands a concession to human limitation, but it is no ground drawn from the matter itself. That ground lies elsewhere than in a consideration of what would otherwise befall us in science and in immediate consciousness. If we ask what the ground in the matter itself is for the rationality of the organs and of consciousness, it leads immediately into the inner end; and if we ask further whence we are immediately conscious of this rationality, then the human trust in the conditions of spiritual life in which we find ourselves, this faith in an original destination, leads into the same intuition.

(1) Dialektik §. 188. p. 121.

(2) Entwurf des Systems der Sittenlehre. §. 23. §. 26.

The ethical process, according to Schleiermacher's exposition, realises the progressive union of reason with nature, in such a way that nature is permeated with rational content. In the organising and in the symbolising process it becomes more and more the instrument of reason, whether of action or of knowledge.

This goal is properly the opposite of the principle, the opposite of the pure identity of knowing and being; for permeation with rational content is the superordination of the ideal over the real and the subordination of the real as a means. From an indifference of knowing and being no ethical direction, no measure of the ethical process can proceed, and this for the simple reason that it is pure identity.

This incongruity could, were this the place, be traced further into Schleiermacher's Christian ethics, whose presupposed [p. 491] concept of God scarcely agrees with the pure identity of knowing and being. The feeling filled with this indifference of the ideal and the real, which in the sense of his philosophical ethics would become religion, cannot have the significance of the feeling that resounds in the words: "In the beginning was the Logos."

(1) Entwurf des Systems der Sittenlehre. §. 124 ff. p. 88 ff.

Thus neither in Spinoza nor in Schelling and Schleiermacher has the endeavour to express the absolute through the unity of opposites reached its goal. The formula sounds deep; the intuition is bold. But its inner indeterminacy and its results bear witness against it.

12. We turn back into our former path. The last investigation set out to examine what the expression of the absolute as a unity of opposites accomplishes in modern philosophy, and since it proved insufficient, the general view was confirmed that the means for a direct and adequate knowledge are lacking.

This reserve does not answer to the longing that drives us towards the concept of God, towards the concept which has all worth in itself and gives all things their worth. Practically a power in the soul, it becomes theoretically a limiting concept, which we only approach. We want more; we want to go further. As we think ourselves into the finite and, comprehending it, create it anew, so the same impulse drives us to transport ourselves, with the life of our formative thought, into the infinite essence of God.

But criticism can be neither undone nor disdained; it remains at the side of philosophy on its path as a warning. Whoever, then, is not conscious of that contradiction between the finite means and the infinite object, whoever imagines that he reproduces God within himself as a process of nature, deceives himself, like the profound theosophist. For here no insight into a becoming is opened; all knowledge is only indirect. "God alone can comprehend God." Theosophy imitates him in this. It seeks to open unfathomable depths, [p. 492] to behold God's essence in becoming and to transform his being into a history. The share of extravagant fancy, without which this does not come off, lifts theosophy on high, but also beyond sober metaphysics.

No one holds it against the eye when it is quietly conscious that not the changeless pure light, but only the subdued and reflected light, or light broken in the play of colours, that not the sun of heaven but the brightness of the earth has been assigned to it as its domain of activity. But in human thought it is censured as unbelief or sloth when, like the eye, it knows that the circle of the finite and conditioned, which is after all wide enough, is its free and joyful field of play. When the eye is delighted by the harmony of colours, it does not deny the sun; rather, it knows, as it were, that the colours are born of light. When thought happily exercises itself upon things, it does not deny God, but sees him in the reason of the world and knows that this reason comes from God. But by the sight of the sun itself the eye is dazzled and then sees only its own phantasms; and by the intuition of God finite thought is swallowed up and yet produces only a mirror-image of the finite.

The unconditioned becomes the transfigured analogy of the conditioned, and yet, considered logically, all analogy from the conditioned to the unconditioned is lacking; for the specific difference between the two has, as it were, become infinite.

All proofs of God resemble the attempt to find pure light from the colour in which the light is dimmed, as though one could simply subtract the dimming. They are nothing but a faint glimmer and a cold semblance. Compared with the living idea, they remain at a great distance. But whence the idea of God before the proof and apart from the proof? Sceptical criticism has a wide field here, but it does not explain what it would like to explain away. The profound intuition of faith and the powerfully unifying spirit answer de[p. 493]cisively. Taken logically, the conditioned would fall apart for us if there were no unconditioned, and the unconditioned, by its concept, towers above the little fragments of the conditioned which human thinking interprets as a reduced image of the unconditioned. So the sun, which illumines planets and moons, towers above the colours that shine for us, above the day that gives us light.

Accordingly it is not given to us to develop the essence of God with that logical necessity with which the mind is able to penetrate finite things. All construction is only an image of God drawn from the world. How, it is asked, must the unconditioned being be constituted that reveals itself thus and not otherwise in the world? All grounding is here indirect. Whoever goes beyond this composes a theosophical poem, whether with Jacob Böhme he grasps the groundless [Ungrund] in ground and takes adversity as the revelation of the hidden life, or with the later Schelling, pointing his phrases dialectically, he sketches a process in which immemorial blind being is raised into that which can be, the unity of both forms the necessary spirit, that which possesses itself, and in the tension of the divine potencies the world becomes the suspended act of necessary divine being; or whether with Hegel he posits God as the syllogism of reason in which all three terms permeate one another; for the type of "being in itself," of "coming out of itself" and of "returning to itself," which always underlies the scheme of Father, Son and Spirit, is only a human likeness, by means of which the [p. 494] concept does indeed imagine that it immerses itself in the rich life of God, but in which it has only a barren formula.

(1) Cf. e.g. Die Idee der Gottheit etc. by Dr. Karl Philipp Fischer etc. Stuttgart 1839. The little book is distinguished by its disposition and its direction. There too, on closer examination, every proof is indirect, and even the dialectical ones come down to this, since the mere refutation of subordinate standpoints is without further ado regarded as the proof of a supposedly higher one. In this connection we partly miss the strict disjunction of the possibilities.

Let us be permitted a parallel, in which, taking life and art together as one, we compare the world with an artistic whole.

When we read a poem, we gather, as it were, little by little from the parts the thought of the whole and combine it into an image, which then in turn illumines the sense of the parts. Only from the parts do we understand the whole, and again only from the whole the parts.

We read the world no otherwise than such a poem. When we strive from individual appearances to the ground, from the parts to the whole, we go the way of experience. And when the parts receive new light from the provisionally grasped whole, the idea leads us.

Experience and idea accordingly demand each other; and the greatness of knowledge lies in their permeating each other.

When the idea of the poem stands before us, clear and significant in itself, and shaping and animating every word, then an image of the creative spirit of the poet stands before us. He does not, indeed, appear to us wholly as he is in himself, but only so far as his soul and his genius poured itself into this one work and sought its likeness in it.

As in this way the spirit of the poet speaks from the poem, so God speaks from the world. The poem is a single play, and hence the spirit of the poet appears in it only in the form of an isolated metamorphosis. The world that we read is also only a fragment, but, like the single drama of an ancient tetralogy, whole in itself. Enough is given us in it to recognise the glory of the creative spirit. The world is the counter-image of his essence. The further we embrace this counter-image, the deeper we look into it, the more is it his revelation. Nature and history are only two different leaves of *one* whole, and history becomes [p. 495] itself, if the whole is to come together in *one* idea, a living member, indeed the most significant member, of a great view of nature, or more correctly of our whole intuition of the world.

It may happen that we read a poem only carelessly, and then we lack the necessary points for sketching the thought of the whole. Or we may read a poem carefully indeed, but nevertheless without spirit, and then the clearly recognised parts do not come together into any whole; they remain parts and at most struggle with one another, instead of mutually animating one another into members of *one* thought. Neither to him who reads carelessly nor to him who reads without spirit does the idea appear. The sciences that fail to recognise the unconditioned behave like careless or spiritless readers.

We read even the first verse of the poem on the presupposition that it serves, along with the rest, to reveal to us a greater thought. On the same presupposition we give ourselves up reflectively to all that follows. So too, in the first step of knowing that the mind takes in the world, the idea of the divine thought realised in the world is its tacit, if often uncomprehended, presupposition. In it all thinking and willing is transfigured. Without it thinking has at most the charm of an idle riddle, and willing at most the worth of a sounding string which, instead of joining in a great harmony, vibrates senselessly and purposelessly.

The knowledge of the finite mind, however far it may advance, is nonetheless piecework for each individual; and whether someone has come to know a particle of the world or a part, the thought of God is always the completion of this piecework.

We are still always reading that beginning, but on the presupposition that the divine thought from which it springs is mirrored in it.

Accordingly the peculiar intuition of the unconditioned rests upon the view of the world which strives to master the various cognitions by a unity.

[p. 496] 13. Every system has its own view of the world and is a system of its own only in this view. In agreement with the preceding investigations, however, essentially two intuitions stand opposed to each other, which are only determined and carried out differently in the individual systems. The one recognises only the efficient cause as the power of the world; the other founds the dominion of the end. The former may be called the physical (or mechanical) view of the world, since it rests solely upon physical causes; the latter the organic, since in it things become organs of a purposive thought. The former was developed consistently and in its own peculiar way in antiquity by the atomists, and in modern times boldly and unsparingly by the *système de la nature*; the latter is the essence of Platonism and of all the tendencies akin to it. If in Spinoza's substance thinking and extension really permeated each other, and did not merely stand side by side like two expressions of one and the same thing, then an organic view would be possible there too. But for Spinoza this is only an alien consequence. Since he abolishes the end, he abolishes thought in the ground of things. Thereby, although differently disposed, he falls to the physical view of the world and to that extent forms an opposition to Plato.

These contending views of the world do not first appear in the philosophy that completes them. They wrestle with one another in the individual sciences and are a question of fact. Mathematics and the physics of natural forces widen their circles and thereby push forward the boundaries of the physical view of the world. Ethics holds fast to the end, but the advancing study of nature wrests concessions from it, and already a tendency shows itself to abolish the distinction between natural and moral law. Physiology stands in the middle between the dominion of the efficient cause and that of the concept of end. The end confronts it irresistibly in organic life, [p. 497] but in particulars it wavers between the two views and believes it gains as much in necessity and reason as it pushes back teleology through deeper investigation of the co-operating forces of nature. But in the great fundamental features the governing end nevertheless remains, and ethics may appropriate it for itself from nature itself.

(1) Cf. above vol. II. p. 41 ff.

(2) Cf. above vol. II. p. 483.

The physical view sees the world from the standpoint of driving causes and effects, like a sea moved by the wind. Nothing has a ground in itself, as it may well seem to have in the domain of life. The individual is only a fragment torn loose from the whole, in that what seems to be its own is only a continuation of what is alien. Whatever great thing arises is not properly produced, but only knocked into shape in fortunate co-operation. The force of past states determines the present. The motion of causes goes forward like a river, forward and ever forward. Matter and motion are the factors of all appearances. They are the first and the last. The end is only semblance, and life nothing but the overweening force that tore itself loose from substance in order to fall back to it again. Thinking is a product of physical cause; it is not the ground of creation, but its consummated effect. Hence God first comes to consciousness in man. Things have no truth; for no thought underlies them. Truth is only in human thinking, and there is no other truth than the sum of [p. 498] erring understandings. Necessity rules all things, but it is only the inevitable compulsion of the efficient cause, recognised indeed by thought, but as something alien that does not spring from it. For the mind that asks after mind, this necessity is after all only chance. The view, carried through consistently, yields in the ethical sphere nothing higher than brute force or subtle cunning; for might alone has right; the efficient cause is might; therefore wrest the victory (the effect) from it, by either making it powerless through your force or felling it through its own weakness. Naked pragmatism in history is only an expression of this view of the world in the ethical sphere. Success alone decides; for the unconditioned is might.

(1) In this sense a great French physiologist expresses himself openly, and German ones have followed him. Dividing the phenomena of life into physical and vital, he says: "Every time that one of the vital phenomena can be transferred into the class of physical ones, a new conquest has been made in science, whose domain thus finds itself enlarged. Words are then replaced by facts, hypotheses by analyses. The laws of organic bodies then coincide with those of inorganic ones and, like these, become capable of explanation and simplification." Thus it is called a simplification when explanation explains thought away.

This view of the world rests in the first place upon the power of the mathematical, which pours itself with motion through the whole world. But if only motion belongs in equal measure to the formative mind, it does not follow that the physical force of the mathematical element holds sway originally free and unbound from thought and its ends. To a mathematician the saying is ascribed that he had searched the heavens and nowhere found the finger of God. In the mechanics of the heavens one does indeed find only the efficient cause, which holds the masses together and relates them to one another. But the masses become, at least according to experience on our earth, means for the existence of life and of mind. To that extent they are demanded by thought, and gravitation becomes the first condition of the world-whole. The outermost and last force, which passes through everything and in and for itself does not make thought known, reveals it by serving it. The physical view of the world grows, further, because the ends fancifully thought into the world suffer defeats at the hands of sober science. The childlike representation animates the forms of the world, which are necessary in strict connection, with contingent ends homogeneous with its own mind. When [p. 499] this illusion retreats before more manly thought, it easily takes more with it than it should; and with faith in the invented symbols of particular ends there also falls, as like as not, faith in the divine end altogether. Finally, the advance of the physical view of the world proceeds from the isolation of the sciences. The end springs from the whole and is the thought of the whole in the midst of the parts that produce the whole. If now the parts are set up on their own, as though they were independent and existed of themselves, they must thereby forfeit the thought of the whole that encompasses them and realises itself in the parts. Consider the hand by itself, and you see only the extensors and flexors that move the little levers of the bones in manifold play. But consider together with it the eye, which directs and guides the hand, and mind and end enter into this instrument of instruments; yet eye and hand agree only under the great presupposition of the living body that embraces both. As in this example, so it goes with the sciences in general. The one considers the matter of the earth, the other the light of the heavens. In both the efficient causes are sought. They are the ultimate opposition in the knowledge of nature. But in the whole they exist for each other, and, separated by an infinite distance, a common end binds the two. Matter is dead without the animating light, and light is blind without the matter against which it strikes. If, therefore, philosophy at every time fulfils its calling to sketch from the isolated sciences, as parts, an image of the whole, so that in it the sciences have communion with the whole of knowledge, then it will always mediate the organic view of the world. And from the side of the spiritual, which in the physical view becomes a play of chance, like a big prize in the lottery, and comes to ruin before the superior power of the efficient cause, another light then pours also over the view of the efficient forces and of matter in motion.

[p. 500] The organic view sees the world from the standpoint of the end and of the forces permeated by the end, like a living body. One must not let oneself be misled by the name of the organic view of the world, as though the organic consideration were merely a more "physical" one, as has been objected, for example, against the organic view of language. Only thought is able to form an organon (instrument) for itself, and only thought is able to direct it. Hence the organic view is precisely the spiritual one, the view of mind realising itself. The individual now receives in the end which it realises a centre of its own and has from there a life of its own. All the categories which, determined by the mere efficient cause, remained alien and blind in themselves, are illuminated by thought, as was shown above. Thought is not born afterwards, as in the physical view, but is the creator himself, almighty from the beginning. The truth of every thing is a ray of this thought; as a concept underlies things, so they are to satisfy this concept. Truth thus traces itself in the forms of creation, and we contemplate it in them devoutly and piously. As in the wonderful structure of the limbs and organs a thought reveals itself "before which all the problems of physics are solved from the very beginning," the problems of light and sound, of chemism and of motion, so this thought becomes the absolute prius of the natural and the moral world. If one succeeds in carrying the end through the world, the merely mechanical cause appears only as a side-effect. One can then indeed consider the efficient cause by itself; but only by lifting it out of its connection with the end and persisting in the consideration of the part. The necessity of the world is now no longer blind, like chance, but conscious, like reason; [p. 501] and human reason is now no longer in the world like a stranger, but like the first-born son in his father's house; it is now no longer like a feeble consonance that infallibly perishes in the roar of sea and wind, but like a unison within a greater harmony. All knowing is now the trustful deed that creates after thought, all perceiving a listening for its revelation, all thinking a thinking-after. The organic view is heightened in the ethical domain when it is able to take freedom up into itself. Things and men now confront the agent as organs out of which an end speaks, and in this they bear their significance and their worth. Hence the task appears of knowing this thought of things, this end of the individual in the whole, and of treating men and things according to this divine element that is in them. Love, in contemplation and in action, gives itself freely to this thought, which goes beyond the self-contained life of the part. Hence we might take Plato's words more deeply and call love the bond by which the universe binds itself together with itself. Thought is before all things, and all things consist in it; all things are created through it and for it. Therefore the love that is grounded in this view is the "bond of perfection." The beautiful is now no longer a contingent charm of force, but an expression of inner harmony. The organ of the body, the eye for example, is the more a microcosm of the whole the higher it stands. So the moral man appears as a microcosm of the free thought realised in the world.

(1) See above, Section X., the categories from the end.

(1) Paul to the Colossians 3, 14. cf. 1, 16. 17.

(2) 1 Cor. 12. Ephesians 4. 15. 16. cf. John 15.

No one has characterised the organic view within the Christian sphere more beautifully than the apostle Paul. The organic view of the world would be only a generalisation [p. 502] of what appears in the Christian sphere as at its highest summit. Paul characterises the moral forces released from the end, when they govern the world as in the physical view, with the striking words:¹ "But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another."

In this way the organic view of the world takes shape when it is carried through. Without it a dualism is unavoidable. For the end is a fact of the world, and the only question is whether wholly or in part. If it is so only in part, then it is in the world like an inconsistency. From this indirect grounding arises the endeavour to extend the analogy of the end from the most significant members over the whole. Once it has permeated the whole, that external teleology ceases which subjects nature to alien ends. For nothing is outside the all-embracing whole. The ideal sketch is easy, but the real demonstration lags far behind it. The fact is to be investigated from itself and not reinterpreted. The tendencies of the sciences waver to and fro. Deeper investigation brings now a deeper end, but now, instead of any end, an efficient cause. The mediations between the members of the world will not appear so visibly that they point, as it were spatially, to the centre. The sciences quarrel over their queen, and they cannot be released from striving to fathom particulars solely from the matter itself. But this cannot lead the mind astray. According to the most significant appearances and according to its own nature it decides and supplies what is lacking.

14. In the organic view of the world the thought which Plato once placed at the head in the *Timaeus* will remain the theme of metaphysics: "God was good, and because he was good he was without envy and willed that the world should become as like him as [p. 503] possible." As the knowledge of the world grows in fullness and depth, it at last completes itself through this thought of unity. As the human mind always represents the absolute to itself only relatively, so too, where the content of the relative is recognised as richer and greater, the representation of the absolute will receive new and greater impulses. Religious representation often believes it is losing where it receives back more than it loses. When the mathematical understanding did away with the heaven of fixed stars enclosing the world, that last celestial sphere modelled on what the eye beholds, opened up infinite space and recognised the countless lights of heaven as distant worlds, the mightily stirred imagination of mankind expanded, and it was in danger of losing the transcendent unity over the unmeasured many. But at bottom the chords that introduce the thought of the unconditioned have also grown all the mightier, as when, for example, Klopstock, enlarging the old restricted representation of heaven, begins his psalm: "Around earths wander moons, earths around suns; the hosts of all the suns wander around one great sun: Our Father, which art." When in recent times life is discovered in the smallest space, when the history of the body of the earth opens a view into unmeasured ages and brings to light from the remotest periods traces of life, and of life ever arising anew in struggle with the elemental powers, then our representations grow at that expression with which already the Book of Wisdom addresses God, when it says: "thou lover of life, thine incorruptible spirit is in all."

(1) To the Galatians 5, 15.

15. The passage cited from Plato's *Timaeus* leads to the optimism that found its expression in Leibniz's *Theodicee*, to the doctrine that the world is the best of the worlds that were possible. Today optimism is widely held to be a pious wish, and it is deemed a task of progressive metaphysics to teach pessimism; indeed Schopenhauer took the word in the strict sense [p. 504] and even undertook the philosophical proof of the superlative that lies in the word pessimism. Our world, he holds, is the worst of all worlds possible at all; for it is so arranged as it had to be in order to be able to subsist by the narrowest margin; were it but a little worse, it could no longer subsist at all; it itself is therefore the worst among the possible ones.¹ Much is lacking for an actual grounding of this presumptuous thought. Does philosophy know what the conditions are under which a world can subsist and under which it cannot? As in a ledger of existence, the sensations of pleasure which the world offers are set down on the one side of the page, and on the other side the sensations of displeasure to which we are subject, and in the reckoning of plus and minus the pessimum, namely an enormous surplus of the sensations of displeasure over pleasure, is found as the sum. Thus, in contrast with the earlier optimism, pessimism is to become the doctrine of metaphysics.

Meanwhile the question arises whether pessimism can at all become the consistent doctrine of any metaphysics, i.e. of the science of principles. In principle, namely, as has been shown, two fundamental metaphysical views stand opposed to each other in the systems: the one the system that asserts the sole dominion of the efficient cause, the other the system of the inner end, which sees reason in things and presupposes thought and will for the world. The systems of the latter genus, which we designate as Platonism in the wider sense, necessarily arrive, with the providence they teach or with the reason inborn in the world, at the faith of optimism; the opposite genus [p. 505] of systems, which seeks the naked necessity of blind forces, takes as the ultimate the strict concatenation of physical causes, to which the ancients gave the name of fate. It would be foolish to wish the necessary, which as such cannot be otherwise, to be otherwise, and these systems therefore seek either to win from the necessary what is useful to man, by laying their own striving into the necessary as well, or, where this is not possible, to rid themselves of foolish wishes, which are only illusions of something impossible, and to resign themselves calmly to the necessary. From such a tendency fatalism, or something similar, may follow, but no pessimism. Such a metaphysics must rather regard pessimism as an inconsistency of empty longing. In the systems of the end it can appear only where the ends are taken blindly and singly, like individual forces, without an ultimate all-embracing thought of unity to which they are subordinated. Such a view will have in the ends of the unconscious little more than another form of blindly efficient causes. That faith in the good God, and therefore in a world that is as perfect as possible, belongs to Platonism and to the kindred Christianity; it produces resignation to the will of the good God.

(1) Schopenhauer die Welt als Vorstellung und Wille. vol. 2. p. 667. 3rd ed. 1859.

(2) See above II. p. 496. cf. on the ultimate distinction among philosophical systems the author's historische Beiträge zur Philosophie. vol. 2. p. 1 ff.

A critique of pessimism will go back partly into psychology, partly into ethics. Psychology has to know the nature of pleasure, which pessimism makes its measure of worth, in its distinctions, and in particular to bring out the eminent significance of the peculiar sensations of pleasure that stand in connection with the inner destination of man. Ethics will have to examine the measure of worth itself. In so far as the portrayal of joyless, frail existence which is supposed to ground pessimism can at the same time serve to spur men on to united help, an ethical motive cannot be mistaken, and the picture can act ethically in the sense of compassion, which Schopenhauer holds to be the proper [p. 506] principle of the good. For everything that excites and enlivens fellow-feeling will further the good, if at the same time it takes the affect, blind in itself, into the service of reason. If, however, pessimism seeks to become a general way of thinking, it comes into contradiction with itself in so far as it, for its part, increases the sensations of displeasure which for it are the evil of the world, and has as its necessary consequence a discontent that embitters every stirring of life. The healthy force of life sickens in a pessimistic mood.

This contradiction becomes still more palpable when, as in v. Hartmann's *Philosophie des Unbewussten*, pessimism is taught theoretically (for, good as the world is, it is nonetheless thoroughly wretched and worse than none at all), but practically the affirmation of the will to live is upheld, and the human task is placed in full devotion to life and its pains and not in cowardly personal renunciation and withdrawal.¹ The deeper the roots this practical maxim strikes, the more vigorously will it defend itself against the theoretical doctrine of pessimism and seek to overcome it. That pessimism cannot find a soil in every ethics is evident. Whoever, for example, with Kant in the *Metaphysik der Sitten*, ascribes to the human being, as the being destined for reason, a worth absolutely, the worth of the person, that dignity of humanity by virtue of which man is an end in himself and can never be merely a means, disturbs the plus-and-minus reckoning of pleasure and displeasure on whose outcome pessimism raises its gloomy banner. For this worth in itself, this worth above all worths, does not fit into this addition of finite, changeable worths.

Accordingly we may exclude the so-called new problem of pessimism from our metaphysical consideration.

16. In the domain of the conditioned the old [p. 507] saying that like is known by like has in a certain sense been confirmed for us. Through the activities of the mind those sides of things were disclosed which are grounded in corresponding activities. In the knowledge of the unconditioned something similar shows itself to us. We know God, so far as we know him, only through that in us which is of divine lineage, through the necessary in knowledge and through the good in the will, and above all through the union of the two.

(1) Cf. v. Hartmann Philosophie des Unbewussten p. 633. 638.

17. With the organic view of the world, which lets the world and what is therein take root in the thought of the whole as what is original, the concept is transfigured in the idea. The naked view of the efficient cause knows no idea, but as the ultimate only the concept, in so far as it is the representation that has taken up into itself the producing, efficient ground of the thing. There is a concept of the circle, of falling, of magnetism, but no idea of them, unless they are related organically to the prefiguring thought of a whole. Language, however, speaks of the idea of an organ when it is traced back in its function to the whole of the living body and when its appropriate formation is comprehended from this.

In the history of philosophy the idea arises with a teleological and ethical consideration; and it is incorrect to derive it, in Plato, its originator, from a merely aesthetic intuition or merely from a dialectical reconciliation of opposites. For the idea of the good stands for him at the summit as the all-determining one.

The idea is the concept of the thing, known in the organic determination of a conditioning whole. Thus we speak of the idea of right when we grasp it not as an efficient appearance, and accordingly, for example, with Kant as the sum of the conditions under which the freedom of one can coexist with the freedom of another, but in a higher connection, say as the organ through which the ethical realised in common life main[p. 508]tains and further develops itself.
